en: Skandapurāṇa: Revākhaṇḍa (RKS), Chapter 1:
[The river] whose swarm of bees is intoxicated by the fragrance of the wine-like ichor flowing from the temples of the herds of bathing elephants;
Tawny from contact with the saffron flowing from the pair of breasts of the perfected women (siddhāṅganā) during their baths.
May the waters of the Narmadā protect you— waters whose banks at dawn and dusk are covered with heaps of kusha grass and flowers,
and whose ripples are touched by the trunks of young elephants.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: On a delightful peak of the Himavat, frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas,
crowded with Yakṣas and Vidyādharas, and inhabited by various hosts of beings.
All the gods, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the Suras; Skanda, Nandin, and the lords of the Gaṇas; the Moon and the Sun together with the planets; and the circle of the constellations and the Pole Star.
Vāyu and Varuṇa, Kubera and likewise Yama,
all the deities beginning with Indra, and the hosts of Gandharvas as well.
The Mothers beginning with Brāhmī, the sages whose wealth is asceticism, the personified sacred fords (tīrthas), and Caṇḍa, Bhṛṅgi, and Mahābala;
The Dānavas, Asuras, Daityas, Piśācas, Bhūtas, and Rākṣasas [beheld] that [palace],
which was as radiant as ten million suns and adorned with jewels and rubies.
It possessed thousands of ponds and wells with staircases made of jewels and lapis lazuli,
filled with lotuses and blue water-lilies, and endowed with various kinds of trees.
It was filled with flowering and fruit-bearing trees that grant the fruits of all desires,
crowded with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, and resounded with the cries of *cakravāka* birds.
All of them reached that place of Hara, which resounds with the cries of cuckoos and koels, is crowded with various birds, and is frequented by the Siddhas.
There, some were praising Mahādeva Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, as he sat; others were dancing before the Lord of Gods.
Rising up in their midst, Skanda addressed these words to Hara, who was seated upon a divine throne together with Umā.
Having joined his palms in reverence and prostrated with all eight limbs,
[he worshipped] the creator and destroyer of the universe, who is honored by gods and asuras alike.
To the one who grants boons to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra; who is affectionate toward his devotees;
who possesses three eyes and a white throat; and whose true nature is both known and unknown.
To the Lord, the imperishable, who is draped in an elephant hide, and who wears a garland of skulls and a tiger skin as an ornament; RKS 1.15.
Salutations be to you, whose body is smeared with ashes, the wielder of the Pināka bow,
who possesses infinite and boundless forms, Time itself, and the Supreme Lord.
Salutation to you who are Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, and likewise Ghoratattva;
salutation to you, the Tatpuruṣa; salutation be to you, the supreme Īśāna, the eternal Śiva.
Salutations be to you, who are Atharvan in the form of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas;
salutations to you, who are in the form of the fire of time and who dwell in all the worlds.
Homage to you whose body is half-woman, and homage to you, the most ancient;
Oṃ, homage to Śiva, who possesses form, who is formidable, and whose nature is existence.
To Śiva, who takes the form of worldly existence, who possesses a formidable appearance and matted locks—
to you, the entire universe, the three worlds with all that is moving and unmoving, is pervaded.
O Lord, you have been troubled by me through the fickleness of my tongue;
O Īśāna, forgive me for this, whether it was done out of ignorance or even knowingly.
Īśvara said:
"Choose a boon—may it be well with you—for by this hymn, O observer of noble vows, I shall grant you the boon desired in your heart; of this there is no doubt."
Skanda said: "O God, if you are pleased with me and desire to grant me a boon,
let there be auspicious palaces made of gold in the northern quarter."
The seven levels, however, have expansive golden walls and archways;
they are adorned with various jewels, pearls, and the like, and embellished with diamonds and lapis lazuli.
Right there, sweet voices arose along with thousands of flutes and lutes,
accompanied by spectacles of dance and song that were divinely beautiful and captivating.
"O Śiva, whose houses are these to the north of Meru?
By your grace I ask this, for my curiosity is indeed great. (RKS 1.26)
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Skanda, best of gods; understand what is being told by me regarding those in the city of Bhṛgusthāna when there is a conjunction of Rāhu and the Sun.
At Kurukṣetra and Prabhāsa, at Mokṣa and likewise at Rudrapada;
at the site of Kedārakṣetra, and likewise at Rudra and Kanakhala.
O son, having meditated upon Śiva in the field of Lalitā at Bhairava,
those who have died in the river of Śiva remain devoted to the meditation on Śiva.
Their homes are delightful, acquired through the fruits of their own karma;
they possess divine seven-storied mansions and abundant clothing and enjoyments.
"And I have bestowed upon them the pleasures of palatial enjoyments;
Skanda said:
[palaces] with hundreds and thousands of stories, adorned with lapis lazuli and jewels."
With many doors secured by bolts and panels,
they were filled with eternal festivals of desirable, divine, and captivating dances and songs.
"O Maheśvara, whose are these innumerable, delightful mansions on the eastern side here, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns?"
In the south and in the west, there are thousands of various enjoyments;
the pleasures in the abode of the Lord of Gods do not equal even a sixteenth part of them.
By what ripening of karma— whether auspicious or inauspicious—
are the inhabitants of Kūṣmāṇḍa plunged into this terrible, dark realm?
In pits of pus and blood dwell worms, insects, and moths;
those born of animal wombs and humans are tormented by their sins.
O Lord, by what ripening of karma do those who are miserable with poverty, wretched, tormented, and hungry come to exist in auspicious or inauspicious states of rebirth? RKS 1.37.
"Please explain all of this correctly and with favor.
Īśvara said:
"Those who have died on the bank of the Narmadā at the confluence where the waters are fiercely swift..."
O Six-faced One, their delightful dwellings are located in the eastern part,
to the south of Oṃkāra and to the east of Amarakaṇṭaka.
And those best of men who die at the Narmadā-koṭi tīrtha as human beings dwell in delightful and charming celestial palaces.
Whether on Mount Bhṛgu, in fire, or in water, or at the confluence of the Revā and Kapilā,
whatever gift was given or austerity performed— those dwell here in these very houses.
At the confluence of the Godāvarī, the Payasvinī, and the Tapatī;
at Tryambaka, Dhautapāpa, on the Himavat mountain, and on the Vindhya range.
On Mount Sahya, which consists of Maheśvara, and at the mighty Gokarṇa;
in Hariścandrapura, Candra, Śrīśaila, and Tripurāntaka; RKS 1.43.
O son, those who die on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight at the Mahānada river, or at Yonikuṇḍa in Kārtika, [attain liberation] along with the ocean.
In a golden palace to the south, the most excellent among them, the self-born ones,
enjoy various pleasures just as Śakra does in Triviṣṭapa.
One should give up one's life at the Sarasvatī, at Prabhāsa, at Śaśibhūṣaṇa,
at Pāriyātra, at Mahākāla, at Prayāga, and on the Great Path (Mahāpatha).
Their houses are delightful, with abundant and diverse enjoyments, radiant with the luster of jewels and rubies; in the north, there are thirteen crores of them.
In this manner, twenty-one such grounds were established;
on the right, nine crores of golden palaces were filled with provisions.
In the western quarter, there are sixteen crores of houses resembling pearls,
due to his specific pilgrimage to sacred fords and his excellence in the practice of giving.
"O son, when I am pleased, they enjoy various pleasures on the northern part of Meru, as well as on the southern and western parts."
And they sport in a captivating palace created by the gods;
there, Vārddhaki, the architect of all works, is the creator for the gods.
O Mahāsena, you behold a palace made of all kinds of jewels atop the world; in its eastern part, one enjoys the fruit of the Narmadā.
O Skanda, O sinless one, all that you have asked has been told to you by me for the benefit of the gods.
Thus ends the first chapter in the Revākhaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS, Chapter 2.
Skanda said:
All these—the foremost among the gods, Brahmā and Viṣṇu—desire to hear [this].
Such is the power of this sacred site, whose great fruit is [immeasurable].
Likewise, [he recounted] the origin of the Narmadā, her confluence, the worship of the Liṅga,
and the festival of the gods on Mount Amarakaṇṭaka during the auspicious occasion.
O Lord, tell me truly, together with the associated narratives,
the full fruit of pilgrimage, as well as the lineages and the Manvantaras.
"Out of grace, please tell me whatever you have, endowed with devotion.
Sūta said:
"Having heard this meritorious narrative, the Purāṇa proclaimed by Skanda..."
Then Mārkaṇḍeya, who knew the truth of the past and the future and who endures for seven kalpas,
arrived there accompanied by other ṛṣis.
With his every desire fulfilled, he was honored as truly superior even by the sages of fierce splendor, who numbered more than one hundred and twenty-five thousand.
Surrounded by these— brahman-sages, divine sages, and other royal sages— the illustrious one proceeded toward the forest hermitage in their midst.
Having obtained the fruit of his pilgrimage to sacred fords and taken refuge on the bank of the Narmadā,
Lomaharṣaṇa heard of the great power of Mārkaṇḍeya.
Then he came to see the sage who destroys all impurity,
at the holy confluence of the Narmadā, frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas.
It was crowded with yakṣas and vidyādharas, adorned by kinnaras,
filled with various hosts of gods, and frequented by diverse assemblies.
Having heard of the descent of the Revā and its power associated with merit,
the gods, Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and men danced there.
With white water-lilies, lotuses, *punnāga* trees, and *nāgacampaka* flowers;
likewise with mangoes, rose-apples, wood-apples, pomegranates, and jackfruit.
Adorned with nimba, jambīra, and nāraṅga trees, with groves of plantains,
with water-lilies, betel vines, and the like, as well as with rice fields and tamāla trees.
With citron and dates, grapes and sweet *pāṭala* flowers, with *bilva*, sandalwood, *pīlu* and the like, as well as *kadamba* and *kuṭaja* trees; RKS 2.14.
It was intensely laden with blossoms and fruits upon trees that bore every kind of desirable fruit;
it was crowded with swans and kāraṇḍava ducks, and adorned with ruddy geese.
Resounding with the cries of various birds— cuckoos, peacocks,
and parrots— the birds, who remembered their former births, spoke in human speech.
Accompanied by Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Yakṣas, Vidyādharas, and Uragas,
the divine couple sports gently upon that most excellent of mountains.
And in the mountain cavern, it was adorned with divine gandharva dances and thousands of flutes and lutes,
as well as with celestial spectacles of exquisite beauty.
Making heaven and earth resound with the sound of the chanting of songs,
there were Brahman-sages, celestial sages, and other royal sages.
From the illumination of the Agnihotra sacrifice by the sound of the Vedas,
the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāman, and Atharva [Vedas] arose for the best of the twice-born belonging to the four castes.
Pulastya and Vasiṣṭha, Pulaha and Kratu, as well as Bhṛgu, Atri, Marīci, Bhāradvāja, and Kāśyapa.
Manu, Yama, Aṅgiras, Śātātapa, Parāśara, Āpastamba, Śamba, Kāvya, and the sage Kātyāyana; RKS 2.22.
Gautama, Śaṅkha and Likhita, Dakṣa, Kātyāyana,
as well as Jāmadagnya, Yājñavalkya, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, and Vibhāṇḍaka.
Garga, Śaunaka, Dālbhya, Vyāsa, Uddālaka, Śuka,
Nārada, Parvata, and Durvāsas, the fierce ascetic.
Śākalya, Gālava, Jābāli, and likewise Mudgala;
Viśvāmitra and Kauśika—these sages are honored by the gods.
Likewise, Dharmaśata, Ānanda, Vaiśampāyana, Vaiṣṇava, Śākalāyana, Vārddhakya, Juhuti, and Avasu; RKS 2.26.
The high-souled Bālakhilyas, who dwell upon the circle of the earth,
ascend the staff of Brahmā and proceed to the world of the gods.
These and other virtuous sages also went there,
all blazing with splendor like smokeless fires.
Some fast for a month, some fast for a fortnight;
others observe the three-night fast, the *sāntapana* penance, or likewise remain without food.
Some subsisted on flowers and fruits, while others were peaceful and subsisted on air;
some fed on cow dung, and others likewise subsisted on water.
They were learned men who maintained the sacred fire-sacrifice, who contemplated the meaning of liberation and the Vedas,
and who were experts in the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and other scriptures, as well as in the Śrutis and Smṛtis.
These and many other ascetics, dear to Mārkaṇḍeya,
stood together with him like the moon surrounded by bears.
Having heard the fruit of pilgrimage to sacred fords, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma,
set out together with learned Brahmins and his beloved Draupadī.
Learned scholars, knowers of the Vedas, most devoted to Brahman, and contemplators of Brahman,
arrived at the bank of the Narmadā toward the hermitage of Mārkaṇḍeya.
Having circumambulated him three times and prostrated himself with all eight limbs again and again,
the son of Dharma then sat down there together with his brothers.
Seeing the king seated, the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya spoke these words to the god-like Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma.
"Is it well with you, O tiger among kings, along with your brothers and the brahmins?
Laughing, he spoke these words to Mārkaṇḍeya, the best of sages.
Today my birth has become fruitful and my life well-lived;
today I have achieved my purpose through the sight of your lotus feet.
"Today my inner impurity has been destroyed, purified by the eradication of evil,
having seen this entire penance grove blazing with the splendor of the sun."
O Lord, being liberated from this sin after seven future births,
you shall sport in the enchanting divine realm in the northern quarter.
The goddess Gaṅgā who flows through the three paths, the Yamunā, and the Sarasvatī;
Gaṅgādvāra, Himasthāna, Kubjāgra, and Brahmayonika.
Ugra, Kanakhala, and Kedāra as well as Bhairava;
Naimiṣa, the sacred site of Gayā, Kurukṣetra, and Puṣkara.
Vārāṇasī, Prayāga, the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, Kālañjara, the great tīrtha of Atīrtha, Prabhāsa, and Śaśibhūṣaṇa;
O you of noble vows, having abandoned these and other meritorious fields,
for what purpose is the great river Narmadā alone resorted to?
O knower of the reality of the future and the past, O knower of the three times, O master of the three Vedas;
all these people desire to hear—please speak out of your grace.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen, O mighty-armed king, together with your brothers, the brahmins;
I shall relate to you that ancient account proclaimed by Skanda.
Then, in the Svāyambhuva Manvantara, during the first Kalpa and the Kṛta Yuga,
at that assembly of the gods on Mount Kailāsa, the abode of Śiva.
On the full moon day of Kārttika, they came to behold Hara, the Lord of the gods;
[therein] was recounted that exposition of dharma and adharma which had previously been requested by Kārttikeya.
This was previously told by Śiva to Pārvatī and Ṣaṇmukha, while Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the other gods, as well as the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, were listening.
And it is sung that for eight hundred and fifty thousand [years] one dwells in the world of Śiva;
half of that in the world of Viṣṇu, and half of that again in the city of Brahmā.
In the world of mortals, it is sung that eighty-four thousand [verses] exist;
Śiva was previously propitiated by Brahmā and the other gods and asuras.
Then the Lord of the Gods, being pleased, was ready to grant a boon as desired.
The gods said:
"If you are pleased, O Lord of Gods, become the granter of boons to the gods."
The earth, consisting of seven islands, is the ground for the ripening of karma;
they declare Jambūdvīpa to extend as far as the ninth island.
There were thousands of ponds and wells, rivers with fresh water,
and flowing streams that descended from the terrible Pitṛghora of Śarva.
"Indeed, for the sake of enabling the ancestors to drink the water-offering of sesame seeds now,
O Savior of all worlds, cause the Narmadā to descend!"
Īśvara said:
"O gods, that which is difficult for all the thirty deities to attain and cannot be requested is now being asked for.
Who is able to endure the force of the whirling of its waters?"
"The entire world is becoming water and will soon fall [into it] with great speed;
therefore, beg for another river, one whose waters are easy to cross."
The gods said:
"Who else is capable of delivering us, except for the meritorious Narmadā, the best of rivers, who crosses over sorrow and is the mistress of the three-eyed Lord?"
Having heard the words of the gods, that best of rivers was summoned;
and then the goddess arrived, adorned with all her ornaments.
Manifested in the form of a sea-monster by the command of the God of gods, she said:
"O Lord, grant me what must be spoken; let compassion be shown toward me."
Having heard those gentle words of Narmadā, the Three-eyed One spoke these smooth words: "Go now to the world of mortals."
For the sake of the welfare of the worlds, and especially for that of mortals, Narmadā said:
"O Lord, I shall carry out your command; yet, how can I do so without a support?"
"Who is able to hold me back? The earth will undergo dissolution.
Then the Supreme Lord commanded all the mountains.
Having thus commanded them all, the divine Śiva himself [departed].
Then the mountains said:
"We are all unable to sustain the force of the Narmadā."
"The earth will indeed suffer division, and the mountains will shatter into a hundred pieces.
O Lord of the Thirty-three, bestower of commands, please grant us your permission," said Ṛkṣavān to the god.
And by my truth, O Lord of Umā, through your grace,
the Goddess was then brought down to Jambudvīpa, O King.
Having split the entire earth, including its mountains, forests, and groves, she was then addressed by the hosts of gods: "O you of virtuous vows, maintain the boundaries [of the world]."
Measuring twenty-one thousand yojanas in extent,
it pierced through the seven netherworlds and reached the depths of the Rasātala.
Then, when the dissolution had arrived, he went to the world of the gods;
O King, this is declared to be the first conceptualization of the incarnation.
O sinless one, in the second *yuga* of the first *kalpa*, during the Svārociṣa period,
there were no oceans, no rivers, no sacred fords (*tīrthas*), and no confluences.
In former times, during the Tretā Yuga, the river Bhāgīrathī descended;
she was held within the hollow of Jahnu’s palm and remained stationed in the center of his heart.
O King, how is she to be served, having abandoned that which leads to liberation?
[For people] are shrouded by the darkness of ignorance and deluded by the māyā of Viṣṇu.
O King, having indeed abandoned the Narmadā, the gods serve other rivers,
as do the suns and the gods amidst the radiance of jewels and gems.
O King, having heard this meritorious narrative concerning the power of Śaṅkara, one perceives such an interval between the Narmadā and other rivers.
There, the *Skandapurāṇa* consisting of seven chapters is served;
this has been told to you, O King, exactly as it was seen and heard.

Having accomplished all that was to be done, you shall attain the supreme state, free from the destruction of your lineage, along with Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas, after fulfilling all your desires.
Having heard this meritorious, purifying narrative that destroys sin,
those who constantly and perpetually listen to it— thereby even the killing of a cow is destroyed.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Narration of the First Kalpa," in the glorious Revākhaṇḍa.
RKS, Chapter 3.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"The descent of the Revā is meritorious, as is its confluence and its worshipped linga."
And the measurements of pilgrimages, as well as the ages and the periods of the world-ages.
The greatness of Parvata and that of the river there is as it should be;
for it is a festival time for the gods, especially at every sacred ford (tīrtha).
The greatness of Pattana, the appropriate manner of residing there,
and the meritorious glorification of Bhṛgu— which grants liberation from the sin of killing a Brahmin— [are described].
O great sage, tell me this: for what purpose did that best of rivers descend into Jambūdvīpa, and how did she go to the world of Śiva?
"Tell me by your grace whatever has been said or remains unsaid.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Listen, O king of kings; understand from me what is being told."
In the first age, there was a great asura named Hiraṇyakaśipu,
who was endowed with the grace of Śiva and was exceedingly powerful through his mother’s strength.
Defeated by him, the deities, intent on flight,
went for refuge, agitated, afflicted by fear, and overwhelmed by terror.
We have taken refuge in the god Mādhava, the slayer of Madhu, who bears the conch and the discus, and who carries us across the ocean of saṃsāra.
Neither the Agnihotra nor the Vedas, nor the officiating at sacrifices for the gods;
neither Vedic study nor sacrifices, nor the offering of oblations, nor the libations to the ancestors.
O King, in the meantime, the world was oppressed by wicked Dānavas and the practice of dharma was destroyed; then the powerful Viṣṇu [intervened].
All those Daityas were slain by him in the form of Narasiṃha;
then Dharma was set in motion once more, including the performance of sacrifices for the gods and Brahmins.
All the Dānavas were destroyed— those base ones devoted to evil deeds—
and for that very purpose, Narmadā, the sustainer of the world, arrived.
When the Svārociṣa interval had arrived, at the beginning of the Kalpa in the Kṛta Yuga,
the Goddess, worshipped by the thirty gods, took birth again among mortals.
O best of men, desiring the welfare of the worlds,
he who is honored by the hosts of gods will act [thus] upon knowing that mortal man to be devoted to the practice of dharma.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
In former times, there was a universal monarch named Purūravas in the Lunar dynasty;
he ruled the entire earth just as Śakra rules the triple heaven.
Once, that best of kings, Purūravas— who was devoted to serving the elders and firm in his vows— questioned the aged brahmins in the midst of the assembly.
Tell me truly: by what means, other than sacrifices and the like, have men deluded by sin attained heaven? Please explain that to me as it really is.
The Brahmins said:
"O Great King, the Narmadā, the purifier of the world, resides in heaven;
cause her, the remover of the sins of the worlds, to descend from heaven."
Having heard those words of the twice-born who were firm in their vows,
he propitiated the God for more than ten thousand years.
Even though he subsisted on roots, tubers, fruits, vegetables, and water,
he remained constantly devoted to Śiva with a perfectly pure inner self.
Then Mahādeva, being pleased, said: "Choose a boon, my son;
I shall grant it to you without a doubt, whatever is desired by your heart."
Purūravas said:
"O Mahādeva, if you are pleased and desire to grant me a boon,
then for the welfare of all the worlds, cause the Narmadā to descend."
I have heard that the entire world— consisting of nine regions, seven islands, oceans, and likewise rivers— is submerged in a terrible hell.
Even the gods, as well as mothers, fathers, and humans, do not reach satiety with Jambūdvīpa, which extends for a hundred thousand yojanas and is without support.
Having heard these words spoken by Naradeva, Mahādeva Hara said:
"O King, that which is difficult for even the gods to obtain and should not be asked for is now being requested."
"I shall grant you another boon, with the exception of the Narmadā.
Purūravas said:
"O Mahādeva, even at the cost of my life, I do not seek any other boon."
Having understood the king's resolve regarding the accomplishment through fierce asceticism, Mekalā was commanded: "Descend, O Goddess of the Gods!"
"By means of the ripening of Purūravas, bring about the welfare of the mortal world.
Thus commanded, she arrived and stood before Śiva.
Having joined her palms in reverence, she said, "Let my command be given today.
Hara replied:
"O Revā, by my command, depart from heaven to the world of mortals."
"Purūravas, perform penance and truth now, O auspicious one. Narmadā said:
"O Lord, how shall I go from heaven to the earth without support?"
Then, having heard those words, the God of gods, the Lord of Umā,
invoked all eight of the most excellent lineage-mountains.
The God said to the mountains, "Who among you is capable of supporting the river?
The mountains replied,
"Great mountains would shatter into a hundred pieces from the impact of the waters."
Then Vindhya spoke:
"O foremost of the lords of gods, by your grace my son is capable of holding back the river; of this there is no doubt."
Known as Paryaṅka, he possessed the firm prowess of Kandarpa;
he was the eldest, accompanied by all his hosts, and honored by all the mountain lords.
"Even by the gods he is difficult to discern; he is devoted to the worship of Śivā.
O Maheśvara, although all the mountains are indeed present here," [RKS 3.35]
Nevertheless, he alone is capable of supporting it here; of this there is no doubt.
All other mountains—whether powerless, crippled, or aged—are incapable.
"Grant permission; the couch is capable of supporting that river.
And being thus permitted by the Lord, that couch, the best of mountains, [prepared itself].
He said, "O Maheśvara, by your grace I shall uphold [this]";
thereupon the Goddess moved from the summit of the mountain Paryaṅka.
Due to the whirling force of the flood of waters, the entire earth, along with its mountains, forests, and groves, was submerged; the world was overtaken by untimely calamity.
Then, praised by all the hosts of gods, the daughter of Mekala said:
"O auspicious one, you who bring benefit to the worlds, maintain the bounds of propriety."
By you all this triple world, including the moving and the unmoving, is pervaded;
therefore, by your concealed form, Mekalā was commanded by Śiva.
Having gratified her ancestors, she entered Rasātala, which measured twenty-one thousand yojanas in extent.
When he was told, "Touch me with your own hand," Purūravas did so;
and having drunk water, he offered the libation of water with sesame seeds (tilodaka) to his ancestors.
He went to the supreme abode, which is difficult even for the gods to attain;
it is pure and encompasses all the three worlds, including everything moving and unmoving.
For that purpose, O King, the Narmadā, which flows through seven kalpas, is served by him. Thus has this narrative, spoken by Śiva, been told to you.
Now, at the conclusion of the Dvāpara age, when the time for Vaivasvata has arrived,
you shall be king together with your brothers, true to your word and firm in your vows.

As long as they did not form the resolve that "we have no need for [him]," all of them remained composed and performed their daily threefold duties.
When spring had arrived, those women went to Indra’s palace by means of the Puṣpaka chariot in order to witness a performance as it was practiced of old.
Having played according to custom, they— overwhelmed by the intoxication of wine—

Having seen the incomparable beauty of Citrāṅgada, the excellent women were so infatuated that their minds, intoxicated by passion, did not recognize him.
And all those Gandharva women, their faces joyful, being desired by them,

In the past year, they arrived at the city of the Gandharvas;
they came to the city of Umā, the domain of Maheśvara, in order to behold Gaurī.
Then, having paid homage to the Goddess, they spoke these words:
"O Sovereign Lady, protect us who have fallen from our own religious observance."
Then the Goddess became enraged toward those who were intent on evil deeds—
those who had violated their vows and the like, and those who had defiled the wives of others.
Shameless, of evil conduct, and excluded from all the world—
such is the atonement for that unrighteousness and sin upon the surface of the earth.
He who, deluded by lust and greed, should desire a maiden,
shall be born as a worm in excrement for sixty thousand years.
In the meantime, O King, Citrāṅgada, offering praise,
bowed his head to the goddess and spoke these words:
Out of great fear of the curse, that lord of men lamented:

"What atonement is there today for this sin? What is the remedy for the disease?
Thus the Goddess spoke these words to the Gandharva, who was deluded by desire.
For one who has abandoned the performance of dharma and fallen from the heavenly world,

"No atonement is prescribed for the sin of defiling a maiden;
even my Gandharva daughters have been mocked by you with drinks of honey-wine."
"But you Gandharvas, deluded by passion through this sin,

For a thousand divine years you shall wander in the world of mortals;
due to the fault of having deformed a maiden, you shall have the faces of hunchbacks and monkeys.
"May they suffer their sin on the surface of the earth due to the fault of their own actions.
Having been thus cursed by the Goddess, they all returned to the mortal world.

"A great curse has been bestowed upon us to turn us back from the path of evil.

"Entreat Mahādeva, the God of gods, the Supreme Lord.

"Let an atonement for this sin be performed according to my word.

six [yojanas] to its north and likewise six to its south.

In this interval, O Great King, the field of Śiva (Śivakṣetra) is proclaimed;

By the offering of water with sesame seeds, his maternal ancestors, paternal ancestors,
and forefathers remain satisfied until the dissolution of all beings.
There, in former times, Brahmā performed innumerable supreme sacrifices;
and Śakra, the king of the gods, attained his sovereignty there by performing sacrifices.
O King, in ancient times, Kārtavīrya— who was devoted to sacrifice and charity— performed a hundred sacrifices right there in Ayodhyā.
And there was a lord of the earth in the solar dynasty who was the son of Āditya;

The universal monarch named Manu was superior in virtue even to Śakra and the other lords;
likewise, death, disease, and old age do not enter that supreme city.
It was adorned with five hundred auspicious golden houses possessing seven stories,

Like the city of Kubera, or like Amarāvatī belonging to Śakra,

Two and a half million people lived there;

There was no country, no sacred ford, no kingdom, and no hermitage that he did not burn with thousands of various sacrificial fires.

While she was thus constantly nursing him over a long period of time,
