there were eleven Rudras present, as well as twelve Ādityas.
The Viśvedevas, as well as the Sādhyas, the Maruts, and the Vasus;
the eight world-protectors, as well as the oceans and the rivers.
Likewise, the lords of the forest, the mountains, various sacred fords,
the guardians of the directions, the guardians of beings, and the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras;
All the Soma-drinking ancestors bestow the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
as do the Rākṣasas, Guhyakas, Bhūtas, and Uragas.
Likewise, during the festival, there were dwellings for those who live in the wind as well as those who dwell in space;
and there were rivers flowing with ghee and milk, with mud made of curd and milk-rice.
During that great festival of the king’s sacrifice,
there were various kinds of foods and edibles, as well as vehicles and other desirable objects, provided according to everyone's wishes.
The gods and sages were satisfied, as was the fourfold host of living beings;
thus was the sacrifice brought to completion by the Brahmins who bestowed abundant sacrificial fees.
Then Indradyumna was praised by the gods and asuras, as well as by the divine beings;
he then assigned separate sacrificial portions for each of the deities.
For such was the portion of the Rudras as it was created by the Self-born One.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
[Tell me] of the Rudras, Ādityas, Vasus, and the Viśvedevas who consume the sacrificial oblation.
"O Great Sage, please tell me the names of the lineages and their branches.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Atri, Aṅgiras, Sarpis, Marut, and Bṛhaspati."
Dhruva, Dhūmra, Ketu, Dhara, Dhātṛ, and Hara—
these eleven are remembered as the Rudras, all of whom bestow the fruits of one's desires.
Āryamā, Varuṇa, Indra, and Pūṣan who possesses the hand;
and Mitra is likewise celebrated, as well as the last, who creates the waters.
Vivasvān, Parjanya, and Dhātṛ—these twelve are remembered;
they were born in the hermitage of Kaśyapa and arose as repositories of splendor.
By means of a practice lasting less than a month, all these wander at will throughout the heavenly world day and night.
O Great King, listen indeed as the eight Vasus are being described: Dhruva, Dhara, Soma, Sāvitra, Anila, and Anala; RKS_34.73.
Pratyūṣa and Kalpa—these eight are remembered as the Vasus;
and likewise, the sons of Viśvā are proclaimed as the Viśvedevas.
Kratu, Dakṣa, Satya, Kāla, Kāma, Ghana, Purūravas, Mārdravas, and Rocamāna— these are the ten.
Likewise, the sons of Muhūrtā are proclaimed as the Sādhyas;
and the Maruts are proclaimed to be forty-nine in number.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, the names of all these are indeed well-known;
O sinless one, I have told you everything that I was asked by you.
Then, having dismissed Dhruva as well as the sages who were the sons of Brahmā,
and having understood the significance of the syllable Oṃ, the king performed worship.
The linga was adorned with jewels of gems and rubies,
and with various perfumes, incenses, camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite with banners, parasols, canopies, fans, and divine chowries, that hymn of mine was recited.
Yogins constantly meditate upon the syllable Oṃ joined with the Bindu;
it is the bestower of desires and the bestower of liberation—homage again and again to the syllable Oṃ!
O bestower of boons, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra, O you who are all the gods, homage be to you!
To Kadrudra, the wise one, the thousand-eyed, the one praised by the immortals.

O Rudra, that form of yours which is auspicious, not terrible, and free from the appearance of evil—O you who possess all faces, heads, and necks, for the sake of the welfare of all beings! RKS 34.83.
And the Blessed One is all-pervading; homage to him who has gone everywhere!
His hands and feet extend everywhere, and his eyes, heads, and faces are on every side.
Possessing ears everywhere in the world, he stands encompassing all.
"O Maheśvara, you have been wearied by the fickleness of the tongue;
this hymn was composed for the Lord by Indradyumna, O Bhārata."
O descendant of Bharata, he spoke to that king regarding the supreme Liṅga in the midst of the [other] Liṅgas, which was seen blazing with the brilliance of the fire of cosmic destruction.
Choose a boon—may prosperity be yours—whatever dwells in your mind.
Indradyumna said:
"O Lord, if you are pleased with me and desire to grant me a boon,"
O Lord of Gods, together with Umā, being duly honored here in this divine grove,
please always make this Sacrifice Mountain your abode.
O Lord of the gods, whether one is helpless or self-possessed, may he who gives up his life at this sacred site go to the world of Śiva.
He was a performer of a thousand sacrifices, a knower of Dharma, and likewise a lord of the sacrifice of giving;
yet there were also those who were blind, dwarfs, and humans born of animal wombs.
O Maheśvara, in this regard, there would be equality between the two at death for one who encircles a mountain with a single thread on a festival day.
By him the earth, together with its mountains, forests, and groves, has been circumambulated;
he attains the fruit of all sacred fords and goes to the world of Śiva.
Oṃkāra said: "O best of kings, may all this desire of yours be fulfilled."
Having spoken thus, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the god vanished right there; then, together with the gods, asuras, Ādityas, and Sādhyas,
he ascended his own vehicle and departed for his abode on Kailāsa.
The king also caused the fourfold assembly of living beings to hear:
"By the power of my sacrifice, may all be free from disease."
"May all, however, attain satisfaction through the power of my sacrifice.
Then, O Bhārata, Indradyumna praised Brahmā.
The Creator, being pleased, said to him, "Choose a boon, O lord of people.
The king said:
"If you are pleased with me, O God, and if you wish to grant me a boon here—"
"O Lord, if you are pleased with me, I consider this to be my boon: may you abide on the southern bank of the Narmadā, assuming the form of a Liṅga."
"Once the sacrifice of life has been performed there, let him indeed go to the world of Brahmā.
"So be it," O king of kings, Brahmā replied promptly.
Having spoken thus, O Yudhiṣṭhira, Brahmā departed for the world of Rudra along with the gods;
and then the king prostrated himself before Viṣṇu with all eight limbs.
Keśava, Mādhava, Viṣṇu, Govinda, Madhusūdana,
Padmanābha, Hṛṣīkeśa, Śrīdhara, and Trivikrama.
I bow down to Dāmodara, Vāsudeva, and Hari,
who is adorned with the conch, the discus, the mace, the Śārṅga bow, and a garland of forest flowers.
I bow to the Lord of the World, the Lord of the Universe, the glorious Lord, the supreme knower of all; to the beloved of Śrī, the bearer of Śrī, the Lord of Śrī, the abode of Śrī.
O Acyuta, O Infinite One, O Lord of Sacrifice, O Sovereign of Sacrifice, homage be to You!
Homage to You who are the form of the Ṛg, Sāman, and Atharva Vedas, and whose very form is the sacrifice!
Salutations to you who assume the forms of Nṛsiṃha, Matsya, Vārāha, and Kūrma;
salutations to you, O Garuḍa-bannered one, mounted upon the vehicle of the sacred ford.

The Lord Nārāyaṇa, the master, the primordial one— the deity with a thousand heads, who is both with parts and without parts, the supreme, the object of knowledge, the Puruṣa, and the sovereign witness.
I am forever prostrate before the God Hari, the destroyer of the Daityas,
who is the womb of Hiraṇyagarbha, the womb of the earth, the womb of sacrifice, and the source of the nectar of immortality.
O Vāsudeva, whose essence is glory and whose essence is wisdom, homage be to you!
O Lord, this entire world, both moving and unmoving, has been created by you.
You are indeed the creator, the protector, and the destroyer in age after age;
you are the all-seeing, the unmanifest, the one to be known, and the one whose face is everywhere.
O Soul of the Universe, O God who is everywhere, Vāsudeva, homage be to you!
You are Āditya and you are Vāyu; you are Agni and you are Candramas.
You are the Sustainer, O Lord of the gods; you are Indra, you are Prajāpati.
By your grace, O best of the gods, the success of my sacrifice has been achieved.
Having heard this hymn of praise, the Lord, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace, [was moved].
He spoke these truthful words: "Choose a boon, O lord of people!
I shall grant it to you, of this there is no doubt; you shall attain the success of your sacrifice."
The King said:
"O Janārdana, in the gentle portion of the syllable Om, you who exist in the form of a Liṅga,
become the purifier of the world upon the peak of the Vaidūrya mountain."
I consider this to be the boon, if you wish to grant one here:
that those who worship here according to the prescribed rite shall indeed go to the abode of Viṣṇu.
Those men do not go to the animal realm, nor likewise to the world of Yama;
when they have given up their life there, those men go to that state.
"By the gift of food to the ancestors, may the ancestors indeed go to the station of Viṣṇu through your grace; this I speak as the truth, the absolute truth."
Having heard those words of King Amitatejas,
O lord of the people, Viṣṇu spoke these words to Indradyumna.
"I shall manifest an incarnation right here, O best of kings;
everything, O most excellent of monarchs, shall come to pass through my grace."
Having spoken thus, O Bhārata, the god who bears the conch, discus, and mace departed toward the third heaven while being praised by the gods and asuras.
O King Indradyumna, this great sacrifice of yours has been described;
because of it, that mountain became sacred and renowned throughout all the worlds.
Know that Siddheśvara is Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa is Hari;
by hearing of and chanting his name, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Then the king, established in his vow of truth, praised the sacred fords for the sake of delivering his ancestors, saying: "Homage, homage to the sacred fords!"
The holy fords said:
"Choose a boon, O highly fortunate one, whatever dwells in your mind.
Having heard the words of the holy fords, Indradyumna spoke.
"By my grace, you must remain at this sacred ford in the presence of Oṃkāra.
Having said "So be it" to the king, they offered a hymn of praise to the river.
We pay homage to you, who flow for an eon, the supreme portion of Hara,
the best of rivers, renowned throughout the world upon this earth.
She is purified not by our power, but by her own nature,
just as the radiance of the sun is pure and so too is the light of fire.
"And likewise, O king of kings, this great river belongs to Himāṃśu.
Having spoken thus to that king, the sacred fords then vanished.
Then the best of kings, having offered the *argha* oblation, praised Gaṅgā—
the goddess Bhāgīrathī, as well as the auspicious Bhogavatī.
The Jāhnavī bestows liberation, she is auspicious, the savior, and the destroyer of sins;
in heaven she is indeed the Mandākinī, saluted by the God of gods.
You are Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas; you are Umā and likewise Kātyāyanī.
What else is there for you, O Goddess, who are borne upon the head by Hara?
"Who has the power to praise you, except for the one who bears the crescent moon as his crest?
Gaṅgā said:
"I am pleased with you, O Great King; choose a boon, O observer of noble vows."
Having heard the words of Gaṅgā, the king replied to her.
The king said:
"O Goddess of gods, if you are pleased and desire to grant me a boon here,"
Let your residence be made right here; let this boon be granted.
Gaṅgā said:
"So be it, O Indra among kings; I shall indeed carry you by means of my portion."
Then he praised Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, who flows for an eon: "O Goddess, you are the most excellent, flowing for an eon; you are worthy of homage and possessed of long life."
And by the power of your water, purity has come to me;
yet at the end of the eon, rivers, oceans, and the like go to their destruction.
You alone abide right here as all the sacred fords;
O fortunate one, you are worthy of worship, adored by the thirty gods, and long-lasting.
"At the tip of your matted locks you shall indeed become the form of Hara, equal to Gaurī.
Having spoken thus, Gaṅgā then paid homage to Mekalā.
Mounted upon the divine vehicle and being praised by hosts of apsarases,
Sarasvatī said: "Indeed,
this daughter of yours has been protected by me in accordance with dharma."
O blessed one, I have come to you, devoted to your service, seeking to behold your lotus feet, for you are a vessel of merit that carries across seven kalpas.
"O Goddess, likewise for twenty-four years I have been performing my ablutions; do you not know me, O illustrious one, O Dharā, O Mistress of the Earth, O River? (RKS 34.144)

Assuming the form of a female elephant, she arrived at Koṭitīrtha when the sun and moon were eclipsed by Rāhu; at that time, there were one hundred and twenty-five million sacred fords (tīrthas) present.
O Goddess, at the command of Viṣṇu himself,
you were appointed for the purpose of bathing during the fourth part of the Dvāpara age, amidst the armies of the Kuru and Pāṇḍava hosts.
In that auspicious assembly, which embodies all sacred fords, whatever gift is given or whatever austerity is performed for the sake of battle— RKS 34.147.
Indeed, all that becomes a hundredfold when performed in your water at the end of an eon;
and that same act becomes ten millionfold when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu.
Having spoken thus, O Great King, the Sarasvatī,
who flows through the eon, returned once more to her own abode along with King Indradyumna.
Then, O Bhārata, King Indradyumna himself offered praise:
"By the power of your water, the ancestors and the gods have been gratified."
And by you, O Goddess, the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile, have been purified;
you are the mother of all beings and the one who carries men across the ocean of saṃsāra.
O Great Goddess, you are Mekalā, as well as Kalpagā and Narmadā;
renowned as Jalapūrṇā, you are the ornament of the Vindhya mountains.
"O auspicious one, who would be capable of praising you even in a thousand years?
Having heard this hymn, the Goddess then spoke to the king:
O King, this sacrifice performed here by thousands of Kṣatriyas is equal to yours, O Great King; it has never been equaled before, nor will it ever be again.
"O King, I grant you a boon by which you shall attain perfection.
Having heard those words of her who flows through the Kalpa, O Yudhiṣṭhira...
Then the king, who was eternally devoted to Śiva, spoke laughingly together with the brahmins: "O auspicious one, who carries [us] through seven kalpas! (RKS 34.156)
"If you are pleased with me, O Goddess, and you wish to grant me a boon,
then create seven channels on both the southern and northern banks."
O Goddess who pervades all things, if you hold me in high regard from every side,
O lady of noble vows, I consider this to be a boon if you are pleased with me.
O descendant of Bharata, having heard those words of Indradyumna, Narmadā spoke these words to Indradyumna, O lord of men: RKS_34.159.
All this shall come to pass through my power and by my grace;
and whatever gift is given during this interval, there is no doubt regarding that.
"There is no number for them; I tell you this truthfully.
There is no returning for them again," so said the Blessed One, O King.
Whether they be outcastes, dog-cookers, wild animals, or even reptiles,
all of them go to the third heaven at the confluence of the Nīlagangā.
O lord of the people, O descendant of Bharata, having performed a sacrifice and having paid homage to the Narmadā and to Oṃkāra, Indradyumna, the best of kings, [attained his goal].
Mounting his own vehicle, devoted to truth and righteousness,
the king was surrounded by a thousand [attendants] and praised by hosts of apsarases.
He entered the holy city of Ayodhyā, built by the gods.
Thus, O King, has this ancient history been narrated to you.
Then, after ruling the kingdom for a long time, that king of great strength went to the third heaven, having completed ten thousand years and more in this world.
By hearing and reciting this, one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows;
one shall not behold the world of Yama, nor go to a sinful womb.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Descent of the Nīlagangā at Indradyumna’s Sacrifice," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS, Chapter 35.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
[Tell me of] the beautiful Vaidūrya mountain, frequented by gods and siddhas.
For what purpose did Māndhātā indeed go to [the realm] that lasts for seven kalpas?
Likewise, having destroyed Tripura with the Pāśupata weapon,
Hara split open Pātāla and went to the depths of Rasātala.
For what reason did the Jāleśvara Liṅga likewise arise there?
And how did the Nīlagangā, flowing from Kalpa, reach a division at that place?
O great sage, Bāṇāsura was a devotee of Śiva, pure and having obtained boons from Śiva; by him those liṅgas were worshipped here.
"Indeed, nine crores of them were cast there by number;
O Great Sage, tell all of this in brief."
Just as it was heard in a former age, in the ancient narrative celebrated by Skanda,
concerning the gods beginning with Brahmā and Viṣṇu, and concerning Pārvatī and the Six-faced One.
"O dear one, let it be told then, exactly as it was indicated by Śiva.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Listen, O mighty-armed king; understand what is being told by me."
When the Svārociṣa interval had arrived, during the first kalpa in the Kṛta age,
there was a gathering of the gods on Kailāsa, the best of mountains.
And on the full moon day of Kārttika, all the gods came to see Hara;
there, Skanda spoke these words to all the hosts of deities:
I have heard and seen what was spoken by Śiva in the past;
eight hundred and fifty thousand [verses] are proclaimed in this work.
Just as they are bound by Śiva himself in the world of Śiva,
half of that [merit] is in the world of Viṣṇu, and half of that is in the city of Brahmā.
And the world of the Sun is established at one hundred and twenty-five thousand [yojanas].
Likewise, eighty-four thousand [years] are proclaimed in the world of mortals in that sequence; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
The Sūta is the compiler, and the Saṃhitās are contained therein;
they know the Purāṇa to be sevenfold: the Kalpaskanda and the Mahāskanda.
Primary creation, secondary creation, genealogy, the periods of the Manvantaras,
and the accounts of the dynasties— thus the Purāṇa has five characteristics.
In the Kali age, human beings in this world will be powerless, sustaining themselves through meager livelihoods; they will be devoid of martial prowess and will become immoral in conduct.
There is no private recitation, no *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, no austerity, and no officiating at sacrifices;
the Brahmins, lustful for women and greedy, are merely supplicants performing rites for their own desires.
Constantly intent on receiving gifts and seeking only to maintain their households,
those who have fallen under the power of affection for women do not understand themselves at all.
When the Kali Yuga has arrived, even the most righteous ascetics will perform evil deeds; likewise, there will be Kaulas and those who go naked.
All subjects will be of a single caste, and the king will be a barbarian;
such will be the case when the inferior age has arrived and Keśava has taken refuge in the Buddha.
O Great Sage, mortals will indeed have short lifespans, with little vigor and prowess, and there will be calamities from various regions.
Indeed, twice-born men born of the lineage of Cāṇḍālas will appropriate the Vedas;
they will even perform the imposition of the Vedas [upon themselves] as well as the sale of the Vedas.
Desiring the acquisition of wealth, they will go to the king’s gate;
likewise, they will sell the *agnihotra* fires and the selling of daughters.
All the twice-born, though learned in the Vedas, will be devoid of their vows;
when the twelfth year is complete, men will have grey hair even in their youth.
A woman who has been pregnant for ten or twelve years should not regard herself as a woman, nor should a son regard his parents as his mother and father.
A daughter-in-law regards her mother-in-law as such, and likewise, a daughter [regards] her mother;
this has been declared by way of illustration. Now hear what is relevant, O Bhārata.
O Great King, Māndhātā, the best of monarchs, went to the Vaidūrya mountain in order to perform a sacrifice for the sake of delivering his ancestors.
For the sake of the welfare of the gods, Hara indeed destroyed Tripura;
in ancient times, it was consumed by the blazing Pāśupata weapon.
And by him was brought from Pātāla the Liṅga Jāleśvara,
which grants desires and liberation, and is always saluted by the gods.
For the sake of delivering the worlds, the supreme Nīlagangā has arrived;
born from Megharāja, she is the remover of all sins.
One should perform a śrāddha ceremony for the ancestors there with the desire for their inexhaustible [merit],
at the Śivālaya in Koṭitīrtha, where the liṅgas of Bāṇāsura are located.
O lord of men, those [bones] which have fallen into the waters of the Narmadā are honored and purifying, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O Indra among kings, the Bāṇaliṅgas are renowned throughout the three worlds;
for them, there is no consecration, no purificatory rite, nor even the ritual invocation and so forth.
In this very way, O Bhārata, the forms of Śiva are to be worshipped.
All this that I was asked by you, O sinless one, has been told to you.
Listen, O King, to another divine story that destroys sin;
O sinless one, I shall relate to you that which is known to me as the destroyer of evil.
Here there is a glorious mountain known by the name Vaidūrya;
there dwell sacred fords and holy shrines.
It was filled with trees that yield the fruits of desire, both in flower and in fruit,
as well as with the songs of celestial birds and rows of groves of reed-bamboo.
O Bhārata, there the holy river Narmadā, which removes all sins, flows, adorned with *śāla*, *tāla*, *sarala*, and *tamāla* trees.
Whatever sacred fords, holy shrines, rivers, oceans, mountains, and gods, including the Grandfather Brahmā, exist within the three worlds;
O best of kings, O Bhārata, Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Cāraṇas all come to the Narmadā to bathe; indeed, every perfection is found there.
O King, what is there on that mountain where the sage Viśvāvasu dwells,
yet where Kubera, the lord of the Yakṣas and rider of men, is not present?
On that meritorious peak of vaidūrya, the very presence of the Sun himself resides;
there, the trees with their green foliage are perpetually laden with flowers and fruit.
Great wonders are likewise seen there on that best of mountains—
holy, divine, resembling heaven, and eternally frequented by celestial sages.
O royal sage, there indeed flows the river Hlādinī, the most meritorious of sacred fords,
when the Vaivasvata interval has arrived, O King, in the first created age.

Through the descent of the syllable Oṃ, the mountain was composed entirely of lapis lazuli in the Tretā Yuga; in the Dvāpara Yuga, it was made of jewels, and in the Kali Yuga, it takes the form of gold.
In the Kali age, the mountain is declared to be the remover of sins just like the God himself;
all this ancient account has been related to you exactly as it was seen.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vaidūrya Mountain," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS, Chapter 36.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
In ancient times, there was a royal sage and universal monarch named Vasudāna.
The illustrious lord of Ayodhyā, whose prowess was equal to that of Indra.
Then he enjoyed the entire earth as if it were a single village,
and he performed a thousand sacrifices, including the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
All the subjects live for more than one hundred and twenty-five thousand years;
nor is there anyone there who is dejected, suffering, or even poor.
O lord of the earth, while he was thus protecting the world, the earth— rich with crops— became a cow that yielded all desires of its own accord.
On the southern bank of the Narmadā were the Daityas, thorns to the gods:
Ketumālin, Suketu, Sumukha, and Dundubhi.
And some who had arisen in the abode of the gods became obstructors of the Dharma;
at that time, out of fear, they were unable to perform sacrifices here.
Vasudāna spoke these words to Vasiṣṭha, the foremost knower of Brahman:
"In which sacred ford (tīrtha), indeed, is the horse sacrifice performed without obstacles?"
"Having pointed out [the ritual] according to the injunctions of the science of sacrifice, let it be told to me.
Having heard those words of the wise Vasudāna, [he replied:]
And Vasiṣṭha spoke these words to the king, O Bhārata:
"It is not possible to perform the horse sacrifice, especially with such a face."
The form of Amareśvara indeed stands facing the southern direction;
there, all the gods, including Indra, were defeated by the Dānavas.
They are never able to receive a share of the sacrifice;
for this reason, O King, what has been spoken to you is the truth.
Having heard those words of the high-souled Vasiṣṭha,
Vasudāna became enraged and replied to the domestic priest.
"Having slain these wicked Rākṣasas today, who are indeed thorns to the gods,
I shall perform the supreme sacrifice through the grace of the gods."
Having spoken thus, the wise king departed, accompanied by all the necessary provisions, together with learned brahmins who were masters of the Vedas and officiating priests.
And five hundred thousand cows with their calves that yield milk,
one hundred and twenty-five thousand horses, and likewise ten thousand elephants.
Jewels such as gems and rubies, gold, silver, and wealth,
various kinds of food and edibles, clarified butter, rice, and sesame seeds likewise.
Taking up the sacrificial pavilions and the sacrificial posts, O best of kings,
the sacrifice proceeded thus without any obstacle, O Bhārata.
The earth, moistened by the waters of the purificatory bath (āvabhṛthya), appeared as if fashioned of gold;
and the beasts and birds that had wallowed in the mud became [as if] made of gold.
O Bhārata, all of them there became golden-hued,
where Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara were worshipped simultaneously.
And from that sacrifice, O best of kings, streams of milk and ghee issued forth separately, as did a stream of cow urine there.
O best of kings, the bathing water used by the sages who had mastered the Vedas for the gods became a flowing stream there.
And when all those currents had then merged together, O King,
the river named Kapilā was beheld by the celestial Brahman-sages.
There, the confluence with the Narmadā is celebrated as Rudrāvarta;
thereafter, all the Brāhmaṇas were honored with sacrificial fees.
Then all the hosts of gods, mounted on elephants, horses, and chariots, adorned with various ornaments, being well-pleased, spoke to that king:
"Choose a boon, O highly fortunate one, O observer of noble vows, for this sacrifice.
Vasudāna said:
"Having bathed at the confluence of the Revā and the Kapilā and having worshipped Maheśvara..."
"May those who have died and are not subject to rebirth go to the third heaven by means of celestial chariots;
I consider this a boon—let it be granted as a favor to me."
The gods said:
"O King, having granted this boon, the deities are indeed pleased; your every thought and desire shall bear fruit according to your wish. (RKS 36.27)
Having ascended their respective celestial chariots, they departed joyfully for the third heaven;
the royal sage Vasudāna also [departed] with brahmins who had mastered the Vedas.
Then, filled with supreme joy, he returned to Ayodhyā together with his harem and retinue, by virtue of the power of this sacred ford.
Having enjoyed abundant pleasures, he went to the city of Maheśvara.
Thus, everything concerning the confluence of the Revā and Kapilā has been told to you.
By hearing and chanting this, one is liberated from the bondage of existence.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Incarnation of Kapila," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS Chapter 37.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
When the Svāyambhuva Manvantara had arrived, in the first Kalpa, during the Kṛta Yuga.
He was the son of Dākṣāyaṇī, who had been born of Arundhatī.
There was a king named Viśravas, equal to Śakra in prowess;
he was the illustrious lord of Mathurā, a universal monarch (cakravartin) of great strength.
That king was like Maghavan himself, having conquered both gods and demons;
and the Brahmins as well as other people had all their desires fulfilled.
While he was thus governing the earth, which was abundant with wealth and grain,
there was neither famine nor poverty anywhere upon the surface of the world.
When this interval had arrived, he set out for Amarakaṇṭaka;
having bathed at Koṭitīrtha, he indeed worshipped Maheśvara.
O Bhārata, having taken recourse to the southern form of that deity,
one should remain established in meditative absorption for as long as that king, who is devoted to dharma, remains so.
Then, at midday, he sees two suns that have gone to the eastern quarter and two to the southern quarter, emerging from the solar disc in the western direction.
O King, two [suns] were below in Pātāla and likewise two suns of fierce form were above;
then the fire of the Saṃvartaka eon blazed forth.
Fierce and terrible winds, capable of bringing about universal destruction, blew;
there was a conflagration of the quarters, an earthquake, and dreadful portents of falling meteors.
The Siddhas and Gandharvas, along with the Kinnaras, Vidyādharas, and Yakṣas, fell from the world of the gods like those deprived of their merit through the exhaustion of their karma.
The Vidyādharīs wept, as did the Apsarases;
then the great fire blazed forth, consuming the mountains, forests, and groves.
Having reduced the entire earth to ashes,
that best of kings then arrived at the bank of the Revā, afflicted by thirst and tormented by burning heat.
As he prepared to drink water, he beheld the Mekalā river;
however, on that very path, not a drop of water was to be found.
The current was seen as nothing but dust, and the Narmadā river itself was no longer visible;
he wandered among rivers, oceans, mountains, and lakes.
That best of kings found no water to drink anywhere;
he beheld the goddess Narmadā and Vindhya, the most excellent of mountains.
Having entered into the midst of the Narmadā, the king became overwhelmed with anxiety:
"Without water, my death today is certain; of this there is no doubt."
Having reflected that the entire world had vanished and that nothing remained except water, the best of kings took refuge in the syllable *oṃ*.
Just as the king, afflicted by thirst, desired to ascend the mountain, he beheld there indeed a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpaśākhin).
Having seen that tree, which was laden with fruit, in bloom, delightful, and adorned with branches,
the king lay down there, having found its most refreshing shade.
Then his body became immortal and his hope for life was fulfilled;
he saw there a man lying down, blazing with splendor.
Then, O Yudhiṣṭhira, by his exhalation the worlds were indeed shaken upward,
and likewise the seven netherworlds (pātālas) by his inhalation.
And four water-pots stood at his side, filled with water;
seeing them, that best of kings, afflicted by thirst, reflected.
"I shall not take [the water] while he sleeps peacefully for the sake of enlightenment, nor shall I drink it myself;
what shall I do?"—having reflected thus, the king bowed to him and stood there.
Having assumed a human form, this Supreme Person remains here;
he is himself the divine Prajāpati, the destroyer, the creator, and the Lord of the world.
Then he beheld a second person of blazing splendor,
mounted upon a bull, three-eyed, and bearing a trident and a *pināka* bow in his hand.
His body was radiant with ashes, he wore a crown of matted hair,
he was adorned with a garland of skulls, and his splendor was equal to the light of lightning.
Seeing that man with fangs bared, tawny eyes, and the moon as his crest— such a form that caused the hair of all to stand on end.
The king praised the Lord of Gods, who is saluted by all the gods:
"Victory to you, O God, Great God, Primordial God! Homage be to you! (RKS 37.28)
"O Lord, wielder of the trident, listen to this: thirst afflicts me.
Grant me cool water, O Śaṅkara, by which I may live."
Having heard those words of his, Śiva spoke while laughing;
and as that god was speaking, [the gods] were seen on all sides within his mouth.
The celestial sages, the worlds, the seven [realms] with their mobile and immobile beings,
the netherworlds, all creatures, as well as the Gandharvas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas.
Then he saw a woman who had arrived, deeply distressed,
her entire body covered with dust and drenched in blood.
With infinite radiance and splendor, her hair tossed by the wind,
she placed the boy upon her left thigh and the girl between her breasts.
Having seen her adorned with the sacred thread, the triple staff, and two earrings,
the king then spoke these words.
Victory to you, O Goddess, Great Goddess, who bestows grace upon the worlds!
My body is overwhelmed by thirst; grant me water here to drink.
Having heard those words of his, the Supreme Goddess said to him:
"O King, drink my breast-milk if thirst afflicts you."
Having heard those words of hers, the king reflected:
"O Queen of the Gods, I shall suckle at your breast. To this, the woman spoke these words.
"O best of kings, I previously made a vow to you, O one of great splendor:
'Having placed my breast before you, I shall indeed give the child to you afterwards.'"
"Therefore, O illustrious one, drink my breast-milk; there is no sin in this.
Then the king spoke to that woman who could assume any form at will.
"This is improper for all those like me; what talk can there be [of it]?"—while they were thus conversing with one another, she vanished there.
"Where have you gone, O Great Queen? Having said this, he was struck with wonder;
for news obtained in a dream appears as something unsubstantial.
As he reflected that this was like a magician’s trick or like the water of a mirage,
she stood once more before him.
Upon seeing her, the king then prostrated himself with his eight limbs touching the ground and said:
"Who are you, O lady of excellent hips? Tell me this truly."
Umā, Kātyāyanī, Gaṅgā, Vedamātā, Sarasvatī,
Brahmāṇī, and Mahālakṣmī— please describe them out of your grace.
Who is this man who is equal [to all]? What are these four jars?
And who is this three-eyed one mounted upon a bull, bearing the trident and the Pināka bow?
"Who is this boy placed upon your lap, and who is this girl?
I am a fool; I do not understand birth or death."
The woman said:
"O King, know me to be the Earth, adorned with the seven continents,
along with the seven netherworlds, mountains, forests, and groves."
The rivers, the oceans, and the mountains dwelling within my belly—
the entire world, the three realms with all things mobile and immobile, is pervaded by me.
Know the Lord Hari, who reclines upon his couch, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace, to be the source of the universe and the one who enables the crossing of the ocean of saṃsāra.
Know the three-eyed, trident-bearing god Maheśvara;
know him as Mahādeva, mounted upon the bull, the lord of the worlds and the master of the universe.
Know that the infant resting on my lap is Brahmā, the creator;
the entire universe is pervaded by these three: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
Brahmā is the creator of the world, Hari himself is the protector, and Rudra is the agent of destruction; thus the universe is pervaded by these three.
Know that there are four jars situated on the mountains, representing the oceans;
know the maiden situated between the breasts to be the purifying Narmadā.
Having heard these words, the king was struck with great wonder;
then, after a long period of time, creation proceeds once again.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, for the sake of the welfare of the entire world, I have witnessed all this— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara— in kalpa after kalpa.
Nyagrodha, Kalpavṛkṣa, Oṃkāra, Saptakalpagā,
I myself, and Vaidūryaśaila— these, O Bhārata, are the supreme liṅgas.
Know all this in truth to be both imperishable and undecaying;
O sinless King, I have told you that which I was asked by you.
"You are devoted to listening to the Purāṇas; of this there is no doubt.
Through hearing and chanting of this, one is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence."
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Vision of the End of the Kalpa," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS, Chapter 38.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O scorcher of foes, such is the supreme majesty of this sacred ford (tīrtha).
O best among the knowers of the Vedas, I do not attain satiation while listening.
O high-minded one, further describe the greatness of this sacred ford by means of Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and are capable in all undertakings.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O great king, there is another holy place, the Liṅga known as Yameśvara;
by seeing and worshipping it, one does not behold the world of Yama.
On the southern bank of the Narmadā and to the west of the Kapilā,
there is the beautiful city of Viṣṇu, like Amarāvatī belonging to Śakra.
And Mādhava remains there for a period of ten million kalpas;
formerly, in the war between the gods and the asuras, he was [afflicted] by the dānavas, the thorns of the gods.
Then all the deities were utterly defeated and the earth was oppressed;
all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, [sought refuge] with the one who reclines upon the ocean of milk.
Having prostrated before him—the one worthy of praise, who dwells within and is imperishable—they lauded him:
"Victory to you, O God, Lord of the World, Destroyer of the Daityas, Janārdana!"
Assuming the form of a boar, the earth was lifted up by you;
assuming the form of a fish, the Vedas were recovered from the midst of the ocean.
In the forms of the Tortoise, Śeṣa, and others, you destroy the suffering of the gods;
as the enemy of the Asuras, you bound Bali by assuming the form of a dwarf.
The Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu, who caused terror to all the worlds and was a thorn to the gods,
was slain by you in the form of Nṛsiṃha.
"O Lord of the World, whose root is the Veda, protect us who have come to you for refuge.
Having heard this hymn, the God spoke these words to Brahmā:
And for what purpose, O Brahmin, have I been awakened by you in the Ocean of Milk?
Brahmā said:
O Lord of the World, without you, the earth is covered by the enemies of the gods.
For it would be like the world deprived of the sun, shorn of all light.
Viṣṇu said:
"O Brahmin, cast away your fear immediately; this Dānava is difficult to overcome, yet in a very short time I shall cause the Dānava to be slain."
Having spoken thus, Janārdana arrived together with the gods;
and with his Sudarśana discus, he [struck] the heads of the Dānavas.
The Blessed Viṣṇu indeed cut [them] asunder for the welfare of all the worlds;
all the Dānavas, afflicted by fear, became intent on flight.
Out of fear of Viṣṇu, they all fled to the depths of the netherworld (rasātala);
then the sacrifice of the twice-born, the gods, and the ascetics was resumed once more.
In that city, O illustrious one, there was a god who was the slayer of the Daityas;
whoever casts off their life-breaths there, whether against their will or by their own choice, [attains liberation].
One is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu by means of a Vaiṣṇava celestial chariot;
at the confluence of the Kapilā and the western Nīlagangā, however—
Indeed, eighty thousand sacred fords (tīrthas) were sent forth by Viṣṇu:
Cakratīrtha, Vāmana, Koṭitīrtha, and Yugandhara.
Having bathed there, O King, a person obtains the fruit of ten million holy sites (koṭitīrtha).
There is also the sacred site named Sudarśana and that which is the slayer of the Daityas.
At Viṣṇvāvarta, Śivāvarta, and likewise at Lakṣmyāvarta,
there is no limit to the merit of whatever gift is given there.
By performing propitiation of Viṣṇu, one enjoys infinite fruit;
for the sacred field (kṣetra) of Viṣṇu is proclaimed to be exactly one krośa in measure.
"The sin of killing a Brahmin shall not enter him; this is the truth spoken by Śiva.
He who performs a month-long fast as well as the Agnihotra sacrifice [is likewise freed]."
You are devoted to your husband, as well as to truth, the private recitation of sacred texts, sacrificial rites,
the Cāndrāyaṇa vow, the Parāka penance, and the offering of water with sesame seeds to the ancestors.
His ancestors are satisfied and indeed sport in the world of Viṣṇu by performing the Ekarātra,
Trirātra, Kṛcchra, and likewise the Sāntapana penances.
The *atikṛcchra*, the *parṇakṛcchra*, and likewise another Vaiṣṇava vow:
he who does not eat on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) of both fortnights [performs these].
He goes to that supreme abode where the Blessed Lord Hari resides;
Keśava has indeed declared that the fruit from another sacred field is ten million times greater [there].
Whatever chanting or austerity is performed there, may it all become inexhaustible.
The twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) is meritorious when conjoined with the Śravaṇa asterism, and the eighth (aṣṭamī) is auspicious when conjoined with Rohiṇī.
Having fasted there, O Great King, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu—
even if one is a Cāṇḍāla, a Śvapaca, or even born of an animal womb.
Whoever gives up their life here goes to the world of Viṣṇu;
and whoever observes a fast during the months of Kārttika and Vaiśākha [attains the same].
A human being obtains the fruit of ten crores of fasts;
this was sung by Śaṅkara in the past in the Skanda-purāṇa.
Seeing those who have fasted for a month and likewise those devoted to their husbands,
Dharmarāja himself shall go there and offer them the guest-offering (argha).
The Lord, the Master, arrived with sixty thousand vehicles;
the Lord Yama came for as far as a thousand yojanas.
Clad in white garments and bearing a body of radiant Dharma-splendor,
he stood before the vehicle and reverently prostrated at [his] feet.
Having beheld the world of Viṣṇu and gone there, he returns;
when the vehicles have returned, Yama questions them according to his own will.
The seven great seers were the mind-born sons of Brahmā;
for what reason, O Dharma, did you yourself go on foot?
"Speak, O highly fortunate one! We have come to a state of supreme wonder.
Laughing, Dharma replied, "Listen, O best of sages!"
Unable to behold the splendor of the devoted wives and the radiance of those who fast for a month, they remained at a distance from these celestial chariots.
"All my terrifying servants have returned from them;
for this reason, O Brahmins, I have indeed gone on foot."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Due to the majesty of Hari of immeasurable splendor, his residence and his sacrificial worship in Amarāvatī are celebrated there as the destroyers of the Kali age.
Now, there is another supreme deity renowned as Brahmeśa;
he is situated on the northern bank of the Revā and is the destroyer of sins.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, by worshipping that deity, one’s sin shall perish;
the ancestors attain satisfaction and reach the world of Brahmā.
To the south of Laṅkeśvara, the Siddhaliṅga is proclaimed;
by worshipping it or touching it, the state of being a Gaṇapati is attained.
This auspicious Viśveśvara, the great liṅga containing all the gods,
bestows the fruit of ten thousand liṅgas upon one who worships it on the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Vaiśākha.
By worshipping that *liṅga* of Śiva, one shall become an attendant of Śiva;
from there, O Great King, one should go to the northern bank of the Revā.
The Liṅga known as Pāpapraṇāśana bestows supreme accomplishment;
through worship, libation, and bathing, it removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
The liberation from debts and the linga that destroys sin— by these,
his debt, which arises from manifold causes, is utterly destroyed.
Because it is seen that by the offering of water with sesame seeds one is released from debt,
his ancestors remain satisfied as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure.
Now, how can those who are afflicted by impurity behold that other supreme *liṅga*, renowned throughout the three worlds, the *siddha-liṅga* in the Forest of Wood?
Having performed the bath at the confluence of the Narmadā and the Caru according to the prescribed rite,
and having bathed the Lord with water and worshipped Him with bilva leaves;
There is no returning for him from the city of Umāmāheśvara.
The *siddhaliṅga* Catuṣkeśvara, which is the size of an *āmalaka* fruit and is worshipped by both gods and demons— mortals do not behold it.
But when a most righteous son performs a *śrāddha* here,
his ancestors remain satisfied until the dissolution of all beings at the end of the kalpa.
Having reached the sacrificial mountain at Śākalya’s meritorious hermitage, which extends for ten thousand yojanas, the river Carukā flows forth.
In ancient times, Śakra performed a sacrifice there with Bṛhaspati as his domestic priest;
this place is proclaimed by all the deities as the most meritorious in the world.
Whatever fruit is obtained at Kurujāṅgala during an eclipse of the moon or sun,
that same fruit has been proclaimed by Śiva for the conjunction of the Revā and Caruka.
There, on earth, was the forest known as Dāruvana, frequented by all sixty thousand sages who were established in the ascetic practices of the Tretā age.
Subsisting on roots, tubers, and fruits, and devoted to the *agnihotra* sacrifice,
they went to the city of Brahmā through the power of this sacred ford.
Having slain Andhaka there, the Blessed Lord Śiva danced,
while all the leaders of the Gaṇas played various musical instruments.
There the Lord of Gods dances, and all the deities dance;
therefore that sin-destroying Liṅga is known as Dāruvana.
By worshipping that deity, one shall attain the status of a Gaṇapati;
there is the auspicious Vimaleśvara Liṅga, which embodies all the gods.
By bathing there, those who die go to heaven and are not subject to rebirth;
indeed, the gods and asuras have their bodies purified there.
O great king, they were all led to heaven by the wielder of the Pināka bow;
that man who gratifies the ancestors with offerings of water mixed with sesame seeds and the presentation of funeral cakes (piṇḍas) [attains the same].
He goes to the supreme abode where the god Maheśvara dwells;
when an eclipse of the moon or sun occurs, there is no limit to the merit of giving.
Having worshipped Śiva right there, one shall attain the status of a Gaṇapati;
know that the Liṅga Vimaleśvara there is Maheśvara himself.
Where the Vyāghreśvara Liṅga is located, and where the tigress ascended to heaven—
by offering water with sesame seeds, by oblations, and by the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas)— [one attains the highest goal].
A son delivers his ancestors, as well as a hundred preceding and succeeding generations;
he shall dwell in the world of Varuṇa for as long as fourteen Indras endure.
By worshipping that deity, by praising him, and even by hearing of him, one attains the world of Indra; this which I have spoken is the truth.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Cakrasvāmī," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS, Chapter 39.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
There is a Liṅga named Vyāghreśvara at the meeting point of those who create obstacles.
O highly fortunate one, that which brings liberation from all sins has been told.
"O Sage, I wish once more to know its power.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Listen, O King, to this divine story which destroys all sins."
In former times there was a most righteous king named Babhru,
a resident of Puṇḍravardhana who was devoted to truth and dharma.
When the anniversary of his father’s death arrived, the time for the śrāddha ceremony, he, being well-restrained,
performed the obligatory and occasional rites intended for his father.
Then, O Bhārata, when the time for the sacrifice had passed and he regained his composure,
that king reflected and said, "What shall I do?"
The sages are indifferent to worldly desires and subsist on bulbs, roots, and fruits;
I see no brahmin guest whom I might feel inclined to feed. (RKS 39.6)
Having intentionally thrown the cooked food into the water for the purpose of feeding the Brahmins,
the Ṛgveda then spoke these words in anger.
Now, at the end of the Dvāpara age, the arising of evil prevails;
when the Vaivasvata interval has arrived, the Brāhmaṇas have become seekers of their own desires.
While all those lustful men were consuming the king’s property along with its attendant sin, once, on an auspicious day, they went to the hermitage of Bhāradvāja in that region.
Having saluted and paid homage to the sage, Bhāradvāja stood there; having offered him a great seat, he spoke these words to him.
Welcome to you, O Great King; may it be well with you and your wife.
It has been a long time since we last saw you, O knower of Dharma; why have you come alone?
The king said:
"O Brahmin, today my welfare is secured by the sight of your lotus-feet;
O great sage, the time for the ancestral śrāddha ceremony for my forefathers has now arrived."
"You ought to act in such a way that you feed me just as you would a brahmin.
Having heard those words of his, Bhāradvāja spoke this speech:
If you are able to feed thousands of great sages who are contented, whose vital energies are drawn upward, and who are led by Haṃsa and Lomaśa; ||| RKS_39.14 |||
Thereafter, the ancestral rite proceeds; this I declare to be the truth.
One should offer a seat made of gold, and likewise offer grain and wealth.
Likewise, O lord of the people, one should give a divine cow of honey and a cow of milk,
as well as a loin-cloth for one purified by fire and a garment.
Having heard those words of Bhāradvāja, the king said to him,
"So be it," and reported everything to his wife.
Having prepared a great bull, I shall perform the ancestral rites;
the ritual acts prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, as well as the libations for the ancestors, are accomplished through this sacrificial meat.
Having reflected again and again upon such scriptural passages from the Smṛtis,
he then killed a great bull and offered libations to those ancestors.
Then Bhāradvāja and the others, perceiving that the animal was an ox,
became enraged at that deed and [cursed] both the queen and the king.
Tormented by the accumulation of their anger and uttering reproaches, they then said: "Having prepared liquor from grain, meat, and honey, and having consumed beef! (RKS 39.21)
A Brahmin shall perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance and is purified by the tying of the *mauñjī* girdle;
having consumed forbidden food, the twice-born man shall enter a fire of dried cow-dung.
Eight thousand ascetics have been slain by you;
how then can the gods accept the sacrificial offering, and likewise the ancestors?
Indeed, the sacrifices performed by you have gone to the wombs of dogs;
your asceticism has become fruitless today, for you have brought about its total destruction.
Babhru said:
"He who, having abandoned the dharma declared in the Vedas, practices another dharma,
will certainly be born in the womb of a dog for ten thousand years."
Those Brahmins who revile the meaning of the Vedas and are weak in knowledge are Śūdras in this very life; once dead, they become dogs.
The Gomedha, the Hayamedha, and likewise the Naramedha—
by these Kṣatriyas live and are honored by gods and men.
Having heard those words of the king, Bhāradvāja cursed the monarch:
"Since the Brahmins have been gratified by you with the meat of a great bull..."
"By this sin, may you become a tiger and your beloved a tigress;
for a thousand divine years, you two shall roam the earth."
Having heard those words of the sage of immeasurable splendor,
the illustrious royal consort Sudharmā spoke these words:
For my husband, who performed the rites prescribed by the Vedas, has been cursed;
likewise, I am devoted to my husband, faultless, and truly righteous.
For ten thousand years, you shall suffer from that sin;
indeed, you shall become most terrible brahmarākṣasas.
In waterless desert lands and others covered with thorns,
they were afflicted by hunger and thirst, pursued by crows and vultures.
And Bhāradvāja and the queen, having cursed one another there,
O King, Bhāradvāja then performed meritorious deeds together with them.
Then, O Bhārata, he went to the world of Brahmā along with the Brahmins;
having saluted Brahmā, the best of the gods, according to the prescribed rule, he [proceeded].
He reported everything there, including what had been prepared as food and what was not fit to be eaten.
Brahmā said:
"An action that is contrary to the world's practice should not be performed, O best of gods."
In the investigation of dharma and adharma, both what is prescribed and what is prohibited have been stated;
worldly custom has been set forth, and the path of the three Vedas has been examined.
"However, that which bestows heaven and liberation must be performed with effort.
Having been thus enlightened by Brahmā, the king then addressed the Brahmins.
"The end of their curse was declared by that very Supreme Lord;
the end of the curse for you evildoers has now been witnessed by me."
When their merit was exhausted and the transition to another age had arrived, they were cursed;
meanwhile, there was the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya, who dwelt on the banks of the Narmadā.
He will give you instruction by which you shall attain liberation;
then, after a long time, they went to the sage Mārkaṇḍeya.
By the turn of fate, they all approached the sage who dwelt on the bank of the Kalpagā; having saluted him according to custom, they prostrated before him.
Standing right there, engaged in their own work and conversing with one another,
the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya beheld them and reflected.
"A pair in the form of tigers speaking with human voices—
by what ripening of karma, O Brahmins, do they become Brahma-rākṣasas?"
Having reflected thus, Mārkaṇḍeya then spoke to Bhāradvāja:
"O Brahmins, couples who have become *brahmarākṣasas* assume the form of tigers."
"And you, being of deformed appearance, tell us how that happened.
Bhāradvāja said:
"Listen, O Brahmin, as my words are told to you in brief."
A universal monarch named Babhru, who knew the truth of past and future events, was a knower of the three times and a master of the three Vedas; he resided in Puṇḍravardhana.
His lawful wife was named Sudharmā, devoted to her husband;
once, however, at the time of a śrāddha ceremony, she did not obtain a brahmin guest.
Then, having intentionally come to my hermitage,
he took hold of my feet with his head and spoke these words.
"This is the time for the ancestral *śrāddha* rites; let favor be shown to me.
