Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O King,
learn from me the destiny of those heroes who, through fasting, by means of weapons, fire, water, or in battle, cast off their lives.
O Bhārata, their individual dwellings and their respective deeds number twenty-four crores and twenty-seven [lakhs].
In ancient times, Umā declared that those men who shall give up their lives by this rite are [destined for] middling or superior maidens.
"And eat them, for they have been granted to you by me through my great favor;
those who fall down from Amareśa after dying there shall not be cast down."
O best of kings, upon seeing the Bhṛgus, one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin;
eighty-four Bhṛgus are proclaimed to exist in Jambūdvīpa.
Likewise, seven others are specified as the supreme stairway to heaven;
however, Bhairava, the best of the Bhṛgus, is to be known at Amarakaṇṭaka.
O King, Śūdras, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and even the lowest-born outcasts likewise give up their lives, provided they avoid a twice-born man.
A Brahmin who falls there becomes a slayer of a Brahmin and a slayer of himself.
O King, when there is a conjunction of Rāhu and the Moon, one becomes a king in the city of the Vidyādharas for twenty-two thousand years.
When the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, one experiences double the fruit—
whether against one's will or under one's own control— even if struck by floods or fire.
Whoever dies having reached Bhṛgu shall become a king of the Vidyādharas;
Bhṛgu appears in the form of Bhairava, resembling the Vindhya and Kailāsa mountains.
"Those who revile Bhṛgu are destroyers of the Liṅga-Brahman;
Bhairava does not tolerate them," so it was proclaimed by Skanda.

A Brahmin who has fallen from his vows, as well as one who kills his mother, kills his father, goes after his sister, goes after his daughter-in-law, or likewise goes after his own kinswoman; RKS 46.14.
The falling of these [into the fire] is prescribed as the means of purification;
by that, one is liberated from sin and goes to the world of Śiva.
In Hariścandrapura, in Candra, at Śrīśaila, near Tripura, at Traiyambaka, at Dhautapāpa, at Vārāha, and on the Vindhya mountain; RKS 46.16.
Likewise, by falling into the pool of the Kāverī, one shall attain heaven;
and on the southern side of Bhṛgu is indeed the Capaleśvara Liṅga.
For the protection of this sacred field, it is renowned as the destroyer of sins;
therefore, the field extending sixty bow-lengths is to be known as Cāpaleśvara.
But that man who ascends the mountain without having seen him takes away all of his merit; of this there is no doubt.
And having painted the sun upon a cloth, adorned with banners and staffs,
and having placed a ring upon his hand, he should be fanned with chowries.
A hero, however, may go to fall [from a cliff] or ascend Mount Bhṛgu;
Śaṅkara has declared that for him there shall be the fruit of a sacrifice at every step.
At all times, celestial nymphs, deluded by desire, wait upon him,
mounted upon divine vehicles and adorned with divine ornaments.
But Vīra, having fallen there and abandoned his own body,
instantly possessed a divine form with prowess equal to that of Śakra.
Having mounted the vehicle that grants all desires, he shall go to the city of Śiva together with celestial nymphs, even while engaged in mutual dispute.
For one who is impotent, devoid of vigor, or who has leaped over a sacrificial pit (bhṛgu),
there is no doubt that he incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin at every step.
A mortal would not have a long life; why then does he fear death? No one is able to protect one who has fallen under the power of the appointed time of death.
That most wicked man of evil conduct, a caṇḍāla despised by the world, is he who, having undertaken renunciation and the like, falls away from it.

Upon seeing a Brahmin who has fallen from his renunciant status (saṃnyāsa), one should perform a ritual bath and gaze at the sun with every effort; it is traditionally taught that from touching such a person, one must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
One should never speak untruth even in the company of the truthful;
one should remain in silence, for otherwise one may incur sin. (RKS 46.29)
When death has been determined and has arrived, how can one remain indifferent to it?
Old age, death, and diseases are the surging waves of the ocean of saṃsāra.
Knowing this, O best of kings, one should indeed ascend Mount Bhṛgu.
Thus, O King, has this supreme majesty of Bhṛgu been told to you.
In the Kali age, one should not speak to those of wicked intellect who perform heretical acts,
especially to the Digambaras, the Śvetapaṭas, the Buddhists, and others.
Those of evil conduct who revile the ancient Smṛtis are not to be spoken with;
indeed, one should never engage in conversation with them.
The bull-bannered god himself spoke thus to each of all the gods:
"Those fools who do not believe in the King of Tīrthas proclaimed by me [shall suffer]."
Those who descend from Bhṛgu go to a terrible hell.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Bhṛgupati Mountain," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS Chapter 47.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
The chanting of the syllable Om, the giving of gifts to Brahmins, sacrifice, and likewise austerity—
The origin of the five-faced [deities] and likewise the origin of the lingas.
O great sage, please graciously recount the number of the ages (yugas), as well as their divisions (kalās) and the history [of each],
exactly as it was taught by Śambhu.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen, O king of kings, to this ancient account proclaimed by Skanda,
consisting of eighteen lakhs and thirty-two thousand verses.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, this is the calculation for the Kṛta Yuga, including the measures of its dawn (saṃdhyā) and twilight (saṃdhyāṃśa): eight hundred thousand and likewise eight thousand years.
In the Dvāpara age, they desire the measurement of the day to be equal to the measure of the morning and evening twilights;
[the day consists of] four hundred thousand and four thousand [years].
This is the measure of pride during the twilight and the sub-twilight periods of the Kali Yuga:
cows yield little milk, and the earth yields little grain.
Likewise, the clouds contain little water, and the twice-born possess meager learning;
yet at the completion of their sixteenth year, men have the grey hair of old age even in their youth.
In the tenth or twelfth year, a woman shall become pregnant;
in the Kali age, Śūdras will be constantly devoted to dharma, and people will go about naked.
All subjects will be of a single caste, and the king will be a barbarian (mleccha),
when the Kali age has arrived in its form as Mādhava.
There is no Agnihotra sacrifice, nor the Vedas, nor dharma, nor officiating at sacrifices;
there is no truth, no austerity, no charity, no goodness, and no deities.
Brahmins who sell the Vedas will, in every house of the outcastes,
carry out the instructions of the Vedas, acting as bringers of ruin to the Vedas.
For those who sell their daughters and those who live off their daughters,
not even a thousandth part, nor even a single fraction, of righteousness is produced.
Wherever he attains perfection, there shall be a sacred ford where men will bathe in the water;
moreover, Śūdra women shall become the wives of the twice-born in every household.
In the Kali age, men will exist in a state of inversion, with the low becoming high;
there will be Buddhists, Kṣapaṇakas, and sinful men who are naked, filthy, and defiled.
Deluded by evil karma, they mock the ignorant;
the disciple does not respect his teacher, nor does the son likewise respect his father.
Those who steal the property of their own lineage, those who wear the robes of renunciation,
those who live off their religious emblems, as well as the wicked who subsist on ashes— these are [to be avoided].
When the Vaivasvata interval has arrived and the Kali age begins, all this shall come to pass.
O King, I have thus told you everything that will occur during the Kali age.
O sinless one, I shall explain in brief the origin of the syllable *oṃ* and its ritual application according to the prescribed rules, as I have been asked by you.
By chanting the name of this deity, one is released from the bondage of worldly existence;
O King, by uttering and constantly recollecting the single syllable "Oṃ."
He who departs, casting off the body, attains the supreme goal;
likewise, Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas, originates from the syllable Om.
Within the single-syllabled reality of *oṃ*, there reside Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara;
the syllable *oṃ* is indeed the root of the Vedas, established upon the branches of the Śrutis.
The fruit, the flower, the leaves, the Smṛti, and the Āgama—
just as the syllable Oṃ is recited at the beginning of all branches of knowledge.
Likewise, at the beginning, Maheśvara, the primordial god of all gods,
is proclaimed as the three junctions (saṃdhyā) and the three times within the syllable Oṃ.
The triad of fires, the three worlds, and the threefold set of goals are established there;
and sixty-eight sacred fords were proclaimed by Śiva to Brahmā.
And one hundred Rudras are proclaimed to be complete with one [additional];
at Kedāra there is one hundred, and at Oṃkāra there is one hundred plus one.

The five Brahmās, the five-faced one, the syllable Oṃ, and the supreme Liṅga—whatever Liṅgas exist upon the earth within the range extending to the edge of the oceans; [all these are contained therein].
O Yudhiṣṭhira, when the Svāyambhuva interval had arrived and the Kṛta Yuga of the first kalpa had begun, those [beings] abandoned their five faces and adopted the syllable Oṃ.
Defeated by the Dānavas, the gods took refuge on the banks of the Narmadā;
they were pursued by the Kaṅkolakas, the Kālikeyas, and the Kālakas.
Those gods, together with Brahmā, went for refuge to the Lord;
then, O Bhārata, Bṛhaspati spoke to Brahmā.
"Perform a most fierce sacrifice that will bring about the destruction of the Dānavas.
Thus Brahmā then spoke these words to that counselor of the gods.
"Indeed, my mantras have been forgotten due to the fear of the Dānavas.
In that interval, having pierced through the seven netherworlds (pātālas), [he emerged].
O King, preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and proclaiming *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*,
[he beheld] the Liṅga that had arisen from the mountain, blazing with the splendor of the fire of cosmic destruction.
Resplendent like ten million suns and enveloped in garlands of flames,
that supreme reality— devoid of beginning, middle, or end— is not seen anywhere.
Śambhu himself, together with the four classes, the four Vedas, and the Vedāṅgas and the scriptures, spoke these words to Brahmā, the creator of the worlds:
"O Brahmin, perform the sacrifice as you desire, for I have bestowed upon you the Vedas, which are gentle and bring peace to the worlds."
Then Brahmā performed a fierce sacrifice that brought about the destruction of the Daityas,
and he also performed a gentle sacrifice that brought peace to the worlds.
Then, O Great King, having seen that terrifying display, the asuras,
agitated by the fear of Brahmā’s curse, fled in the ten directions.
By the power of the syllable Oṃ, all the gods became fearless;
then, having worshipped the Lord of the Gods, those deities departed for the third heaven.
O King, know that the great *liṅga* which endures until the end of the eon, which is worshipped by gods and asuras, and which bestows both desires and liberation, is indeed the syllable *Oṃ*.
At the end of the eon, all the deities dissolve into that *liṅga*;
they call it the immortal Brahman, as well as Hari and Siddheśvara.
There is the Sun-god Piṅgaleśvara, as well as Soma and Pitṛīśvara;
there the three Vedas, together with the six auxiliary limbs and the Pada and Krama recitations, attained perfection.
Know that Siddheśvara, situated on the summit of the mountain and accompanied by ten million lingas, bestows all spiritual accomplishments; thus it has been described.
By worshipping that *liṅga*, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu;
for in every *kalpa*, O Great King, all other deities perish.
O King, having excluded the five liṅgas— Mārkaṇḍa, Nārmada, Avimukta, Kedāra, and Oṃkāra-Amareśvara— RKS_47.44.
And likewise, O Bhārata, he who rises at dawn and recites these five meritorious *liṅgas*, beginning with Mahākāla, shall attain great merit.
Having obtained the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas), one is glorified in the world of Śiva;
indeed, the one Kālī always dwells pervasively in Mahākāla.
O King, one hundred and twenty-five million sacred fords reside at Mahākāla;
O King, the Kāverī stands within the realm of Śiva as a field of Śiva.
Within a distance of four *krośas*, the sin of killing a Brahmin does not spread;
and on its bank rests the *Siddhaliṅga* of Agni.
O descendant of Kuru, at the sacred ford known as Śivakhyāta,
a man who merely bathes there shall not be born again.
Insects, birds, moths, and others born of the animal realm— even humans—
are liberated from sin there, according to the word of Śiva.
In that regard, if one performs a śrāddha for the ancestors with water and sesame seeds,
those ancestors remain unsatisfied for thousands of millions of yugas.
Among all sacred emblems (liṅgas), the divine one is proclaimed here as supreme;
having bathed there, one goes to heaven and shall not enter again the confinement of a womb.
Having obtained the fruit of ten million sacrifices, one is glorified in the world of Śiva;
O King, it is said that there are eighty million sacred fords at Kedāra.
For men, the fruit of liberation comes from seeing, worshipping, or touching him;
when the water of Kedāra has been drunk, rebirth no longer exists.
For one who, having fasted for a day and night, drinks only milk while observing celibacy,
a linga shall appear in his abdomen within six months.
Merely by beholding Kedāra, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Vārāṇasī is greatly meritorious and renowned throughout the three worlds.
That city is indeed in the intermediate space, outside the world of mortals;
it extends for five krośas, within which distance the sin of Brahman-murder does not spread.
O descendant of Bharata, there are twenty-eight crores of lingas there;
having performed one's ablutions as prescribed between the Gaṅgā and the Varuṇā, [one attains the fruit].
Completely liberated from all evil, that man who gives up his life there while meditating upon Śiva rejoices in heaven like a god.
Having uplifted a thousand lineages, he goes to the world of Śiva;
there, no measure can be found for the gift that is given.
By the offering of sesame-water, there is inexhaustible satisfaction for the ancestors;
whoever abandons their life there, whether against their will or by their own choice, [attains that state].
One shall become a three-eyed attendant of Śiva, bearing a trident in hand;
through the touch of the Avimukta Liṅga, liberation is attained.
Indeed, three parts (kalās) reside there in the city of Kāśī, without a doubt;
at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, four parts are traditionally taught.
Where the Gaṅgā, with its thousand mouths, enters the ocean—by bathing and immersing oneself there, by drinking the water, by offering funeral cakes, and by performing libations; RKS_47.64 //
There, that man shall go to the city of Śiva together with his ancestors;
[and he shall see] another, Kālarudra, who dwells in the seven netherworlds.
Know that god to be Hāṭaka; yet mortals do not perceive him.
He is worshipped by gods and daityas, and is attended by the celestial siddhas.
The second is Gaṅgeśvara, the third is Sāgareśvara, and the fourth is Śūlapāṇi; these are the four Kalās.
One should worship Rudra, who consists of five parts, within the range extending to the edge of the ocean,
with the exception of Maheśāna, Oṃkāra, and Kāmarūpin.
Oṃkāra, which possesses five faces and five Brahmās and is endowed with the nine Śaktis,
was formerly taught by Śiva on the shore of Kalpagā.
In that world consisting of merit, one should worship the western face, which is adored by the three worlds and resembles a conch, a kunda flower, or the moon.
From which the Ṛgveda emerged, Brahmā is the presiding deity there;
to the north is Vāmadeva, yellow-hued and most enchanting.
Know that it originates from the Yajurveda; Viṣṇu is its presiding deity.
Aghora, who has the luster of the color of clouds, is situated in the southern direction.
Know that which originates from the Sāmaveda to have the Sun, Time, and Fire as its deities;
it should be known as Tatpuruṣa, located in the east, and resembling the color of saffron.
The Atharvaveda has emerged as the fourth; the waters are its presiding deities (adhidevatās);
Īśāna is your face, which is five-colored and possesses a great body.
There, the presiding deity is Soma, whose music is the established doctrine of the Vedas;
he is the sixth, named Sadāśiva, partless and free from affliction.
Having known that which is without characteristics and devoid of marks, there is no doubt regarding liberation.
This description of the syllable Oṃ has been told to you, O King.
If we do not have the power for even a thousand [repetitions], what need is there to mention a single recitation?
One should worship by bathing [the deity] with water alone and with a *bilva* leaf.
He who gives up his life at the Oṃkāra-Dakṣiṇāmūrti is honored in the world of Rudra for four thousand years.
One shall dwell in the city of Maheśvara for thousands of millions of years;
moreover, one shall have a palace and a monastery constructed with plaster and bricks.
At the base of the painting, it should be adorned with banners and flags,
provided with a canopy and small bells, and possess an auspicious bamboo frame.
One should cause the syllable Oṃ to be adorned with the richness of five colors;
having bathed it with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), one should anoint it with sandalwood, agallochum, and saffron.
Having wrapped [the image] with various beautiful lower garments and cloths,
one should burn guggulu resin mixed with clarified butter, along with gold, pearls, and gems.
The bell and the lamp, as well as the smokeless *ārārtika* offering,
the mṛdaṅgas and the paṭahas, the flute, the lute, and the singing.
The kāhalī, conch-trumpets, and likewise the bronze cymbals and so forth;
the fan, the ball, the parasol, the fly-whisk, and the banner-staff.
O best of kings, one should offer gold, food, clothing, and so forth, as well as houses, villages, and towns— whatever it may be— to Oṃkāra.
The merit of that gift cannot be calculated here,
even when the moon or sun is eclipsed by Rāhu at the two Siddheśvara and Oṃkāra shrines.
One should cause it to be filled with garlands of banners; hear now the fruit of its merit:
as many times as that [garland] is shaken by the wind, [so many merits shall one obtain].
O King, he shall dwell in the world of Śiva for thousands of yugas,
for thousands of crores of yugas, and for hundreds of crores of yugas.
One whose self is fulfilled in all desires resides in the abode of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
O King, this characteristic of the origin of the syllable Om has been told to you.
Now listen to the hymn of praise composed for him by Brahmā.
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Oṃkāra," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS, Chapter 48.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O sinless one, the mantra was then told to Brahmā by means of the syllable Om.
Brahmā too, having heard those words, recited this hymn of praise.
Oṃ, to the one reckoned as the number of space, the destroyer of space, the all-pervading,
the infinite, the protectorless, the immortal, and the eternal.
To Śambhu, the eternal one, who is established upon the seat of yoga,
the perpetual practitioner of yoga, the destroyer of the sky.
Oṃ, homage to Śiva, the source of all, to Śiva, to Īśāna.
Salutations again and again to the Head, to Tatpuruṣa, to the Face, to Aghora, to the Heart, to Vāsudeva, to the Secret One, to Sadyojāta, to the Embodiment, and to Oṃkāra.
Beyond time, immutable, the Buddha, who crushes the vajra-body;
the presiding lord, the moon, the Teacher, the wielder of the Pināka bow, the sovereign of the thirty gods;
Agni, Rudra, the consumer of oblations, Piṅgala, the purifier, and Hara.

He is the blazing one, the burner, the substantial entity, and that which ends in ashes; he is the end of the earth, the remover of untimely death, the sustainer, the ordainer, and he who is designated as the agent.
Kāla, Dharmapati, Śāstṛ, Viyoktṛ, Navama, Priya,
Nirmita, Vāruṇa, Hantṛ, Krūradṛṣṭi, and Bhayāvaha.
Ūrdhvadṛṣṭi, Virūpākṣa, Daṃṣṭrāvat, Dhūmralocana,
Bāla, Atibala, and the mighty Pāśahasta.
Śveta, Virūpa, Rudra, Dīrghabāhu, Jaḍāntaka,
Śīghra, Laghu, Vāyuvega, Bhīma, and Vaḍavāmukha.
He has five heads and matted locks; he is subtle, sharp, and the ender of the night.
He is the lord of treasures, possessed of ferocity, the wielder of the bow, gentle-bodied, and the crusher of foes.
Anantapālaka, Dhāra, Pātāleśa, Vṛṣadhvaja,
Sadhūmra, Śāśvata, Śarva, Sarvapiṅga, and Karālavat.
Viṣṇu, Īśa, Mahātman, Sukha, the one freed from death,
Śambhu, Vibhu, Gaṇādhyakṣa, Tryakṣa, and Divaspati.
Dialogue and dispute are powerful and increasing;
they are recorded as numbering one hundred and one Rudras in total.
Having thus composed a hymn of one hundred and one verses, Brahmā established them all within the syllable Oṃ for Maheśvara, the God of gods.
Having prostrated on the ground with all eight limbs and performed a circumambulation,
the Grandfather of the Worlds stood there, mentally recollecting the God.
O Bhārata, having heard that hair-raising hymn of praise from Brahmā,
the God of gods spoke these words to Brahmā.
"Delighted by this divine hymn of praise, I grant you a boon; choose one, for I shall give it to you without doubt—even that which is difficult to attain even for the gods."
Brahmā said: "O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to me,
let there be here a sacrifice in five faces under the name of Brahmā."
Hara said:
"So be it, O Brahmin; this which you have spoken is indeed true.
From that time forward, O Bhārata, the worship of Brahmā has been established as a duty."
Brahmā said: Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, with their minds always fixed upon you, shall recite this fierce hymn of Oṃkāra before you.
They shall obtain every desire, both in this world and in the next;
whatever desire a person longs for, that very thing he shall attain.
"By constantly reciting it one hundred and one times, one shall go to heaven.
Having spoken thus, Brahmā then paid homage to Maheśvara.
Mounted upon the divine vehicle, he went joyfully to the world of Brahmā.
A period of four thousand yugas is proclaimed to be one day of Brahmā.
Indeed, by this very measure Brahmā lives for a hundred years;
the lifespan of Viṣṇu is ordained as a hundred times that of the Grandfather (Brahmā).
In half the blink of an eye of the syllable Oṃ, fourteen thousand and countless grandfathers (Brahmās) perish in the supreme realm of Viṣṇu.
Having thus known the state of Brahman, one should always worship Śiva within;
since the command of Śiva resides in the *liṅga*, therefore one should always worship the *liṅga*.
But he who, out of delusion, hates the *liṅga* which is worshipped by all the gods, goes to a terrible hell; such is the word of Śiva.
The Buddhist mendicants and heretics, who are experts in false doctrines,
have perished and been destroyed because they were devoid of the worship of Śiva.
Due to practice throughout many successive births, they go to the netherworld (rasātala);
therefore, having fought according to the Purāṇas, one should practice the dharma taught by Śiva.
But he who, being wicked and evil-minded, practices another dharma—
this ancient account, O King, proclaimed by Skanda, has been told to you.
By hearing and chanting this, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Hymn Consisting of the Five Brahmas," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS, Chapter 49.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O highly fortunate one, one should go to the confluence of the Revā and the Kapilā.
Having bathed there, those who die go to heaven and are not subject to rebirth.
By the offering of sesame-water, the ancestors attain the supreme goal during the nine and a half days when the moon is eclipsed by Rāhu.
O Great King, there is no doubt that one’s merit increases through this increase;
however, when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, it lasts for exactly ten days.
O lord of the people, in the same way, the distinction of Kapilā increases at the confluence of the Revā with the Kapilā and at the meeting with Vārāṇasī.
The fruit is declared to be equal even by means of water with sesame seeds;
the Revā at the confluence of the Kapilā is equal to Vārāṇasī.
When the Svāyambhuva interval (antara) arrived, those born from the boons granted by Brahmā [established] Rudrāvarta,
Brahmāvarta, and likewise Sūryāvarta.
Furthermore, these three should be known to exist at the confluence of the Kapilā and the Narmadā,
where the Narmadā is split apart to a measurement of four cubits.
O King, it is remembered that there is a pair of whirlpools at the confluence of the Revā and Kapilā;
there flows the Pippalāvāhinī, which dwells in the seven netherworlds.
In that very place are Kapilāvarta and Pippalāvarta;
indeed, the ancestors desire this holy ford which bestows satisfaction.
Therefore, a son should with effort, according to the prescribed rule, offer to his ancestors a handful of water mixed with sesame seeds, and he should also diligently offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa).
A person who, having bathed while pure at the confluence of the Revā and Kapilā, performs a śrāddha ceremony, shall deliver his ancestors from terrible suffering.
Whoever should behold an immortal there, his merit is equal to that of an Aśvamedha sacrifice,
especially during an eclipse of the moon or sun and at other auspicious times.
One should provide incense, smoke, food offerings, and rows of lamps;
whoever performs the worship of the Liṅga with offerings mixed with sesame seeds and rice, [attains great merit].
Having anointed [the image] with saffron, one should clothe it in red garments;
likewise, one should perform worship with flower garlands and with gold, jewels, and so forth.
As long as the moon and the sun, the Himavat mountain, and the great ocean endure,
for that many thousands of yugas shall he be honored in the world of Rudra.
One should increase the silk, the woven thread, the cotton, and the red-dyed cloth,
as well as the Vaijayantī canopy above the water-pot.
O Bhārata, endowed with the five jewels and accompanied by the sound of tinkling bells, [the drum] should be beaten for as many moments as there are threads [in its cord].
For that duration of time, one shall dwell in heaven in the city of Umāmaheśvara;
for Īśāna and the other [faces] as well, it has been stated previously that they are equal.

by the gift of gold and jewels, they go adorned with gems.
One whose self is enriched with all desires goes [to that realm] by the gift of land;
by the gift of food and drink, one goes while drinking and eating.
By means of such gifts as these, they go happily to the abode of Śiva;
and by the gift of food, one obtains vast enjoyments in heaven.
Among all gifts, they know the gift of food to be supreme;
it is a merit that brings joy to all and increases strength and nourishment.
The gift equal to the gift of food is renowned throughout the three worlds;
the gift equal to the gift of food is renowned throughout the three worlds.
From food all beings come into existence, and they die for lack of it.
Blood, flesh, marrow, and semen arise in succession from food;
from semen beings are born; therefore, the world consists of food.
There is no happiness equal to food, whether it be gold, jewels, horses, lordly elephants, women, garlands, sandalwood, or other such things; there is no enemy equal to anger.
For this very reason, O Bhārata, the gift of food is of great merit; the giver of food is said to be the giver of life. Therefore, one should become a giver of food.
Therefore, by the gift of food, all other gifts in the three worlds— whether they be objects of enjoyment, women, or vehicles— are as good as given.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, whatever food, drink, and so forth, as well as any kind of sovereignty,
is recorded as the fruit of the gift of food, both in this world and the next.
For it is by means of food that one whose limbs are nourished performs the accumulation of dharma—
[food which is] pure, immortal, divine, stainless, a living essence, and an elixir.
Food and drink, horses, calves, beds, umbrellas, and sandals—
these eight gifts, O Yudhiṣṭhira, are praised in the world of the departed spirits.
In this way, by means of specific acts of giving, men go with ease to the city of the King of Dharma; therefore, one should practice righteousness.
O Great King, one who is self-restrained should offer abundant food and water to the ancestors at the sacred ford of Amareśvara.
Those holy fords and sacred fields which have indeed been proclaimed here as bestowers of desire and liberation, and as granters of all perfections;
Indeed, Narmadā is proclaimed as the mother of all of them; she is the best of rivers, auspicious, and flowing through seven kalpas.
"The number of austerities, sacrifices, and gifts found at sacred fords is known;
however, there is no such count for them on the Narmadā—so said Śaṅkara."
Just as Śiva, so too should Revā be worshipped with great effort;
yet those among these who are of evil deeds, sinful, and devoid of charity— RKS_52.24.
By that terrible path to the south they go to the abode of Yama,
which extends for eighty-six thousand yojanas all around.
The city should be known as Mahāraudra, presided over by various forms;
it appears as if standing close at hand to men of cruel deeds.
Even for sinners, they travel by a fierce path situated far away,
one filled with sharp thorns and strewn with gravel.
Some, moreover, are struck by this great [mountain] composed of sharp stones covered with razor-edges,
and by felling trees that serve as executioners.
In some places he was seized by fierce iron needles,
and in others by mountains rugged with spreading creepers and thick with trees.
Afflicted with suffering, they travel along paths strewn with glowing coals,
and in some places with pits of poison, as well as with heated clods of earth and bricks.
And with sands heated by intense fire, as well as with sharp spikes,
it was covered here and there with many broken branches.
Indeed, some go to the abode of Yama with great hardship through darkness,
seized by glowing embers situated along the path as well as by forest fires.
In some places it was covered with heated stones and mud knee-deep;
in other places it was filled with foul water and, in yet others, with the fire of wicked chaff.
In some places there are vultures, cranes, tigers, and most dreadful wicked insects;
in some places there are great crabs and the like, and in others again there are pythons.
In some places there were fierce flies, in others serpents with virulent venom,
and on all sides were herds of rutting elephants, causing havoc.
And by lions with sharp horns and great strength that were tracing their paths, by fierce rhinoceroses, and by intoxicated beasts of prey; RKS_52.36 //
And by fierce ḍākinīs, by terrifying rākṣasas,
by most dreadful diseases, and by unassailable fires.
Shattered by a great and fierce wind mixed with massive flames,
they are left without support amidst a rain of great rocks.
Indeed, in some places they move along, scorched and blazing,
while being pierced on all sides by a great rain of arrows.
Being struck by falling masses of thunderbolts, by terrible falls of meteors,
and by a rain of blazing coals, they indeed proceed [to their doom].
Terrified again and again by the terrible and most horrific sounds,
they were overwhelmed on all sides by a rain of sharpened weapons.
Being drenched again and again by great torrents of nectar, as well as by a fierce, great cold, and by [instruments] such as razor edges; RKS 52.42.
In many other ways, by the hundreds and thousands,
and thus by a path that is both harsh and treacherous, they are tormented.
For it was by one who did not rest, O Bhārata, by one who was not far away,
yet by one who was close at hand through hardship and the locus of all suffering.
All embodied beings who are deluded and devoted to sin are forcibly led away by the most terrible messengers of Yama, who carry out Yama’s commands.
Solitary, dependent on others, and deprived of friends and kinsmen,
they grieve over their own deeds and are burned again and again.
Intermingled with hungry ghosts (pretas) and spirits (bhūtas), their throats, lips, and palates were parched;
their limbs were emaciated, they were terrified beyond measure, and they were being scorched by a blazing fire.
Some sinners, bound with chains and sinking deeply,
are dragged along while being intensely scorched by the exceedingly powerful messengers of Yama.
Likewise, the sinners, remaining with their faces turned downward upon their chests and bound by their masses of hair, are dragged along in great suffering.
Having pierced the foreheads of embodied beings with swift arrows, they are dragged somewhere; by means of their evil deeds, they are led along a wicked path while lying face upward.
With their sides and arms bound together and their bellies crushed,
some, dragged by nooses around their necks, go forth in extreme misery.
By means of the "tongue-spike" (jihvāśaṅku) [grasp], having brought the nape of the neck together,
they are seized with the "half-moon" (ardhacandra) as they are being thrown here and there.
Furthermore, others were bound with ropes to their penises and testicles;
some had their hands and feet cut off, and others had their ears, lips, and noses severed.
With their penises and testicles severed, with their heads cut off and their limbs scattered in heaps,
they are pierced by goads and devoured by crawling reptiles.
They run hither and thither, wailing and without refuge,
being struck again and again with mallets and iron clubs.
And on all sides they are struck with various kinds of terrible whips and javelins, vomiting blood repeatedly.
And being cast into the water, they indeed long for shade;
thus do men who have failed to practice charity pass away, even if they have performed penance.
And having taken provisions for the journey, one goes happily to the abode of Yama;
in this way, by such a lowly path, men reach the city of Yama.
Thus, by the messengers sent forth, they are ushered into the presence of Yama;
there, Yama indeed causes those who have performed virtuous deeds to remember them.
"By welcoming you with seats, by offering water for the feet and the respectful arghya, and by your kind words,
you are blessed, O great-souled ones, who act for your own welfare."
But by you who have indeed performed meritorious deeds for the sake of divine happiness, having resorted to the bank of the Narmadā on Mount Amarakaṇṭaka; RKS_52.61.
Gifts have been given, austerities performed, and oblations offered according to the prescribed rites at Vārāṇasī, Kurukṣetra, Prayāga, and likewise at Puṣkara.
At Gayā, in the Naimiṣa forest, at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean,
at Kedāra, at Bhṛgu, and also at Prabhāsa, O Moon-adorned One;
In the delightful Mahākālavana, at Śrīśaila, Tripurāntaka,
Traiyambaka, Dhautapāpa, and likewise at Nīlakaṇṭha;
At Gaṅgādvāra, at Himadvāra, and likewise on Mount Kālañjara—
at these and other sacred fords (tīrtha) and holy fields (kṣetra)— in due order.
The fruit of birth has indeed been attained by you; of this there is no doubt.
Ascend this celestial chariot, adorned with the enjoyments of divine women.
"Go together to auspicious heaven, endowed with all desires;
having enjoyed there great pleasures in accordance with the measure of your merit."
Whatever other slight impurity there may be, even that you shall consume;
this much, however, has been told by me, O dwellers on the banks of the Kalpagā.
They ascend the celestial chariots, standing above all others;
for it was said by Brahmā and the other gods in the past that there is indeed a limit to the number of all holy bathing places.
In that place, whatever gift is given, by that one is glorified in heaven;
and whoever dies there, whether by means of a vow or by fasting, [attains the same].
Relying upon the divine vehicle, he proceeds to the abode of Śiva.
This supreme merit of the Kalpagā, O King, has been recounted to you.
Those of meritorious deeds behold Yama as if he were their own friend;
however, those of cruel deeds behold him as terrifying.
With a face made terrifying by fangs, eyes crooked with a frown,
hair standing on end, a great beard, and his upper and lower lips quivering.
Eighteen-armed and fierce, resembling a mass of black collyrium,
with all his hands raised holding weapons, he roared, staff in hand.
Mounted upon a great buffalo, with eyes like blazing fire,
wearing red garlands and garments, he stands tall like Mount Meru.
With a roar like the clouds at the time of universal dissolution, as if drinking up the oceans,
swallowing the three worlds, and vomiting forth fire.
Death stands near him, possessing a radiance like the fire of time;
Time is like the color of collyrium, and the Ender (Kṛtānta) is terrifying.
Various diseases, sharp, of many forms, and terrifying,
[appear] bearing spears, tridents, and hooks, with nooses, wheels, and swords in their hands.
Bearing adamantine fangs, fierce and cruel, resembling collyrium in color,
with hands raised holding all manner of weapons, they are the messengers of Yama and the slayers.
Those who have committed evil deeds see Yama there in such a form;
yet Yama approaches the evildoer with extreme fearlessness.
And the venerable Citragupta, awakening them to the Dharma, said:
"O you of evil deeds, you who have stolen the property of others!"
Those who roar with pride on account of their beauty and valor, and who violate the wives of others—
whatever action one performs, that very thing is experienced by him again.
Why then have you committed this evil deed for the sake of self-destruction?
For what purpose do you grieve while being tormented by your own actions?
They experience their own karmas; there is no fault here belonging to anyone.
And these protectors of the earth have arrived, O lord of the earth.
"O kings of evil conduct, destroyers of your subjects, who are arrogant in the power of their own wicked wisdom due to their terrible deeds!"
What indeed was that evil deed committed by you— driven by greed for the kingdom, by delusion, and by unrighteous conduct— for the sake of this very brief sovereignty?
Enjoy exactly as it is the fruit that has been gathered;
where is the kingdom or the wife for whose sake this evil was committed?
Having abandoned all your possessions, you shall likewise remain alone;
for your kinsmen do not see that by which the subjects have been destroyed.
"What will it be like now, as you are being cast down by the messengers of Yama?
Thus were they addressed by Yama with many such words.
"O King, they silently grieve over their own deeds"—
having thus instructed those kings with these words, the Lord of Dharma then [departed].
Then, for the sake of purifying their sins, Yama spoke to his messengers:
"O you, Caṇḍa and Mahācaṇḍa, seize these kings!"
"Purify yourselves from sins gradually by means of the fires of hell;
then, having quickly taken your stand and grasped the kings by their feet,"
Having whirled him around with great force, all the servants of Yama hurled him with immense speed onto the intensely heated surface of the earth.
They struck a great tree made of solid stone;
then they were all quickly shattered by those blows.
At that time, O Yudhiṣṭhira, they were unconscious and motionless;
then, touched by the wind, they gradually returned to life once more.
Having brought them forth for the sake of purification, they cast them into the ocean of hell;
there are twenty-eight primary and intense millions of hells.
At the end of the seventh level, they abide in terrible darkness;
there dwell the Atighorā, the Raudrā, and likewise the Ghoratamā.
The fifth is of terrible form and the producer of extreme suffering;
the sixth is named Taraṇatārā, and the seventh is Bhayānakā.
The eighth is Kālarātri, the ninth is Ghaṭotkaṭā,
the tenth is Caṇḍā, and Mahācaṇḍā is even below that.
Caṇḍakolāhalā, Pracaṇḍā, Parāgnikā,
Jaghanyā, Avarā, Lomā, and the leader Bhīṣaṇī.
Karālā and Vikarālā are supported by twenty vajras;
Astā is five-cornered, while Sudīrghā is perfectly circular.
The sevenfold and eightfold [hells], as well as Dīrgha, Māyā, and Itihā—
thus have those ten million terrible hells been described by name.
These are recorded as twenty-eight according to the measurement of the elements;
of these, it should be understood that there are five leaders for each in successive order.
O Lord of the People, although there are millions of such hells individually by name,
Raurava is the first among them, where embodied beings wail.
Indeed, even the great ones weep due to the torments of Mahāraurava;
these five are known as the leaders: Darkness, Cold, and likewise Heat.
Aghora, Prathama, Tīkṣṇa, Padma, Saṃjīvana, Śaṭha, Mahāmāya, Viloma, Kaṇṭaka, and Kaṭaka are recorded [as the names of the faces].
Tīvra, Vāma, Karāla, Kiṅkarāla, Prakampana,
Mahācakra, Supadma, Kālasūtra, and Pragharjana.
Sūcīmukha, Sunemi, Khādaka, Suprapīḍita,
Kumbhīpāka, Supāka, and the most dreadful Krakaca.
Aṅgārarātri, Pacana, Asṛkpūyabhava,
Sutīkṣṇa, Śaṇḍaśakuni, Mahāsaṃvartaka, and Kratu.
The Taptajantu, Paṅkalepa, Pūtimat, Hradasrapu, Ucchvāsa, Nirucchvāsa, Sudīrgha, and Krūraśālmalī.
Uṣṭrita, Mahānāda, Pravāha,
Supravāhana, Vṛṣāśraya, Vṛṣāśva, and those with the faces of a lion, a tiger, and an elephant.
With the faces of dogs, pigs, lions, buffaloes, rams, mice,
and donkeys, and with the mouths of crocodiles, pot-demons, and sea-monsters, they were most terrible and fearsome.
They are all-eaters and eaters of their own kind; they perform every kind of action like horses and crows;
they are vultures, owls, leopards, and monkeys.
Gaṇḍaka, Pūtivaktra, Raktāsya, Pūtimūtrika,
Kaṇadhūmra, Tuṣārāgni, Kṛmimat, and likewise Niraya.
Ātodya, Pratodya, Rudhirodya, Bhojana,
Kālātmaga, Anubhakṣa, and the most terrible Sarvabhakṣa.
Karkaṭa, Viśāla, Vikaṭa, Kaṭapūtana, Ambarīṣa, and Kaṭāha; and the terrible river Vaitaraṇī.
There is the heated iron spike, Ekapāda, Aśrupūraṇa,
the terrible Asipatravana forest, and the one established as Asthiliṅga.
The sesame and linseed oil-presses, which crush fraudulent sinners;
the great furnace and the side-furnace; and the slab made of heated iron.
The mountain called Kṣuradhārā (Razor-Edge), Maya, the Yamalaparvata (Twin Mountains),
Sūcī (Needle), Viṣṭhā (Excrement), Andhakūpa (Blind Well), Patana (Falling), and likewise Pātana (Causing to Fall).
Muśalī, Vṛṣalī, Aśivā, Saṅkaṭalā, Tālapatrā, Asigahana, and Mahāmohaka as well.
Saṃmohana, Asthibhaṅga, Taptācala, Māya, Aguṇa,
Bahuduḥkha, Mahāduḥkha, Kaśmala, and likewise Yamala.
Hālāhala, Virūpa, Śvarūpa, Cyutamānasa,
Ekapāda, Tripāda, Tīvra, and then Vidita.
These twenty-eight are traditionally taught as five groups in sequence.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Hell," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS, Chapter 53.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
There were ten crores [of attendants] corresponding to their names, and five leaders for each.
It is recorded that there are one hundred hells, beginning with Raurava and ending with Marīci.
The mandala of the great hells exceeds forty [yojanas];
men experience them one by one, in accordance with their karma.
Then, due to the rapid accumulation of unwholesome karma, men are bound by hideous desires with a well-concealed chain of burning darkness.
They are suspended from the branch of a great tree by the servants of Yama;
then those servants indeed swing them back and forth on all sides.
And being violently shaken by excessive speed, the sinners fall unconscious;
and for those situated in the intermediate space, there is then the weight of a hundred loads of iron.
Their feet are bound by the exceedingly powerful messengers of Yama;
by that great weight, those men are intensely tormented.
They contemplate their own past deeds and remain silent and motionless;
then, they are struck in succession with iron rods the color of fire, covered in thorns.
Then they are struck forcefully on the head by the messengers of Yama and cast into a pit filled with excrement, which is an abode of worms.
The evildoers are cooked on all sides by terrible servants,
and then especially with alkaline water and fire.
They are cooked like eggplants in a heated iron cauldron,
after being cast into a pit of impurity teeming with aquatic creatures.
Once they have been thrown into that pond filled with fat,
blood, and pus, they are devoured by sharp worms and by crows with iron beaks.
Furthermore, men endowed with evil deeds are roasted like meat upon heaps of blazing coals, and they are impaled upon sharp stakes.
Those sinners are indeed cooked in many ways by the messengers of Yama in cauldrons filled with oil that have been thoroughly heated, and then once again.
And the tongues of those who speak pleasant words that are untrue are torn out;
they are then violently crushed from the feet upward against the chest with a very firm and red-hot [iron].
Likewise, even a twice-born man who is devoted to false scriptures is prodded with sharp arrows into the vast treasury intended for sacrifice.
Those fools who revile their mother and father—
their mouths are repeatedly filled with sand and then doused with it.
Then, its mouth is repeatedly and excessively filled with blazing alkaline liquid and molten, heated oil.
Tormented by soldiers who, like dogs, have feet covered in excrement full of worms,
they enter the iron *śālmalī* tree with their tusks.
Furthermore, they are struck upon their backs by terrifying and exceedingly powerful beings with a very sharp,
jagged saw possessed of great strength.
They are cut from the head down by their own offspring through terrible deeds;
they devour their own flesh and drink their own blood.
Those fools by whom food and drink were neither given nor approved are crushed like sugarcane, being shattered by hammers.
In the terrible Asitāla forest, they are cut into pieces;
with all their limbs pierced by needles, they are then impaled upon spikes.
Though they are being dragged along while trembling, they do not die;
nevertheless, their flesh is torn from their bodies and their bones are shattered with hammers.
They are dragged swiftly and repeatedly by the exceedingly powerful messengers of Yama;
with no breath following their last, they remain in hell for a long time.
In Ucchvāsa they are always exhaling, their mouths covered with sand;
but in the Rauravas, they are indeed crushed by various teeth and instruments.
For even the great weep from the torments of the Mahāraurava hell;
[the pain] attends upon the anus, the sides, the feet, the chest, and the head.
Those who, by their very nature, revile and laugh at the wives of others are struck down by fierce soldiers with well-heated iron mallets.
Other women embrace other husbands and do not recognize their own;
why then do you run with such speed? Do you not remember the eternally abiding [Truth]?
And you have deceived your husband, blinded by sin as you pleased;
we too have been cast into iron jars and slowly cremated.
They are cooked in blazing fires and cast into rocks;
they are thrown into blind wells and violently devoured by pythons.
Those who revile the Great-Souled One, the Teacher who perceives the Dharma,
the Brahmin devoted to Śiva, and the eternal Śiva-dharma;
On their chests, throats, tongues, and bodily joints,
as well as on the lips, they are pinned by the servants of Yama with stakes.
In this way, the initial and most terrible torments of those who have committed evil deeds should be known to exist in each individual hell by the hundreds and thousands.
"O King, the torments are dense for all evildoers;
thus indeed are the endless torments in all the hells."
"How can a human being describe their misery even in a hundred years?"—
thus they are cast down by their own various and terrible karmas.
Without a doubt, all those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakins) are cooked in succession in all the hells.
As long as the moon and stars endure, all those who have committed sins shall be tormented in these hells at all times by various [punishing] agents.
Those who commit major sins will undoubtedly ripen [in suffering] in the hells in all four directions;
furthermore, those men who commit minor offenses go to half of that [duration].
Death is not known, dear one, as to when it will happen to whom;
once death has arrived unexpectedly, what man can find even a year?
Since you will certainly depart all alone, having abandoned everything,
therefore, with every effort, be devoted to truth and righteousness.
All this has been told to you regarding the characteristics of the hells.
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Torments of Hell," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS Chapter 54.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
By what dharma can this ocean of saṃsāra, so difficult to cross, be traversed?
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen to the story being told by those sinful ones who were rebuked by him.
This world, being both lustful and deluded, engages in what ought not to be done;
it does not recognize itself, nor another, nor the divine.
He did not hear what was most beneficial, nor did he see with his eyes;
walking slowly on a level path, he stumbled at every step.
Having been addressed thus, when Dharmarāja explained in detail what he had previously stated in brief regarding those who possess sinful bodies, listen now to that.
Yama said:
Released by me, a man does not understand even when being enlightened by the wise;
he suffers in various ways within saṃsāra under the power of passion and greed.
Due to their state of being prone to abortion, they do not understand the scripture taught;
men neither hear nor perform the action that accomplishes heaven and liberation.
In the meditation on Śiva, which accomplishes all desired aims,
it is a great marvel that one’s own welfare is better attained here than [by avoiding] hell.
All men have become like hungry ghosts and have arrived in the world of Yama;
I shall relate the ancient narrative as it was taught.
The supreme narrative of Narmadā was told by Sūrya to my father out of compassion for the gods and the ancestors.
The *Sapādalakṣa* was further recounted by Brahmā concerning the Sun;
I heard it all from Brahmā, who had himself heard it from Śiva.
Formerly, Śiva spoke this to Pārvatī and Ṣaṇmukha:
"Having reached Jambūdvīpa, he has taken recourse to a human womb."
He who does not resort to the goddess Narmadā, who flows for seven kalpas,
[is deprived of merit] through bathing, immersion, drinking, as well as by acts of giving and so forth.
In this world, what other means for securing a [favorable] rebirth exists for those whose minds are afflicted by sin,
other than meditating upon the Great Goddess Narmadā, the remover of evil?
The sins of those who remember the Narmadā or proclaim her name with their voice perish, just as darkness vanishes at the rising of the sun.
Even one who has arrived in the next world is not tormented by the messengers of Yama,
provided he is that lowest of men, a doer of evil deeds, who recites the praises of the Narmadā.
He never at any time enters the hells that have been described;
there, the Gaṅgā and other rivers exist as many millions of sacred fords (tīrtha).
By the power and majesty of Revā,
those who remember Mekalā, Hara, or Hari while staying in hell attain purification at that very moment.
He is released from the messengers of Yama at that very moment; of this there is no doubt, provided he remains on the Vaidūrya mountain at Amarakaṇṭaka.
Oṃkāra is the Supreme Lord, the bestower of the fruits of enjoyment and liberation;
for what reason, then, do those whose minds are afflicted by sin grieve here?
Therein, in the very center, are Siddheśvara, the Siddhaliṅga which bestows grace upon the worlds, Yajñeśvara, and Śaśibhūṣaṇa.
On the southern bank of the Narmadā, there is the Maheśvara Liṅga and the fourth, Kapileśa; the wise know these to be the sacred field of Śiva.
Those who always worship with devotion through offerings of flowers, incense, and water for libation go to the world of Śiva; of this there is no doubt.
All this has been told to you, O sinless one, exactly as you asked;
[the sage] spoke of those most wicked men who stand outside the dharma, O Bhārata.
[It stands there thus:
The gift of a cow, the gift of gold, and likewise the gift of sesame seeds;
the gift of food, the gift of milk, and indeed every kind of utensil. RKS 54.24.
Those supreme among men who give gifts of palaces and groves do not go to the world of Yama or to the hell of terrible form.
They are liberated from all sins according to the word of Śiva;
they obtain honor through dishonor and union with the beloved through separation.
Youth is seized by old age; happiness is beset by suffering;
and the body is worn out by wrinkles and gray hair.
What can a wise man do when he is worn out by old age,
[considering] that the youth and beauty of men and women are mutually pleasing?
That very same body, when seized by old age, is no longer dear to either of them;
likewise, they perceive themselves as endowed with frailty, as if they were someone else entirely.
Who else would be more senseless than that man, overcome by old age, who, even while seeing [this state], does not become dispassionate toward his wife, sons, and other kinsmen?
Due to his lack of power, he is treated with contempt by servants of ill-conduct; one possessed by old age can no longer pursue dharma, artha, kāma, or mokṣa.
Therefore, one who is capable should practice righteousness beforehand,
O Yudhiṣṭhira, as well as the balancing of the discordance of wind, bile, phlegm, and the other humors.
The collection of wind and the other humors is proclaimed to be born of the body;
therefore, this body of the self should be known as being primarily characterized by disease.
Afflicted by an excess of wind-originated fever and by various kinds of diseases, he experiences manifold sufferings in many ways.
And these are to be known by one's own self; what else shall I say?
One hundred and one deaths are established within this body.
In this regard, one [type of disease] is of the nature of time (kāla), while the remaining ones are considered adventitious (āgantuka).
Those which are declared here to be adventitious are pacified by medicinal remedies.
Untimely death caused by poison, food, and other such causes does not cease for anyone through recitation, fire-offerings, or gifts; nor does the death ordained by time. RKS 54.37.
Therefore, a man who is not overly attached does not fear untimely death;
likewise, living beings possess various painful diseases along with physicians.
Poisons, malevolent spells, and death are the gateways for embodied beings;
even Dhanvantari himself cannot save one afflicted by diseases, serpents, and the like.
Neither asceticism, nor charity, nor friends, nor kinsmen can restore to health a living being whose time has come; this is true even for the King of Niṣadha.
They are not capable of protecting us when we are oppressed by time;
there is no suffering equal to death, and there is no enemy equal to death.
For all embodied beings, there is no time equal to death,
which seizes even one's virtuous wife, sons, friends, kingdom, sovereignty, and pleasures.
O Bhārata, death cuts through all things, however diverse they may be;

Knowing that all food is subject to transformation by time,

Constantly removing all suffering and destroying all grief,

This is knowledge, this is meditation, scholarship, the Veda, and the realization of the Veda;

Sacrifice, charity, austerity, truthfulness, Vedic study, and libations to the ancestors—

Thousands of *brahmakūrca* fasts and ten thousand drinks of *soma* are not worth even a sixteenth part of drinking the water of the Narmadā.

Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Discourse on the Course of Karma," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS, Chapter 55.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen, O mighty-armed king; understand what is being told by me.

Cakravartin was Śaśāṅka, the best among all upholders of the Dharma;

at Kurukṣetra, Hariścandra [gave] ten thousand excellent cows.
A Brahmin seer named Mudgala, who was himself established in the Absolute (Brahman), [offered] a load of gold adorned with every kind of jewel as an ornament.
And all the Mudgala twice-born ones were devoted to truth and righteousness;
there were more than one hundred and eight Brāhmaṇas who were exponents of the Veda.
At the conjunction of the sun and Rāhu, Hariścandra,
having honored the twice-born with supreme faith according to the prescribed rites, gave [the gifts] to them.
Having worshipped Maheśāna, the abode that bestows supreme accomplishment,
he was filled with the highest joy for Cakrapāṇi Hṛṣīkeśa.
O best of kings, by the power of this gift consisting of sesame seeds and darbha grass offered at the Sarasvatī, all the worlds were conquered by him.
A city was attained in the intermediate space, enchanting to all the worlds;

Adorned with truthfulness, generosity, and total renunciation, a king equal to Hariścandra has never existed before, nor will there ever be one again.
Thus were these verses sung of old by Śakra and the other foremost gods;
even the Moon performed everything while residing on the bank of the Narmadā.
On Mount Amarakaṇṭaka, she gave gifts, performed sacrifices, practiced austerities, and upheld the truth;
and she gave a half-born child to a high-souled Brahmin.

having burnt away his manifold karmic sins like a mass of cotton by fire, he was purified.
As long as both the feet and the face of the calf are visible within the womb,

A cow with golden horns and silver hooves, accompanied by her calf and a bronze milking vessel,

Between Oṃkāra and Amara, at Koṭitīrtha,
the lord of men presented these [lands], numbering in the thousands, to the Brāhmaṇas.
In that interval, celestial drums resounded in the sky;
at that very moment, he ascended the vehicle, blazing as if with clusters of jewels.
Being praised by countless beings in celestial chariots standing nearby,
he held a golden parasol and was fanned with chowries.
Even Hariścandra was situated a thousand yojanas below;
having seen that such was the deed of the moon-king, O lord of the people.
Having censured Kurukṣetra, his mind filled with wonder,
he [performed it] at the confluence of the moon and Rāhu on the Mahānadī river.
"In brief, so that the gift given shall not be ordinary," [thinking thus],
Hariścandra, the best of kings, became dejected in countenance.
Having gone quickly to the world of Brahmā, where the Lord, the Master of the Worlds, resides,
he saluted the Grandfather according to custom and questioned him.
By means of his generosity, the high-souled Śaśāṅka conquered the gods.
Furthermore, O Brahmin, what merit does this possess that it excels even Kurukṣetra?
The sacred ford named Amareśvara, which has arisen from the Revā, is unequaled by anything else; it shines ever more brilliantly above all.
Having heard these words of the wise Hariścandra,
Brahmā spoke these words to Hariścandra, the best of kings:
"Abandon your despondency, O Indra among kings; the course of karmic actions is profound.
A king resembling the moon has neither been seen nor heard of by me."
"I am not fit to speak thus, nor even the gods together with Vāsava;
for in the past, indeed, there were many thousands of wheel-turning monarchs."
And, O Bhārata, at Amarakaṇṭaka on the mountain, hundreds of thousands of sacred fords were duly established during the conjunction of Rāhu and the Sun.
Sarasvatī, Kurukṣetra, Puṣkara, and likewise Naimiṣa—

O lord of men, O king of kings, at Hariścandra-koṭitīrtha in Mekalā,
abandon the comparison of other holy sites with Mekalā.
In former times, Vārāṇasī and Kurukṣetra were weighed by me;
by virtue of the power of this sacred site, other holy places do not equal it.
Kurukṣetra is renowned as that which sets the course of worldly existence in motion;
yet it has not been heard by those who are possessed of false knowledge and have not listened to the Purāṇas.
"If you desire the supreme state, let the goddess who flows through the Kalpa be served," said the lord of Ayodhyā at that time, after having paid homage to the Creator.
Filled with supreme joy, he went to the Lord of the Immortals;
all this has been related to you exactly as it happened, O observer of noble vows.
O King, the man who hears this shall obtain the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Gift of Cows," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS, Chapter 56.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
To the west of Māhiṣmatī is indeed a supreme holy place that removes all sins.

with various offerings, and with the kindling of rows of lamps;

O Yudhiṣṭhira, in a former kalpa, a divine sage named Mātaṅga took up residence on the bank of the Narmadā and performed extremely difficult austerities.

staying at Aghamarṣaṇa, he understood all dharmas.
Through his association with the great sages and by beholding the Narmadā,
he abandoned his sinful intent and cultivated a mind devoted to dharma.
"O King, both I and this monk are now weary of births among the outcaste dog-cookers.

Eighty-one thousand [streams] issued forth from the tips of his matted locks;

"Choose a boon—may it be well with you—for this meditation of yours, O observer of noble vows."
Mātaṅga said:
"O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased and desire to grant me a boon here,

Even Cāṇḍālas and Śvapacas, though born of sinful wombs and devoid of the practice of japa and other rites, are liberated from sin even here.
The liṅga named Mātaṅga is situated on the bank of the Narmadā;
for whoever bathes there and worships it, there shall be liberation from bondage.
"O Maheśvara, by your grace, I consider this to be the boon.
Having heard those words of his, the Lord of Śivā replied:
"Let all that be so through my grace; of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus, O God, he departed for Kailāsa, the most excellent of mountains.
Having obtained the boon, O Mātaṅga, he ascended a vehicle that moves at will to the city of Umāmaheśvara, adorned with all ornaments.
By the power of that bath, she quickly went to enjoy pleasures for a long time;
and on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Caitra, which was the new moon day—
Whatever is offered as an oblation or given as a gift therein yields infinite fruit;
even one who has entered a state of sinful birth attains this through the offering of sesame seeds and water.
But he who delights the ancestors with a ball of molasses enriched with groats—

Whoever performs the worship of the *liṅga* mixed with sesame seeds and rice,

O Bhārata, that which is called the Aśokavanikā is said to be the Mātaṅga tīrtha; it is located on the northern bank of the Revā, as has been told to you.
Now I shall describe another sacred site situated in the southern quarter, named Mṛgavana, which destroys all sins.
Having bathed there, O Great King, one should worship Viṣṇu, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace;
on the eleventh day, remaining without food, one should pass the night.
There, in the deer-forest, one should worship Hari with fragrant flowers;
when a single Brahmin is fed, it is as if a hundred thousand have been fed.
By the offering of water with sesame seeds, the ancestors indeed attain the station of Viṣṇu;
right there is situated the supreme sacred site of Vārāha.
Wherein the Earth was uplifted by Hari in the form of a boar,
and likewise another [form], the Universal Form (Viśvarūpa), by the one of immeasurable splendor.
A woman who is devoted to her husband and likewise observes the month-long fast,

Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Mātaṅga’s Hermitage," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS, Chapter 57.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall relate the narrative of how the Deer Forest became renowned.
There was a certain hunter of evil conduct, merciless toward all living beings.
O best of kings, wandering through mountain caves with noose in hand and bow in hand,
he struck down all the deer for the sake of his family.
When the month of Jyeṣṭha had arrived, during the summer heat blazing like fire,
he wandered about, afflicted by thirst, and took refuge at the foot of a tree.
At night he slept motionless, afflicted by suffering and overcome by hunger;
meanwhile, a fire born from the friction of forest trees had arisen from a mountain cave.
And by him that forest, filled with deer and tigers, was utterly consumed;
it was all reduced to ashes and turned entirely into dust.
At the time prescribed for the arrival of the clouds, during the auspicious flow of the Narmadā,
when the sun has entered the zodiac sign of Virgo, on the twelfth lunar day under the asterism Śravaṇa.
Through contact with the waters of the Narmadā, the yakṣas indeed became pannagas;
at that very moment, possessing divine bodies, they ascended a Vaiṣṇava vehicle.
By the power of this sacred ford (tīrtha), that hunter became a king;
for ten thousand years, he enjoyed captivating pleasures.
Even those deer who were burnt there attained the state of Gandharvas;
indeed, by means of a Vaiṣṇava vehicle, they reached the station of Viṣṇu.
Whether against his will or by his own choice, whoever should renounce their life shall rejoice in the world of Viṣṇu for a thousand divine years.
By the offering of sesame-water, the ancestors attain the supreme goal;
there is another sacred ford named Manoratha, which bestows the highest accomplishment.
Renowned throughout the three worlds as being situated on the banks of the Revā,
whatever desire a person may pray for, that very thing they obtain even by bathing there.
And one obtains everything through the power of this sacred ford;
the confluence of the Aṅgārāvarta is the bestower of the fruit of a thousand cows.
And the god Aṅgāreśvara resides there at that confluence;
by merely bathing there, a man shall attain the status of a leader of the Gaṇas.
And when the day of Aṅgāra (Tuesday) falls on the fourth lunar day, O Bhārata,
one should fashion a golden man and wrap him in a red cloth.
A copper vessel filled with ghee, or even one filled with molasses—
one should offer all of that according to the prescribed rules, especially to a śrotriya.
By the power of the sacred ford of generosity, one shall become a sharer in half the throne of Śakra;
for by it, even many intense misdeeds and sufferings [are overcome].
Therefore, one must not commit evil, for it causes suffering to oneself;
regardless of the time, the place, or the stage of life at which it occurs.
Whatever action, whether auspicious or inauspicious, has been performed, that is experienced by the agent in that very way;
therefore, one should always give to the seeker without interruption.
Otherwise, enjoyments are cut off like shallow streams in the summer;
whereas the auspicious goddess who flows for seven kalpas is enjoyed [only] thus.
I shall declare to you the yoga of knowledge for the total eradication of saṃsāra;
knowledge is that which reveals Śiva, and yoga is contemplated as being precisely therein.
The course of Yoga is difficult to comprehend in the presence of Narmadāśiva;
there, the command of Śiva prevails regarding the procedure for bathing and worship as follows.
Without contradicting the established tenets, a person should not oppose [the teachings] with books; thus, for the sake of dharma, knowledge, and liberation, he attains that which is consistent.
Due to contradiction between what precedes and what follows, where could the intended meaning possibly lie?
Having examined reasoning from its very root, one should abandon it along with [mere] scriptural authority.
Therefore, a wise person should always investigate the nature of the self by means of both scripture and reasoning, and not by inference alone.
The fruit of that which is inferior, superior, and so forth is manifold and is known to be of its own kind;
therefore, one should examine merit, for it is excellent and yields great fruit.

A wise person should avoid from afar those who follow heretical paths, those who persist in improper actions, those who act like cats in hypocrisy, the deceitful, those who rely on fallacious reasoning, and those who revile sacred fords.
One should never engage in conversation or association with the Digambaras, the Śvetapaṭas, or any others who are proponents of [mere] logical reasoning.
In the Kali age, dharma is perverted; [people] go naked, have shaven heads, and eat filth. Therefore, having abandoned that, one should practice the dharma of the Tretā age.
The authority regarding all dharmas is that which is proclaimed by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
he who acts otherwise certainly falls into hell.
Such is the definitive conclusion regarding all scriptures:
those who are devoted to the worship of Śiva should always serve the Goddess Kalpagā.
One should perform the libation for the ancestors, give alms to the mendicant,
practice compassion toward all living beings, and contemplate the narrative of the Narmadā.
This knowledge is entirely complete and purifies all karma;
it is the Lord, devoid of beginning, middle, and end, and pure by nature.
In the Śiva-āgama, Śiva should be known as omniscient and perfect;
the knowledge imparted by him undoubtedly accomplishes all goals.
How could he who is omniscient, perfectly complete, pure by nature, auspicious,
and entirely free from all defects speak otherwise?
How could the creation of the world occur even without the command of Śiva,
given that the Pradhāna is insentient and the Puruṣa is ignorant?
Whatever is insentient, such as primordial matter (pradhāna), atoms, and so forth, is not an agent by itself; it cannot act without an intelligent instrument that observes it.
Just as a lump of clay does not of its own accord turn into a jar by means of this [instrument],

Instruction regarding dharma and adharma, but not the investigation of dharma and adharma,

Just as this terrible ocean of saṃsāra has proceeded without beginning,

Just as medicine is by its very nature the antidote to diseases,
so too is the auspicious [state] known as the antidote to the terrors of saṃsāra.
Just as patients suffer without a physician, being left without anyone to call for help,

Therefore, there exists the beginningless, omniscient, perfect, supreme Śiva;

Those who practice the auspicious knowledge, having cultivated the state of Śiva within their hearts—
if the Vedas are indeed authoritative— then such knowledge arises for them.
And this Narmadā on earth is the refuge of all beings;
as a goddess in the form of water, she bestows grace upon the worlds.
This [goddess] rescues from falling certainly into hell the fourfold collection of beings, both the stationary and the moving, within the Blessed One.
Having understood this, O best of men, and having beheld Śiva who dwells through the kalpas, one obtains lofty,
divine mansions endowed with wealth and grain.
One should present all the divine articles of equipment to the Brahmins,

Hear now, O Bhārata, the fruit of merit for that man who causes divine [images] to be made; what need has he of many other gifts given?

Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter in the Narmadā-māhātmya of the Revā-khaṇḍa within the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS, Chapter 58.

he is endowed with the most divine of the divine, possessing the splendor of glorious gold.

Below that is the netherworld named Vitala, which is white; it is the surface of the earth, where the two Nāgas Kambala and Aśvatara dwell together.
The residence of the great-souled lords of the asuras, such as Mahājambha, Hayagrīva, and others, was established there in Vārāṇasī.

the abode of Śaṅkukarṇa, Mahānāda, and Namuci.
Above the seventh netherworld (pātāla), the earth consisting of seven continents is situated,
endowed with seven oceans and adorned with mountains.
And Jambūdvīpa is in its center; beyond that is Plakṣadvīpa.
Beyond Krauñcadvīpa is Śākadvīpa,
and outside of that is Puṣkaradvīpa, which is proclaimed as the seventh.
The Salt-water Ocean, the Sugarcane-juice Ocean, the Wine Ocean, the Ghee Ocean,

Himavān, Hemakūṭa, and Niṣadha are situated to the south of Meru;

O Bhārata, Meru stands in the center of Jambūdvīpa;
Mālyavat is to be known in the east, and Gandhamādana in the west.

The earth is circular, golden, and shaped like the back of a tortoise.

At its edge, extending all around, is the mountain known as Lokāloka;

Half of this [Mount Meru] extends for five thousand yojanas;

It illuminates the light on its far side, while its own [dark] side is eclipsed;
therefore, that great mountain is called Lokāloka.
This Bhūrloka is proclaimed to extend as far as Lokāloka,
and it is inhabited by Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rakṣasas, and Piśācas.
By humans and animals, by beasts, birds, and reptiles,
and by these sixfold classes of beings, including stationary things of various forms.
From the realm of Bhūrloka and Bhuvarloka up to the solar orb,

Dhruva stands above all the celestial mansions as their central pivot;

Standing above the joints, he produces food and the rest;
