There, twenty-eight crores of presiding deities,
having come from the world of men to the celestial realm by the command of the Lotus-born One, [reside].
Remaining there for the duration of a manvantara, they conclude their respective duties;
then, having ascended to Maharloka, they return from there once again.
Within a single day of Brahmā, the fourteen classes of gods,
having performed their respective duties in due order, dwell in Maharloka and the heavenly realms.
Janaloka is elevated two koṭis above Maharloka;
there the Sādhyas and Asuras dwell, always happy.
The ascetic power (tapas) there rises forty million yojanas even above the people;
the Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis), the sons of Brahmā, reside there.
Satyaloka rises six crores above Tapoloka;
there the Virāj resides, surrounded by hosts of gods and asuras.
The realm of Viṣṇu is twice as high as the realm of Brahmā;
above that, it extends in width and is endowed with divine worlds.
And beyond the world of Viṣṇu lies the great and glorious city of Śiva,
extending for twenty-two crores [of yojanas], situated directly above it.
Resplendent like ten thousand suns, endowed with all objects of desire,
arranged with many forest groves, and adorned by celestial rivers.
[He was adorned] with divine [ornaments] endowed with all kinds of jewels, possessing the luster of refined gold,
consisting of a thousand pieces of ground [gold], and complete with every splendor.
The sky was pervaded on all sides by celestial palaces, like the firmament with moons;
it was crowded with throngs of apsaras and filled with all the vidyādharas.
Accompanied by retinues endowed with immeasurable qualities, possessing the speed of thought, and numbering in the countless millions, they were filled with the sounds of dance and song.
In some places there were delightful swing-houses, adorned with tinkling bells and half-moons rising upward, decorated with ornaments of bells.
With canopies of jewels and pearls, with auspicious heaps of precious gems,
with substances honored by every kind of jewel, and with beautiful strings of pearls;
In some places it was filled with divine great lion-thrones adorned with all kinds of jewels,
and in others with meritorious mansions endowed with countless virtues.
It was everywhere filled with delightful trees always laden with flowers and fruit,
as well as hundreds and thousands of most enchanting flower gardens.
The meritorious and excellent river flows there for seven kalpas;
a thousandth part of its flow is seen here in Jambūdvīpa.
Having descended upon the surface of the earth out of a desire to favor the worlds,
the incarnation of all rivers, beginning with the Gaṅgā, has taken place here in its entirety.
It was adorned with rivers flowing with nectar,
and with ponds enriched with gold and jewels, provided with crystal staircases.
They are adorned with fragrant lotuses that are white, red, black, and yellow,
as well as with heavy five-colored flowers and clusters of golden blossoms.
It is greatly expansive, with beautiful and very smooth [walls] measuring five cubits,
ten, twelve, and likewise twenty cubits.
In various places there were oblong ponds filled with full-blown blue lotuses and others possessing charming petals, resembling emeralds in hue.
With divine faces like those of lions and tigers, with faces of elephants, horses, and deer, as well as faces of oxen, goats, monkeys, and birds; RKS_58.68 //
With one face, with great faces, with many faces, and with no faces;
with one foot, with three feet, with many feet, and with no feet.
With dwarfs, those with matted hair, those with shaven heads, those with long necks, those with large bellies,
those with massive bodies, those with large noses, those with large ears, and those without ears;
They assumed various forms and shapes, were adorned with diverse ornaments,
wore various costumes, were divine, capable of changing their form at will, and possessed great strength.
Endowed with various powers and proficient in various sciences,
countless other species of similar kind likewise dwell there.
Hunchbacked, dwarfish, and others tall; with excellent bodies and beautiful faces;
shaven-headed, misshapen, lowly, and likewise short or long.
Some had protruding bellies, short arms, or were hunched; others had short knees;
some had the faces of lions, while others had the faces of elephants or horses.
With short, curled hair and beautiful, pleasing appearances,
fifty crores of Śiva’s female attendants reside there.
Those women sometimes sport outside in houses made of jewels and rubies; in those houses, which have hundreds and thousands of floors, they find delight at the doorways.
There, the various grounds were adorned with diamonds and lapis lazuli,
accompanied by thousands of fair-faced women endowed with every excellence.
The city of the Lord is pervaded on all sides by innumerable [beings];
in its center is a great, divine sanctuary called Sarvatobhadra.
The primordial abode of Umāpati resembles pure crystal;
there dwells the Blessed Lord Soma, being worshipped by the lords of the Gaṇas.
O sinless one, the glorious Dharma is established there in that abode of Īśvara by the Siddhas who have attained their own stations, as well as by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others.
Wherever the bull among heroes resides, there the Mothers of the Cows are eternally present;
there the goddess Narmadā dwells, being worshipped by gods and asuras alike.
By that water, O sinless one, the calves, all the deities, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Sureśāna together with Umā, are satisfied.
The gods, sages, beings, ancestors, and likewise mothers—
this world, this world of Śiva, is here indeed the world of the Narmadā.
Whatever qualities belong to the world of Rudra and likewise to Goloka,
[they reside] in Nandā, Bhadrā, Subhadrā, Suśīlā, and Surabhi.
Thus the five cow-mothers emerged from the world of Śiva;
the sixth, however, was the goddess Narmadā, out of a desire to bestow grace upon the worlds.
All these, O Great King, are the mothers of the entire world and of all people; they constantly satisfy them with their own inherent qualities.
And by virtue of their cause, the abode of Śiva, following the power of the Lord’s will,
they have descended from the syllable Oṃ to this world from among all worlds.
They eat grass, they roam in the forest, and they drink waters that are perfectly pure;
they yield milk and purify the body, for it is from cows that the world of living beings lives.
For how could there be sins for those whose homes are adorned with cows that constantly have young calves, just like women themselves?
Those who always remember the Narmadā together with the syllable Om as being Śiva himself shall have no return again to this terrible ocean of saṃsāra.
Those who offer supreme devotion by providing even grass and water,
through the grace of those cows, go to the world of Śiva.
These mothers, who always grant all desires with favor, protect those auspicious ones;
they go to the world of Śiva.
Those who, being composed in mind, worship Śiva with devotion through the correct rites,
obtain great enjoyments and indeed go to the city of Śiva.
Those men who go with faith to the holy fords that provide refuge in Śiva—
especially to the Kalpagā river and the Amarakaṇṭaka mountain— [attain liberation].
They sport with great enjoyments in the abodes of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva,
[partaking] of milk, nectar, ghee, milk, honey, curd, and so forth.
O illustrious one, being utterly deluded, he did not see [it] on the Kalpagā.
O King, this auspicious account of the descent of the Revā has been told to you.
By means of this narration, may the Blessed One, Śiva himself, be pleased with me.
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the World of Śiva," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS, Chapter 59.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Knower of the Kalpas, I wish to hear the rules for the practice of the duty of giving.
Or how do even poor monks go to the abode of peace?
"O Great Sage, for the benefit of the worlds, please tell us by what rite and what gift one is likewise liberated from evil deeds."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen, O King, sinless one, as I relate to you according to the proper method:
Puṣkara, Bilva leaves, Kuśa grass, water, and [the fruit] of the Narmadā tree.
The Blessed One, the Self-Existent, has declared that the common cause of all phenomena is faith;
all dharmas, as well as the Purāṇas and the Vedas, are purified by faith.
By means of that dharma of instruction, men go to the third heaven (Triviṣṭapa),
[offering] a wide cloth filled with cotton, dyed red and provided with thread.
It may also be made of tiger-skin or covered with new cloth;
it should be provided with a black antelope skin as a sacred thread and perfumed with holy incense.
One should offer [this] with faith to one who is devoted to the meditation on Śiva;
as many threads as there are in the fibers of that cotton cloth, for so long [does he reside in heaven].
For that many thousands of years he is glorified in the world of Śiva;
having enjoyed manifold pleasures, he rejoices in all the worlds.
And again, having attained the earth, he shall become a lord of the lion-throne;
his bedding, coverings, and so forth shall consist of grass, bark, and leaves.
Having given [food] on the ground to one who seeks it, one is glorified in the world of Śiva;
likewise, he who offers an oblation intended for Śiva to one who beholds Śiva [is also so honored].
Listen to the fruit of his merit regarding vegetables, roots, or fruits,
as well as the number of grains of rice and so forth contained within the leaves that yield the fruit.
Having devotedly given alms together with side dishes to a devotee of Śiva, one is glorified in the world of Śiva for as many thousands of years.
O illustrious one, he is honored in the world of Śiva for a hundred thousand years,
having given a beautiful alms-bowl completely filled with curd-rice.
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who gives to a devotee of Śiva:
it is equal to ten million divine years, endowed with great enjoyments.
Having stayed in the divine city of Śiva until the end of his lifespan,
that lord of the earth [is joined] with a devotee of Śiva by means of very cool water mixed with sugar.
Having offered libations, one rejoices in the world of Śambhu for a hundred thousand years;
[one should offer] a water-pot filled with water strained through a cloth and mixed with sugar.
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who gives [this] to a devotee of Śiva:
a celestial chariot resembling pure crystal that fulfills all desires.
Having reached the world of Śiva, he rejoices there for ten million years—
[he who] should make leaf-cups from *palāśa* leaves or other leaves.
He who gives a well-crafted copper vessel to a Śiva-yogin indeed becomes a giver of a copper vessel to the Śiva-yogins.
He who carries a trident in his hand, a spear on his back, and a water-pot [at his side] is honored in the world of Śiva for sixty million kalpas.
Having fed him with effort, one shall attain the world of Śiva;
and one should feed, according to one's ability, one who observes the vow of Śiva.
Established in the world of Śiva, that wise man sports with the most excellent enjoyments,
he who feeds a householder observing the duties of Śiva’s stage of life.
That man who feeds one established in the vow of Śiva’s hermitage with bulbs and other such foods is honored in the world of Śiva with vast enjoyments.
Abiding in the city of the Lord, he shall attain divine enjoyments;
thus, having fed one devoted to the Pāśupata [observance] and having bowed before him.
He who offers alms to one who observes the great vow (mahāvrata) is honored in the world of Śiva with various kinds of great enjoyments.
He is glorified in the world of Śiva with divine and beautiful enjoyments—
that man who is devoted to the practice of self-restraint, observances, and conduct, and who is intent upon devotion to Śiva.
Having fed them according to one's ability, one is glorified in the world of Śiva;
this applies even to those who stand outside the yoga of knowledge and follow the common dharma of the world.
Those who worship Śiva with devotion go to the world of Śiva,
even by means of non-perishable [fuel], such as a fire of dried cow-dung, by the offering of water, and through fierce austerities.
Even by means of sacrifices, men do not attain that goal which even a lowly person who is a devotee of Rudra attains.
O bull among the Bharatas, men do not attain such a good rebirth through means such as sacrifices and gifts as they do by the mere touch of the waters of the Revā.
Thus, this realm of Śiva has been described in passing,
along with Goloka and Kalpagāloka, which are inhabited by the devotees of Śiva.
Those who, being tranquil through the yoga of knowledge, chant the supreme Śiva,
become liberated from all suffering and are forever happy.
And the world of Śiva (Śivaloka) is to be understood as consisting of the enclosures of the mandala:
the five elements, the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), the quality of goodness (sattva), and nature (prakṛti) as the eighth.
It should be understood that there are thousands of millions of such nāgas;
because the principal [being] possesses all limbs, they are situated horizontally, above, and below.
Beyond the world of Viṣṇu is the abode of the high-souled Kumāra,
which resembles clear pearls and is endowed with supreme splendor.
Beyond Skandiloka, the station of the goddess Umā is proclaimed;
it resembles molten gold and is endowed with every excellence.
Beyond the station of Umā is the supreme station of Hara,
which resembles ten million suns and is endowed with all desirable things.
It was inhabited by all the innumerable hosts devoted to yoga,
including Hiraṇyagarbha, Kūrma, and others, as well as the Vasus, Rudras, and Divākaras.
The Blessed One is constantly praised in his presence by those who long for him—
those devoted to knowledge and meditation, peaceful, subsisting on alms-food, and having conquered their senses.

And by those Brāhmaṇas who have burnt away their impurities through the constant performance of virtuous deeds, that supreme station is attained, which possesses a radiance equal to ten thousand suns.
Those who dwell there with perfected intentions, free from afflictions,
and who serve the Narmadā, attain that supreme state.
This has been told to you, O Pārtha, exactly as it was instructed by Śambhu—
this gift which I have described as being performed on the banks of the Narmadā.
Those who go to another heretical path are surpassed by the Thousand-rayed One;
they become omniscient, all-pervading, pure, and perfectly fulfilled.
But those who perform pure actions and are endowed with supreme sovereignty become,
by their own will, both embodied and disembodied once again.
Thus, the primordial station of Umāpati, the divine abode of Lord Śrīkaṇṭha, the sustainer of the world, is eternally pure and remains constant.
The place where the Kalpagā river flows out is thus called Navaka;
it is eternally characterized by the supreme eightfold sovereignty, imperishable and undecaying.
Those men who constantly meditate upon the deity through the yoga of meditation as perpetually taught by their guru, being perfected, go to that state.
Those who practice the auspicious knowledge while dwelling on the banks of the Narmadā,
being completely liberated from the thirst of desire, they too go to that city.
Even if one is devoted solely to meditation on Śiva for but a single day,
being intent upon the dharma of Śiva, there is no end to that merit.
Because it is the essence among the dharmas of yoga, it is indestructible by the hammers of evil;
it should be known as being like a diamond-grain (vajra-taṇḍula). Therefore, its fruit is great.
By that very dharma which ends with the body, a person dwells for ten thousand kalpas in the primordial abode, the sanctuary of Śiva, sporting with vast enjoyments.
Then, at the end of ten thousand kalpas, he shall attain the realm of Kumāra;
there, sporting happily, he shall dwell for a period equal to half that time.
At the end of that, having reached the world of Viṣṇu, he dwells there;
and at the end of that, having gone to the world of Brahmā, the man dwells there as well.
Falling from the world of Brahmā, he shall dwell happily in the city of Śiva;
therefore, from that state, he attains the worlds of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others in due succession.
Having thus enjoyed himself in all the worlds in succession,
he then reaches the world of humans and should take refuge in the auspicious Revā.
O Bhārata, whatever other gifts I have described elsewhere,
all of them are praised on the mountain Amarakaṇṭaka.
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Śiva," in the Narmadā-māhātmya of the Revā-khaṇḍa within the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS, Chapter 60.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Understand from me the dharma of giving pertaining to Viṣṇu as it is being told."
Having thoroughly practiced the yoga of Viṣṇu for the removal of all afflictions.
Having worshipped Viṣṇu according to the prescribed rite with hymns and the bathing of the deity in ghee and other offerings, one should,
on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), dedicate a single milch cow to Viṣṇu.
Having reached the bank of the Narmadā, hear now the fruit of its merit:
he is honored by Dharmarāja exactly as Viṣṇu is.
Whoever should feed a thousand Śaivas and Vaiṣṇavas,
together with a pregnant cow and ten bulls, [attains the fruit].
Having worshipped [the deity] with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and having adorned it with gold and garments,
one should proceed clockwise around it with devotion to the King of Mantras.
Uttering "Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One Vāsudeva," he entered that place crowded with those learned in the Vedas and engaged in auspicious rites for the propitiation of Viṣṇu.
Having reached the waters of the Narmadā, one should light a garland of lamps, [reciting]:
"May cows always be before me, and cows likewise behind me."
"The cows are in my heart, and I dwell in the midst of the cows"—
having arisen, one should recite this mantra in front of these cows.
Having taken a copper vessel mixed with perfumes and *yakṣakardama*,
one who has bathed in water with [cow] horns and tail and is clad in white garments [should proceed].
By bathing and drinking in the Narmadā, as well as by the water from the tails of cows,
he was liberated from all impurities, perfectly perfected, and long-established in his vows.
Having bathed there on the bank of the Narmadā during the full moon, when the full moon was in conjunction with Rāhu, that brahmin departed.
Together with those very lords of brahmins, having fully worshipped [the deity], one should remember Hari,
accompanied by servants, sons, wife, kinsmen, and relatives.
Endowed with faith, one should offer [the food] to Kṛṣṇa with the mantra during a śrāddha rite, a gift-giving ceremony, a fire-oblation, a wedding, or likewise on an auspicious occasion.
These cows, who are of the nature of Śiva and reside eternally in the world of Viṣṇu,
have been given by me for the sake of Śiva and the high-souled Viṣṇu.
Thus, a man who gives cows well-adorned for the sake of a sacrifice to a Brahmin,
having made such an offering, shall obtain the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
Having delivered thirty families of servants and kinsmen from hell,
he shall indeed establish them in the world of Viṣṇu and of the high-souled Śiva.
Omniscient, perfect, pure, all-pervading, and sovereign,
liberated from the ocean of saṃsāra, he becomes equal to Hari.
By this very method, householders may attain heaven even without the yoga of knowledge, through the gift of a thousand cows.
Whether a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or even a Śūdra, with devotion and according to the extent of their means,
[should perform this] at the confluence of the Narmadā and Kapilā.
To a poor Brāhmaṇa who has been initiated and is adorned with auspicious marks,
during an eclipse of the moon or sun, at the Vyatīpāta yoga, and at the transition of the sun into a new zodiac sign (saṃkrānti).

O Bhārata, one should give [the gift] at the mouth of the *ṣaḍaśīti*, on the new moon coinciding with a Monday, on the full moon of Kārttika, at the beginning of a Yuga, or on any other auspicious day.
For the ancestors sing this verse, O lord of men:
"May there be born in our lineage a son who is supremely righteous. (RKS 60.22)
At the confluence of the Narmadā and Kapilā, and at Koṭitīrtha which grants liberation,
may he who gives cows along with their calves deliver us from hell.
For ten thousand years he indeed sports in the world of Viṣṇu;
therefore, O Indra among kings, you too become a giver of a thousand cows.
I shall now relate to you an ancient history concerning that by which those ancestors always rejoice in heaven like gods.
In ancient times, King Yuvanāśva was a highly illustrious universal monarch who,
being devoted to the protection of his subjects, possessed merit a hundredfold greater than that of Śakra.
The city of Ayodhyā, whose splendor was equal to the world of Brahmā,
was at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga the abode of one devoted to all dharmas.
Having saluted his own family priest Vasiṣṭha— the best of sages, who was equal to Bṛhaspati and Brahmā— in accordance with the prescribed rule, he spoke to him.
"In what place should one perform a sacrifice— at a sacred ford (tīrtha), in a specific region, or in a temple of the gods?"—
thus all the sages, headed by Vasiṣṭha, spoke this.
On earth, the holy site of Naimiṣa is auspicious and comprises all other holy sites;
there, a horse sacrifice becomes fruitful, exceeding ten million times ten millionfold.
O King, it was proclaimed in the Purāṇa by Viṣṇu in the form of a fish;
and it was proclaimed, O King, by Sūrya to his own son, the son of Manu.
Among all the Purāṇas, however, the one proclaimed by the Fish is the most ancient;
for in former times, when the Vedas had perished, they were recovered by him in the form of a fish.
"O Yuvanāśva, even the twice-born who are devoid of the Vedas perform sacrificial rites;
such is that sacred ford (tīrtha) which has been described to you."
Having thus heard these words of his priest Vasiṣṭha,
he then commanded his ministers, who were most righteous and speakers of truth.
"Taking the sacrificial implements, assemble quickly!
Let a proclamation be made throughout the kingdom by the servants with staffs in their hands."
Then the gods were summoned to the king’s sacrificial rite:
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Gods (Indra), Skanda, and likewise Vaiśravaṇa.
And Śambhu himself, who is especially honored by gods and asuras,
[bestowed] ten lakhs of cows accompanied by gold and jewels.
One hundred thousand horses and thirty thousand elephants,
as well as jewels, rubies, pearls, and infinite gold.
The king, together with all his followers, [offered] various kinds of substances— both solid and soft foods, ornaments, sacrificial materials, and whatever else there was.
With thousands of various vehicles, with kings arriving from various lands,
and with thousands of diverse musical instruments and enchanting songs of many kinds.
Making heaven and earth resound with a great roar of Vedic chanting,
he entered the sacred site of Naimiṣa, where the god Maheśvara resides.
Upon seeing Hari, the Lord, one is immediately liberated from sin;
this is truly a visible staircase to heaven, like the world of the gods itself.
Having bathed there and worshipped Hari and Hara, one shall attain heaven;
by the mere glorification of this Naimiṣa, a person burns away [their sins] at that very moment.
Like a fire upon a heap of cotton, [he consumed] the terrible multitude of those born of various states;
for the initiated brahmins had gathered there from somewhere like gods.
O sinless Bhārata, the king gave ten thousand of those ornaments to the distressed ones, and one thousand to the god.
"Oṃ, salutation to Śaṅkara and to Mādhava"— uttering this supreme mantra,
the king took water and *darbha* grass and placed them in a golden vessel.
Having thus resolved, O Indra among kings,
he caused a sacrificial enclosure to be constructed extending ten yojanas, complete with sacrificial posts made of gold.
Then the sacrifice was concluded by the twice-born led by Vasiṣṭha;
all the deities, filled with joy, mounted their celestial vehicles.
They raised a cry of "Victory!", yet the king was full of egoism, thinking, "There is no one equal to me; there is no one else like me."
Just as he had mounted his vehicle and departed from the Naimiṣa forest accompanied by his harem and retinue, he then beheld a monkey.
"Stop, stop! he then said, "O King, listen to my words:
what use have you for the performance of sacrifices or the ritual of giving to the deities?"
"O King, formerly, at the sacrifice of the lord of the gods, Satyadharma, you— your soul deluded by egoism— thought, 'I am the doer.'"
Except for my face, everything below my throat became the color of gold;
and as for those who had gone as children, all their limbs were likewise made of gold.
At the confluence of the Kapilā and the Narmadā, due to the flow of the sacrificial waters, by bathing, immersion, drinking, and likewise by stirring up the mud; RKS_60.54 //
The fourfold assembly of beings has reached the world of the Gandharvas,
for your sacrifice originating in the Naimiṣa forest has been disrupted.
"My body was smeared with mud and likewise washed with water;
yet no fruit whatsoever accrued to me, so your sacrifice was useless."
"Though you have given ten thousand cows, as well as much wealth and grain,
all that was rendered useless by King Satyadharma."
Even if the three worlds were acquired through charity or austerity,
Mekalā is indeed remembered as the mother of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
This has been told to you, O King, concerning what occurred at Amareśvara.
May it be well with you; I shall depart, and you should return toward Ayodhyā.
"I myself shall go to the Narmadā, which flows through seven kalpas;
for having heard of your sacrifice, I have come to the Naimiṣa forest."
"Dejected, I shall depart; my face has not been golden.
Having heard the words of the monkey, Yuvanāśva spoke these words:
"Who are you that speaks this truth to me in the form of a monkey?
The monkey said:
"I am the son of Jābāli, renowned by the name Kadamba."
O observer of noble vows, having entered the womb of an animal due to your own ordinary past actions,
you have wandered through all sacred fords while wearing this [animal] attire.
In that supreme sacrifice of truth and dharma, no protection at all came to me;
my entire body became golden, with the exception of my face.
Having heard the words of the monkey, that best of kings turned back and,
having propitiated the Lord of the gods, the Person of Sacrifice (Yajñapuruṣa), at Naimiṣa.
Having prostrated and propitiated him, he spoke these gentle words:
"By means of the gift, austerity, and observance in my sacrifice..."
Desiring peace, he, assuming the form of a monkey alone, caused [the king] to hear:
"Act in such a way that his face shall become golden."
The Lord spoke these words to King Yuvanāśva:
"Naimiṣa is a sacred ford visible before you, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns."
Naimiṣa is the sacred ford on earth, Puṣkara is in the intermediate space,
and Mount Amarakaṇṭaka is renowned throughout the three worlds.
And you have not heard, my dear, the ancient account proclaimed by Skanda,
wherein she is the mother of rivers and the foremost of all sacred bathing places.
By the chanting of its name, one is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence;
abandon your despondency, for Amarakaṇṭaka is the foremost of all sacred sites (tīrthas).
Furthermore, Satyadharma will perform a supreme sacrifice there at the confluence of the Revā and Kapilā, where his golden face is located.
"There will be no doubt for you, O best of monkeys;
having paid homage to Naimiṣa, to Hara, and to Hari, the primordial god."
Then, having heard the words of Naimiṣa, the lord of Ayodhyā likewise departed for his own abode, filled with supreme joy.
The monkey entered the holy city, just as Śakra enters Amarāvatī;
for Truth and Dharma themselves had gone there.
Having prostrated before the one named Satyadharma, he spoke these words: "At the confluence of the Revā and Kapilā, and at your great sacrifice," RKS 60.76.
From rolling in the mud produced by the ritual bath at the conclusion of the sacrifice,
my body has been turned to gold, with only my face remaining as it was.
"Having performed a sacrifice there once more, make my face golden;
thus may I become the lord of the Gandharvas, liberated again from this birth as a monkey."
When that best of monkeys had his body turned to gold there,
adorned with various ornaments, he [resounded] with the sound of divine drums.
Fanned by hosts of apsarases while traveling in a vehicle drawn by swans,
he went to the world of Śaṅkara through the power of this sacred ford.
There, all those wild beasts also bathed and went to heaven.
This ancient event has been related to you, O Pārtha, exactly as it occurred.
By hearing and reciting this, one obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows.
Thus ends the sixtieth chapter in the Narmadā-māhātmya of the Revā-khaṇḍa within the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS Chapter 61.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O great sage, having heard various kinds of dharmas through your grace, [I am now desirous of hearing more].
I do not reach satiety from the narration and recitation of the story of Narmadā.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Cows are an incomparable purifier; cows are the accomplishers of all goals.
Therefore, indeed, by the gift of a cow and through devotion to Śiva, one is liberated.
In whatever land one may constantly be endowed with devotion to Śiva, that land itself becomes purified; how much more so, then, the person together with their kinsmen?
"Six thousand [verses] have been spoken in the Purāṇa on the banks of the Mekalā," so said the knower of reality regarding the yoga of knowledge and the yoga of dharma.
The nature of the courses of dharma and adharma has been described,
along with the excellent narrative of the Narmadā, which is joined with the accounts of various sacred fords.
By chanting and hearing of him, one is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence;
[one obtains] the lore upon a divine throne, scented with garments and flowers.

RKS, Chapter 68.

The holy hermitage of the Vasus, of sages practicing celibacy,

"Therefore, lift up the wheel that has been set in motion and [protect] your own earth!

RKS, Chapter 69.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then [he went to] the auspicious Devapatha Tīrtha, which consists of all the gods.

some subsist on bulbs, roots, and fruits, while others subsist on water.

"All sacred fords come here to bathe; this has been declared by Śiva:
whatever fruit might be obtained at Sthāneśvara during the conjunction of Rāhu and the Sun," so it was said.

likewise, those who give silver, elephants, and slaves [obtain the same as] those who give gold, cows, land, and so forth.

even by Kubera the Giver of Wealth, nor by gods, gandharvas, and dānavas.

He who has entered a sinful womb, he who has entered the womb of an animal,

Wherein, in former times, the Grandfather (Brahmā) performed a sacrifice for the Lord of Sacrifice,

Homage to the subtle one, to the one whose form is subtle, to the cause that is most subtle of all,

Homage to the divine one, who possesses a divine form and a divine body,
the bridge for those who are divine, and to the most divine of all.
Homage again and again to the being of the splendor of space, who is non-terrible;

Salutation to the Supreme, to the Supreme Lord, to the ultimate cause,
to the Supreme, to the supremely liberated, and to the one who is higher than the highest.
Homage to you who have one tongue, two tongues, and many tongues;

to the eternal one who possesses both eternal and non-eternal forms, to the sole cause of both the eternal and the non-eternal.
Homage to the eternal among even the eternal, and to the most eternal;
to the powerful one, whose form is power, the sole cause of all powers.
Homage to the powerful among the powerful, and to the most powerful;
to the pure one, the all-pure, the sole cause of universal purity.
Homage to you, who are Time, who possess the form of Time, who are the sole cause of all time,

Homage to the embodiment of all mantras, the sole cause of all mantras,
the mantra even among mantras, and to the supreme mantra.
Homage again and again to Īśāna, the immeasurable Great Lord;
homage to you, O Yoga, the embodiment of yoga, the Person of Yoga!
Homage to you who have one throat, two throats, and many throats;
homage to you, the blue-throated one, endowed with innumerable throats.
Salutations be to you, the infinite, the great lord, the destroyer and the creator;
salutations be to you, O Mahādeva; salutations be to you, O Sadāśiva.

Homage to him whose limbs are smeared with ashes; homage to the bearer of the skull-topped staff!
Salutations to you, the Self of all; salutations again and again to the Lord of the universe.
Salutations to you, the omniscient; salutations again and again to the one who provides refuge.
Salutations to you, the unmanifest; salutations again and again to you, the eternal.
Salutations to you who dwell on Kailāsa; salutations to you who dwell in the netherworld.
By you all this—this world and the non-world, the moving and the unmoving—is pervaded;

Whoever praises the Supreme Lord with this divine hymn,
having shaken off all sins, is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Praise of Śambhu," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.

"Being alone, how can I mount the vehicle together with a woman?

"In this sacrifice, the Blessed Lord Hari, the Personification of Sacrifice, was not invited;

The mantra that brings about the year, the supreme authority, the highest austerity;
