He is the one of great consciousness, the omniscient, the possessor of seed, the remover, the destroyer;
he holds a water-pot, wields a bow, has the vital breath in his hand, and is full of majesty.
Aṃśa, Anīśa, as well as Śūlī, Khaṭvāṅgin, and Paṭṭiśin; Śuci, Śucirūpa, Tejas, Tejaskara, and Nidhi.
Uṣṇīṣin, Suvaktra, Udakya,
Vitana, Hari, Harinetra, Sutīrtha, and Kṛṣṇa.
Sarvārtha in the form of a jackal, Śuṇḍīśuddha with a water-pot, Aja, Gandhamālin, and [the one] in the form of a deer bearing a skull-cup.
Ūrdhvaretas, Ūrdhvasākṣin, Ūrdhvabāhu, Nabhaḥsthala, Trijaṭin, Nivāsa, Rudra, Senāpati, and Vibhu.
He who moves by day and moves by night, he who is well-clad and the lord of the quarters;
he who is the slayer of kings and the slayer of Daityas, the sustainer whose nature consists of form and qualities.
Hara has the form of a lion and a tiger, wears a moist hide,
is the Yogi of Time, possesses a great roar, dwells everywhere, and resides at the crossroads.
He who moves among the irresistible pretas, he who moves among the bhūtas, the Great Lord;
he who has become manifold, the possessor of great wealth, the one who is all things, whose course is radiant.
He who loves dance, the performer of dance, the dancer, and Balāhaka;
the terrible one, the great ascetic, the dwelling, the eternal, the mountain-bearer, and the sky.
He is to be known as the Thousandfold, Resolve, and Certainty;
he is Indignation, Forbearance, Skill, and the Destroyer of Dakṣa’s Sacrifice.
The destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, Sumahat, Madhyama, Tejo’pahārī, Balihā, Mudita, and Arcita— these are Bhava.
He is of deep resonance, profound, and the carrier of oblations;
he has the form of a banyan tree, the complexion of a banyan bear, and is the Lord, the All-pervading One.
Tīkṣṇabāṇa, Haryakṣa, Maheśa, Karmakālavid,
Dīkṣa, Prasādita, Yajña, Samudra, and Vaḍavānala.
Hutāśa, Hṛtāśāsya, Prasannātman, Hṛtāśana,
Mahātejas, Sutejas, Vijaya, and Jaya.
The course of the luminaries, success, peace, and even war;
the crested, the staff-bearer, the matted-haired, the flaming, the embodied, the weak, and the external.
Vaiṇavī, Pāpavetāla, Kālāgni, Kāladaṇḍaka,
Nakṣatravigraha, Vṛddhi, Aja, Gandhavaha, and Agraja.
Prajāpati, Hari, Bāhu, Vibhāga, Sarvatomukha,
Vimocana, Suragaṇa, Hiraṇyakavaca, and Bhava.
He is free from passion yet bears the dust [of the earth], the great practitioner, and he whose fame is renowned;
he is without beginning, the origin of all beings, the primordial one of all, the father, and the teacher.
He who has the form of a serpent, the great dweller, the one adorned with a garland of skulls, the knower of waves;
he who consists of three steps, the three-eyed, the unmanifest, the liberator from all bonds.
Sāṃkhyaprasāda, Durvāsas—who is served by all virtuous men—Praskandana, Vibhāga, and Tulya, who knows the divisions of sacrifice; [these are the sons].
He who dwells in all, who moves through all, Durvāsas, Bhairava, Yama,
Himavat, the maker of snow, the sacrifice, the sustainer of all, and the supreme wise one.
Lohitākṣa, Mahākṣa, the one named Vijaya, Viśārada,
Saṃgraha, Vigraha, Karma, Sarpa, and Rājavibhūṣaṇa.
Mukhya, Vimuktadeha, Dehacārī, Kardama, Sarvācāra, Prasāda, Khecara, and Balarūpadhṛk.
The serpent is a particle whose nature is to move through space;
it is wicked, fierce in form, like the sun among the gods, possessing rays of wealth and great splendor.
Vasuvega, Mahāvega, Manovega, Niśācara,
Sarvāvāsa, Śriyāvāsa, Āpadīśakala, and Hara.
The Sage, the Self-gone, the World, the Thousand-faced, the All-pervading Lord,
the Yakṣī, the King of Yakṣas, the Falcon, the Radiant One, and the Lord of Men.
Though appearing like one intoxicated with passion, he is great, bringing about both gain and loss;
he is a perfected master of yoga who steals away [the senses] and is the achiever of all aims.
Bhikṣu, Bhikṣurūpa, Vibhu, Ṣaṇṇāmṛdu, Tvaca,
Mahāsena, Viśākha, Yaṣṭibhāga, and Gavāmpati.
Vajrahasta, Viṣṭambhin, Viṣṭha, and Stambhana; Ṛkṣa, Ripukara, Kāla, Madhu, and Madhukalocana.
Vācaspatya, Vājasena, Naiṣṭha— the indicator of the stages of life (āśrama)—
Brahmacārī, Lokacārī, Sarvacārī, and Suratnavit.
You are Īśāna, the Lord, Time, the night-walker, and the sole sustainer;
you are the immeasurable, the unfathomable, the maker of rivers and streams, and the imperishable.
Nandīśvara, Sunandī, Nandana, Nandavardhana,
Nāgahāra, Vihārī, and Kāla, the best among those who know Brahman.
The four-faced one, the great Liṅga, likewise the four-liṅga;
the presiding lord of the Liṅgas, the presiding lord of the gods, the presiding lord of time, and the bringer of the ages.
The Lord of Umā, the beloved of Umā; the one who bears the Ganges, the steadfast, the excellent;
the one whose purpose is all things, the purpose of all beings; the eternal, the observer of all vows, the pure.
O Lord, how can he who is not born as a god by Brahmā and the others, nor by the great seers,
be praised— he who is the Supreme Self, higher than the highest?
O Supreme Lord, forgive our fickleness of tongue;
bring about the welfare of the gods and increase the prosperity of those dwelling in heaven.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard this hymn of praise, the glorious Lord Śiva, the Sovereign of the Island, spoke with a gracious countenance to the gods: "O deities, choose a boon."
The gods said: "If Maheśāna, the lord who grants boons to the gods, is pleased, then,
O Maheśvara, become the protector for the destruction of the Daityas."
Even one who is of evil deeds and base character, if he worships these five emblems,
attains that state which is difficult to reach even through great sacrifices.
There, in ancient times, Śakra honored the God of gods, the Lord of Umā, who is saluted by both gods and asuras, with a thousand names.
Endowed with the grace of Śiva, he then became the king of the gods;
there the Lord, the Master of Lakṣmī, was praised by the Giver of Wealth.
O descendant of Bharata, know that goddess Gaurī is named Mokṣadā;
and there is the Siddhaliṅga of Mokṣeśvara, which is saluted by gods and asuras alike.
By the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and humans,
the state of divinity was attained through the worship of the five liṅgas.
Kubera, Māruta, Varuṇa, and likewise Nirṛti;
Vaivasvata Yama, and after him the Lord of Naraka.
By the power of that *liṅga*, the highly illustrious son of the Sun,
formerly praised by others, became the lord and sovereign of that island.
Praised with devotion by the Thousand Names, Śiva, the most worshipful one,
was then adorned by Soma as an ornament upon his head.
Because Gaurī was worshipped by Rohiṇī, she became fortunate through that;
likewise, the god who wields the Pināka bow was praised by the stars during their favorable conjunctions.
Then, by those very [deities], the solar orb itself adorned the surface of the sky;
as did the diseases, Kālamṛtyu, and Citragupta the scribe.
Likewise, the lord Śakra, surrounded by these hosts of gods,
is most terrible toward the most wicked, yet full of grace toward those who are most righteous.
There were eight koṭis of those with hair standing erect, fierce and with distorted faces,
along with thousands of women devoted to their husbands and those who fast for a month.
And the preeminent city of the King of Dharma was filled on all sides with countless, delightful, and glorious sounds of joyful shouts.
Hearing their cry, Dharmarāja, together with the members of his assembly,
was dressed in white garments and adorned with white garlands and unguents.
Traveling on foot, he quickly went to where those who were seated in their vehicles were;
having joined his palms in reverence, he questioned those of auspicious deeds.
By what powerful yoga did you attain this great Dharma, which is the pinnacle of righteousness?
From which land have you come, and how was this merit acquired?
Mounted upon their celestial chariots, they said:
"Austerity was practiced at Kurukṣetra, and especially at the Gaṅgā;
for that is established as the gateway to all the worlds."
In reality, dharma and adharma, as well as your power and the causal factors,
are present at Vārāṇasī, Prayāga, and the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
The Pitṛtīrtha of great merit, as well as Puṣkara, Naimiṣa,
Kedāra, Bhairava, and likewise Rudramahālaya.
Ten million Sarasvatīs and Rudras, Prabhāsa, and the Moon-adorned Lord—
whatever has been performed as gifts, sacrifices, and austerities at thousands of various sacred fords [is all encompassed therein].
All this has been told to you, O highly illustrious son of the Sun,
regarding how others, having seen the King of Dharma, acted accordingly according to what was right.
They all spoke gentle words to the King of Dharma as he had been addressed:
"You are not the lord of those who perform virtuous deeds; Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva are the lords."
"But for those who delight in evil deeds, Yama himself is their teacher.
Yama said:
"Wait until I have gone to Kailāsa and returned."
Having spoken thus, O King, he went to Kailāsa, that best of mountains,
where Śiva and all the others, as well as Pārvatī and the six-faced Kārttikeya, reside.
All the deities praise the God of gods, the Lord of Umā;
some dance before him, leaping up and falling down.
Seeing Śambhu of such a form, blazing with splendor,
praising the God of gods, the wielder of the Pināka bow, with the Thousand Names;
Having prostrated with the eight limbs, Dharmarāja said this:
"What is said to be the destiny of those who have come to our city?"
Laughing, the god said to Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma:
"Let all those who dwell on the banks of the Revā proceed here."
"Let those who dwell as followers of other sects enjoy their pleasures in heaven";
having heard these words of Śiva exactly as they were, Brahmā and Viṣṇu [acted accordingly].
Pleased by the words of the god, Dharmarāja, the lord of all the hosts of gods,
arrived at that supreme city in a mere instant.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, all those spoken of by Śiva were sent to the world of Śiva;
likewise, others endowed with auspiciousness were dispatched according to their respective instructions.
"In a former age, I beheld this at the arrival of the deity on the full moon of Kārttika;
therefore, O Great King, one should go to that supreme Vaiṣṇava tīrtha."
Janārdana, the God of gods, has declared that the sacred field (kṣetra) known as Kokilā, which grants liberation from all sins, belongs to Viṣṇu.
O Bhārata, one crore and a quarter sacred fords reside right there;
having fasted on the meritorious eleventh day, one should light a garland of lamps.
O Bhārata, there is no returning for him to the mortal world so difficult to reach; rather, he shall travel in a supreme celestial chariot (vimāna) in which all desires are fulfilled.
There is no doubt that the ancestors obtain satisfaction for an incalculable period of time when a brahmin is satisfied; in that regard, there is no limit to the merit of the gift.
In this interval, whether powerless or even self-possessed, one who gives up their life shall become a king for ten thousand years in the city of the Vidyādharas.
Dhruva attained his status as Dhruva in heaven, blazing with the splendor of the stars;
likewise, other multitudes of beings were born among the wombs of mortals.
By worshipping the God of gods, the king attained divinity in heaven;
yet when the merit of the gods is exhausted, they become mortals, while through devotion and meritorious deeds, mortals become deities.
This distinction between heaven and the mortal world arises from the distinction between dharma and adharma;
nevertheless, Maheśvara is to be worshipped in whatever manner possible.
Whatever may be given to Śiva with a mind endowed with devotion—
whether it be Arundhatī, Bharaṇī, or likewise Sāvitrī.
By Ahalyā, Menakā, Marutvatī, and Rambhā,
as well as by hosts of Apsarases and throngs of Suras and Siddhas.
O Bhārata, by him who has worshipped Śaṅkara while taking refuge on the banks of the Narmadā, abundant enjoyments as well as liberation have indeed been attained.
He who, deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Śiva, does not worship the Earth, shall have neither heaven nor liberation; what then can be said of Kailāsa?
Nor, O lord of men, is one a fit recipient for heaven or sovereignty;
Revā embodies all sacred fords, and Hara embodies all the gods.
The intellect that consists of all dharmas is patience, truth, and austerity;
celibacy is the root of austerity, as is the restraint of the five senses.
Forgiveness, truthfulness, recitation, study, austerity, and the characteristics of self-restraint—
this has been told to you, O King, as it was told of old by Śiva.
And by me, O Indra among kings, the queen whom I have described to you was not spoken of as being common to you and your brothers, especially.
Dvīpeśvara, Kapileśvara, and likewise Narakeśvara—
one should rise and duly recite the names of these deities.
Having obtained the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrtha), one is glorified in the world of Śiva;
and when the flood of sins is completely exhausted, one attains a lifespan lasting seven kalpas.
That place where Śiva is present is the supreme Śivakṣetra;
by hearing of it or chanting its name, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "The Description of Dvīpeśvara," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS, Chapter 72.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
[There is] the meritorious confluence of the Narmadā, frequented by gods and siddhas.
Having bathed there and having worshipped Maheśvara, they go to heaven.
O bull of the Bharatas, in former times the Narmadā came into this world,
having been previously praised and saluted by the gods as well as the celestial rishis.
The mortal world, including all moving and non-moving beings, has been sanctified by you;
O Revā, you who have taken the form of water, you are the supreme portion of Hara.
You are Umā, Kātyāyanī, Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and Sarasvatī;
you are the goddess Cāmuṇḍā, Carcikā, and Revā—you who flow through the seven kalpas.
The auspicious Pravahā, the meritorious Mekalādrisutā who is praised, as well as Yajñayūpā, Mūrdhā, and likewise Svargamokṣapradā; ||| RKS_72.5 |||
She is the savior of all beings, the destroyer of sin, and the surging river;
she is Lakṣmī, Svāhā, and Svadhā, as well as Puruhūtā and Yaśasvinī.
O lady of virtuous vows, the entire world is pervaded by you in the form of water;
[you dwell at] Saṅgama and Siddhaliṅga, which are saluted by gods and demons alike.
"O Great King, everything given as a gift or offered in sacrifice here becomes inexhaustible;
the bathing and worship at the Narmadā are most wonderful."
O Yudhiṣṭhira, there were many thousands of celestial mansions,
equal to ten million suns in their splendor due to the networks of light from various jewels.
Having gone to the city of the King of Dharma, they made heaven and earth resound with the sounds of lutes and other instruments, as well as the chanting of the Vedas and similar melodies.
Once, having witnessed a marvel, King Vaivasvata,
as well as Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu [were present].
These seven sages, who investigate dharma and adharma,
were formerly established by Śiva, as well as by Hari and Brahmā.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O best of sages, O you who abide in the cosmic cycles, tell me how a person whose bonds of karma are not yet exhausted attains the supreme state.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: This was previously told by Viṣṇu to the high-souled Brahmā:
"I take refuge in the lotus-eyed god, Nārāyaṇa, Hari."
I take refuge in the Lord of the World, the thousand-eyed one, the imperishable, the supreme state,
the Blessed One, the master of the past, the future, and the present.
I take refuge in the creator of all beings, who possesses infinite strength and prowess,
the lotus-navelled Hṛṣīkeśa, the true and imperishable one.
I take refuge in him who is the golden womb, the womb of the earth, the immortal one whose face is turned everywhere,
the imperishable, the lordless, and who possesses the brilliance of the sun.
I take refuge in the thousand-headed god Vaikuṇṭha, whose vehicle is Tārkṣya—
the subtle, immovable, most excellent one who bestows fearlessness.
I take refuge in Nārāyaṇa, in Hari himself, the eternal one whose nature is yoga, the protector of all worlds, the steadfast Lord.
May that Lord Viṣṇu be gracious to me— he who is the master of all beings, by whom all this is pervaded, and who is the god who brings about the dissolution of the world.
May that Lord Viṣṇu, who is beyond the Grandfather (Brahmā), be gracious to me— he from whom was born in the past Brahmā, the lotus-born Prajāpati.
When the dissolution has arrived in the past and the world of moving and non-moving beings has perished, he alone remains as the soul of yoga; may that Viṣṇu be gracious to me.
May Vāsudeva be gracious—that Vāsudeva who is Truth, Time, Dharma, and the fruit of action; he who conquers the earth and is the source of all forms and speech.
Homage to you, O abode of yoga; homage to you, the abode of all, the bestower of boons; O enjoyer of sacrifice, enjoyer of the five [senses], Nārāyaṇa, let there be homage to you!
O you of fourfold form, abode of the universe, dwelling place of Lakṣmī, bestower of boons;
O abode of all, salutations be unto you, the witness, O Lord of the world!
Invincible one, whose single form is the universe divided into six parts, Vṛṣākapi,
Lord of Beasts, Time— salutations to you, O ocean of knowledge!
From the Unmanifest the Egg was produced; from the Unmanifest arose the other Lord, than whom there is nothing higher; to Him I have gone for refuge.
For Brahmā, Īśāna, and the other lords constantly meditate upon that Lord, who,
as the all-pervading one, stands supporting the entire universe with but a single portion of himself.
The Teacher is ungraspable and devoid of qualities; I have gone for refuge to him, who stands like a light in the midst of the sun and the moon.
May that Great-Souled One, whom they call the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña), be gracious;
as well as the other perfected ones and great seers who have attained realization through Sāṃkhya and Yoga.
May that Great-Souled One, by knowing whom they are liberated, be gracious.
Homage to you, O Auspicious One in every way, whose eyes, heads, and faces are everywhere!
O changeless one, homage be to you; O primordial concept, you who abide in the heart!
O you who transcend the senses, homage to you; O Supreme Self, let there be salutation to you.
And those who truly know you do not dwell in saṃsāra;
they are liberated from passion and hatred, and utterly freed from greed and delusion.
Being bodiless and well-protected, yet consisting of that [Self] within all bodies,
one [perceives] the unmanifest, intellect, ego, the great elements, and the senses.
Those qualities are in you, but you are not in them; they are in those [objects], but you are not they yourself.
You are unmanifest, yet not entirely immutable; you are the Lord, the master of the qualities.
The whirlpool is the cause, the non-beneficial; the Lord is established within one's own self.
Homage to you, O lotus-eyed Vāsudeva; let there be homage to you!
O Lord of the World, you are the Sovereign; what more could be said than this?
You are the bestower of liberation upon devotees, their preceptor, and the Lord of the gods.
For you are indeed the Lord of Beings (Bhūtapati), the master in birth after birth;
whether bound by egoism (ahaṃkāra) or likewise by the groups beginning with the quality of goodness (sattva).
May my sense of smell go to the earth; may my sense of taste go to water;
may my sight go to fire; and may my sense of touch go to the wind.
"May sound enter into space; likewise, may the mind have its cause [in me];
may my ego-sense enter into my intellect, and may my intellect abide in you. (RKS 72.40)
"May there be for me disjunction from all the instruments, the qualities, and the elements;
may sattva, rajas, and tamas enter into my own primordial nature."
I, a man, take refuge in the Lord of lords, the faultless Lord,
the thousand-headed God, the great seer, the creator of all beings.
May that Viṣṇu, the womb of Brahmā and the source of the universe, be gracious to me;
into the wife of Brahmā all things dissolve when the world of moving and unmoving beings has perished.
And at the dissolution of the summoned [elements], the Great Principle (mahat) dissolves into primordial nature (prakṛti);
and again it is offered by those two—may that Viṣṇu be gracious to me.
May that Viṣṇu, whose splendor surpasses the brilliance of Agni, Soma, and Arka, as well as Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, and the yogis, be gracious unto me.
You are the unborn path of the world, formless yet the conqueror of all forms; you are the new primordial matter, the Great One, the Person, consciousness, and the effortless.
He who has gone for refuge to that very one who is beyond all protectors and superior to all;
he who himself brings down a splendor like that of the moon and the sun.
May that Great-Souled One, from whom the directions are born, be gracious—
he who is possessed of qualities and yet devoid of qualities, both conscious and unconscious, and who dwells in his own self.
May that Great-Souled One, whose body is subtle and all-pervading, be gracious;
he is remembered as the Moon situated within the Sun, and [the Self] situated within him.
May that Great-Souled One, who is immovable and radiant because he is the reality itself, be gracious;
those who know your unity and multiplicity attain the Supreme.
He is equal toward all beings, neither hostile nor partial; he treats everyone with equanimity, free from longing, and does not favor those whose minds are set on other things.
May that Viṣṇu, who is to be known by his entire self, be gracious to me—
he who is this entire world of moving and non-moving beings, the fourfold collection of living creatures.
In you, that [universe] is woven like a thread through a string, like clusters of jewels upon a cord;
for you there is neither dharma nor adharma, nor again a womb or birth.
For the sake of liberation from old age and birth, he has gone for refuge to that very one;
[so too have] the senses, the qualities, and the inhalation and exhalation within the wombs.
This body, which perishes in the face of supreme calamity like mere wood, is my solitary state from birth; herein lies my rebirth.
My intellect is fixed on you, my life-breaths have gone to you; I am your devotee and you are my supreme refuge. When death has arrived, I shall remember you alone.
May those diseases committed in previous bodies enter into me;
O Lord, may they release me from that debt, as well as the sufferings caused by wind and the other humors.
It is the supreme excellence among all excellences, and the highest glory among other glorious things;
it is the merit that is the ultimate state for the sake of purifying all sins.
Having risen constantly at dawn, at midday, and at the end of the day, one should likewise recite the mantra incessantly; this brings about the pacification of all sins.
I bow down to Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Hṛṣīkeśa, Vāsudeva, Janārdana, the Lord of the World; may he dispel my sin.
I bow down to the god who holds Mount Govardhana, who is devoted to the welfare of cows and Brahmins, and who holds a mace in his hand; may he dispel my sin.
I bow to Viṣṇu, the bearer of the conch, the bearer of the discus, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the slayer of Madhu, the Lord of Lakṣmī; may he dispel my sin.
I bow down to Dāmodara, the lotus-eyed and imperishable one, who is filled with joy; may he, who abides for the sake of stability, dispel my sin.
Nārāyaṇa, Nara, the gentle one, Mādhava, and Janārdana;
he who bears the Śrīvatsa mark, whose form is auspicious, the glorious one, the bearer of Śrī, and the abode of Śrī.
I bow down to the beloved of Śrī; may he dispel my sin—he who is the Lord of all beings and whom they meditate upon as the Imperishable.
I have gone for refuge to that Vāsudeva, who is indefinable,
by entering whom one is liberated from all bonds and no longer undergoes rebirth.
I have gone for refuge to that Puruṣa,
who has assumed his entire Brahma-form, including all gods, asuras, and humans.
I have gone for refuge to him who creates the world anew— the god Janārdana, who assumes the form of Brahmā and whose form is the source of all beings.
I bow to Janārdana, who is eternally established as the very nature of creation;
than whom there is nothing else superior, and in whom this entire world resides.
I bow to Him who is situated in the center of all, who is infinite, and who pervades everything—
that which exists within all beings, both the stationary and the moving.
He is indeed Viṣṇu; may all my sin perish without remainder, for no action is performed that is not the work of Viṣṇu, whatever deed has been done.
In this way, my sin arising from the actions of many lifetimes is destroyed—
at night, as well as at dawn, at midday, and in the afternoon.
Whatever sin has been committed through ignorance by deed, thought, or word,
and whatever inauspicious act has been done— may all of that perish in an instant.
May all that go to dissolution like salt in water;
for one who inflicts pain upon others and engages in slander, no merit of birth has been earned.
May all longing for the wealth or the fields of others, as well as whatever arises from anger, go to destruction like salt in water.
Salutations again and again, salutations to Viṣṇu, Vāsudeva, Hari, Keśava, Janārdana, and Kṛṣṇa.
The royal sage named Nābhāga, a lord of progeny, performed an incomparable Vaiṣṇava hymn of praise at the confluence on the bank of the Narmadā.
O Bhārata, it was obtained by Aṅgiras from Brahmā, and from him it was received by Indra;
Vasiṣṭha then caused Nābhāga, the best of kings, to hear it.
Having bathed in the waters of the Narmadā and having given manifold gifts,
Nābhāga ascended a celestial vehicle and went to his own city.
He who praises Janārdana with this hymn of a thousand names shall not return again to the terrible ocean of saṃsāra.
Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "The Hymn to Viṣṇu," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS, Chapter 73.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the place known as Meghanāda.
There Mahādeva dwells in the midst of the water, remaining invisible.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O best of the twice-born, for what reason does Mahādeva reside in the midst of the water, avoiding both the northern and southern banks?
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O dear one, I shall relate to you in its entirety this incomparable and meritorious narrative, which brings delight to the ears, as it was heard by me in the Purāṇa.
Long ago, O dear one, in the Tretā Yuga, there was a descendant of Pulastya, a thorn to the gods,
a fierce conqueror of the three worlds who struck terror into both gods and asuras.
By virtue of the granting of a boon, he is unslayable by gods, dānavas, yakṣas, gandharvas, uragas, and rākṣasas as he wanders the earth.
In that delightful Devagiri, O lord of kings, there lived a great Dānava named Maya, who was renowned and arrogant because of his strength.
Then Rāvaṇa, having gone there, stood bowed in humility;
honored with gifts and marks of respect, he spoke these words to Maya.
Whose is this woman with eyes like lotus petals and a face resembling the full moon?
What is her name, and why, O Lord, does she perform such fierce asceticism?
Maya said: "I am Maya by name, the most excellent lord of the Dānavas;
this auspicious daughter of mine is my wife, named Tejasvatī."
Known as Mandodarī, she was performing austerities for the sake of her husband;
but having heard his words, Rāvaṇa became intoxicated with pride.
Becoming humble and bowing down, he spoke these words:
"I am a king named Paulastya, the destroyer of the pride of gods and dānavas."
"I entreat you, O illustrious one; you ought to give me your daughter, for even the high-souled Maya has recognized the lineage of your grandfather."
Having performed the rites according to the prescribed ordinances, the daughter was given to Rāvaṇa;
then the Rākṣasa, being honored by the night-stalkers, took her with him.
O Bhārata, that best among those who possess sons begot a son, and he sported with her in divine vehicles and celestial chariots.
Immediately upon being born, that great-souled one let out a cry by which the world was stunned, like the roar of the Saṃvartaka cloud.
Hearing that terrible roar, the Grandfather of the World was terrified;
he then gave him the name, "He shall be Meghanāda" (Cloud-roar).
Having assumed that name, he too, established in the supreme vow,
meditated upon Śaṅkara, the Lord of Gods, together with Umā.
Through vows, restraints, gifts, burnt offerings, and recitations according to the rules,
and through divine penances such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa*, he afflicts his physical body.
Thus, O dear one, on another day, having gone to Kailāsa, the upholder of the earth,
and having reached the Liṅga, he set out facing the south.
Having reached the bank of the Narmadā, the mighty lord of men, desiring to bathe,
set down [his belongings], worshipped the God, and performed his recitation of prayers.
O best of kings, desiring to go upon the supreme path in Laṅkā,
he held up a single raised *liṅga* with his right hand.
Then, with devotion, the son of Paulastya [Rāvaṇa] offered both the first and the second great divine liṅgas as they fell into the waters of the Narmadā.
Addressed by that supreme being with the sign "Protect!
Protect!", the second [liṅga] fell upon the northern bank of the Narmadā.
There is a most beautiful liṅga renowned as Meghanāda,
situated in the midst of the water under the name Madhyameśvara.
When he, desiring to lift [the earth], reached the seventh netherworld,
that night-stalker, having learned the resolve of the two gods, turned back.
Entering the sky, he departed while being honored by the night-stalkers;
from that time forward, that sacred ford became renowned as Meghanāda.
To the north, the auspicious Kheṭaka is renowned as Meghārava; to the east, however, is that named Garjana, which causes the destruction of all evil.
O Indra among kings, whoever performs a ritual bath at that sacred ford,
having fasted for a day and a night, shall obtain eternal auspiciousness.
O lord of men, whoever performs the offering of funeral cakes at that sacred site,
by him the ancestors are gratified in heaven for twelve years.
O lord of men, he who feeds the Brahmins at that sacred site obtains there the very fruit that belongs to yogis; of this there is no doubt.
Whether Agniveśa enters the water or undertakes fasting unto death, his destination shall be from which there is no return; so Śaṅkara has declared.
Thus, O tiger among men, this supreme Garjiteśvara has been described to you;
by its mere recollection, it brings about the destruction of all sins.
Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Meghanādeśvara," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS, Chapter 74.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Dārutīrtha.
Where Dāruka, the beloved friend of Indra, attained perfection.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O sinless one, how was penance performed by Dāruka in the past? O dear father, I wish to hear the ritual procedure that brings about the destruction of all sins."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall relate to you that wonderful ancient event which occurred there among the sages of purified souls.
The charioteer of Vajradhara was known by the name Mātali;
he once, for some particular reason, cursed his son.
Trembling because of the curse, O Bhārata, he pressed his auspicious feet against those of Indra, the lord of the gods, and addressed him there.
O Lord of the Gods, for me who have been cursed by my father and am now without a protector,
by what action will there be an end to this terrible curse?
Śakra said:
"Resorting to the bank of the Narmadā, propitiate Maheśvara;
remain until the end of the age, and you shall obtain rebirth."
Having been born again in the Yadu clan by the name of Dāruka,
he ascended the Lord of Gods, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace.
"A human being will be present there; from him you shall attain success.
Thus was he addressed by the thousand-eyed god, O Bhārata.
Having prostrated with his head upon the ground, he arrived there with his radiance destroyed;
having reached the bank of the Narmadā, his body was emaciated.
Devoted to various vows, fasts, recitations, and fire-offerings,
he [worshipped] Mahādeva, the Great-Souled One, the giver of boons who holds the trident in his hand.
He worshipped with supreme devotion until the dissolution at the end of the call,
having then become the high-minded one during the partial descent of Viṣṇu.
Having gratified the Lord of the World, he then attained a good rebirth;
this, dear son of noble vows, is the account for you of Dārutīrtha.
"I have previously related exactly as Śaṅkara told it to me.
Thereupon, King Yudhiṣṭhira’s mind was filled with wonder.
O lord of men, having bathed at that sacred ford according to the prescribed rites, the man looked around repeatedly, bewildered and with his hair standing on end.
Having worshipped the members of the assembly there and having satiated the ancestors and the gods,
he who, with a concentrated mind, performs the abandonment of the body right there—
Having obtained the fruit of the horse sacrifice, he rejoices in the presence of Śiva;
indeed, he who, being pure, feeds a Brahmin with devotion at that sacred ford, [attains the same].
He, however, obtains the supreme fruit of a thousand Brahmins;
[namely,] bathing, giving, austerity, burnt offerings, Vedic study, and the libation to the ancestors.
Whatever merit has been performed therein, all of that one obtains imperishably.
Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Dārutīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS, Chapter 75.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Devatīrtha.
Where the thirty-three gods, having performed austerities, attained supreme perfection.
Formerly, in the war between the gods and the asuras, Indra was violently ousted from his own kingdom by the dānavas, who were arrogant in their strength, along with the hosts of gods.
Having crushed the army with floods of elephants, horses, chariots, and vehicles,
those who were pierced took to the path, their bodies shattered by blows.
Oppressed by the powerful Jambha, Śumbha, Niśumbha, and others, along with the Huṇḍas and Grahas, they all approached Brahmā for refuge.
Having bowed their heads to the god Brahmā, the Parameṣṭhin,
Indra, Agni, and the others, led by them, addressed the Lord of Gods.
Behold, behold, O illustrious one! Harassed by the Dānavas and oppressed by their sons and wives, they have come to you alone for refuge.
Save us, O Lord of Gods, Grandfather of all the worlds!
O Sovereign of the Suras, there is no other refuge for us except you, the Supreme Being.
Brahmā said:
"O gods, resorting to the banks of the Narmadā for the sake of destroying the Dānavas, perform austerities; for austerity is indeed the supreme power."
There is no other means, nor indeed any mantra, nor sacred knowledge, nor even valor, that—
without the meritorious water of the Revā— can bring about the destruction of all sins.
Poverty, disease, death, imprisonment, and misfortunes—these indeed are the fruits of evil; such is my conviction.
Knowing this, perform difficult penance according to the prescribed rule;
it is honored by all as pertaining to Śambhu, and from that one shall obtain fearlessness.
Having heard those words of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin,
all the gods, led by Indra and Agni, came to the Narmadā.
O King, there the Viceroys performed extensive and most difficult penance with ritual resolves, and thereby they attained supreme perfection.
From that time forward, that holy place has been known as Devatīrtha;
it is celebrated throughout all the worlds as the destroyer of all sins.
In that regard, even one who possesses a faithful nature and is endowed with the prescribed rite,
if he performs the ritual bath with devotion, shall obtain the fruit of pearls.
Whoever worships that god, who is honored by all the gods,
obtains the supreme fruit of the horse sacrifice and other sacrifices.
O lord of men, he who feeds the brahmins at that sacred ford finds there the delightful Devaśilā, which increases great merit like a mountain.
For men who die through renunciation, there is an imperishable destination;
and he who enters the fire at Devatīrtha, O Yudhiṣṭhira, [attains the same].
One shall dwell in the world of Rudra for as long as the dissolution at the end of the aeon;
thus [are defined] bathing, recitation, fire-offering, self-study of scripture, and worship of the deity.
Whether it be a good deed or an evil one, at that sacred site it shall become inexhaustible.
Thus much, O Bhārata, has been declared regarding the ritual procedure as well as the origin [of the place].
The account of Devatīrtha is unsurpassed among all sacred fords.
Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Devatīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS, Chapter 76.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the excellent place known as Guhāvāsī.
There, the great god Śaṅkara dwells in a cave as the perfected one (siddha).
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O best of brahmins, for what purpose does Śaṅkara dwell in a cave?
O sinless one, tell me all of this in detail.
"O Lord, I wish to hear all of this, for my curiosity is great.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O king, O highly wise one, you have asked me a most excellent question."
Furthermore, even a detailed account of this from the Purāṇas cannot be told by me now,
for due to my old age I am one who has lived for many years.
Formerly, O Brahmins, there dwelt in the Dāruvana forest those equal to the gods:
the student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and likewise the ascetic.
And for those devoted to their own duty, the supreme state was proclaimed;
meanwhile, during the spring season, due to a certain circumstance...
Seated in his celestial chariot and traveling together with me,
Mahādeva beheld the abode of people resounding with the sound of the Vedas.
Having seen that goddess Muditā— who brings about the destruction of all evils through dwelling with those who have come and those yet to come— he spoke with a voice faltering with joy.
Having seen those female ascetics, the god spoke these words:
"O daughter of Himavat, they do not meditate upon any other god nor indeed upon Dharma."
Having heard these supreme words spoken by the God of gods,
she, filled with curiosity, spoke again to Śaṅkara.
O Mahādeva, as you have said, women are devoted to the duty toward their husbands;
therefore, O Lord, becoming the bodiless one (Anaṅga), disturb their conduct.
Mahādeva said:
"O Goddess, these words spoken by you do not please me, my dear;
for the Brahmins are highly blessed, and one should never do anything that is displeasing to them."
The Brahmins have anger as their weapon; Hari has the discus as his weapon. Anger is sharper than the discus; therefore, one should not provoke a Brahmin to wrath.
Neither those gods, nor those worlds, nor those nāgas, nor likewise those asuras,
are seen by these three worlds, for they have not been deceived by these camels.
He who generally causes agitation among those for whom the highly fortunate Brahmins— the deities of the earth— are pleased, falls away from the fruit of enjoying the celestial realms.
For them, dharma, as well as artha, kāma, and mokṣa, are certain;
knowing this, O illustrious lady, let this obstinacy be abandoned.
"For this is indeed contrary to the world if you desire happiness under your control.
The Goddess said: "O Lord, I am not your beloved; I am not one who acts under your command."
O Great God, O All-pervading Lord, perform here every act of suppressing injustice toward all beings; O you of noble vows, for you there is nothing impossible in this world and the next.
"O Lord, let this be done for me; O Master, my curiosity is great.
Thus addressed by the Goddess, Mahādeva, who is devoted to her pleasure and welfare, [replied].
Having assumed the form of a Kāpālika and bound his mass of matted hair with great serpents, the Moon-adorned One went toward the Dāruvana forest.
Having made a supreme helmet and likewise golden earrings,
he was clothed in a tiger skin and adorned with necklaces and armlets.
Making the earth tremble with the resonant sounds of his anklets,
and with the roar of his great drum that resounded like the bells of heroes;
When the time of dawn arrived, he went there to the Dāruvana forest;
meanwhile, all the brahmins there were subsisting on flowers, roots, and fruits.
O descendant of Bharata, having seen that great and wondrous sight of the god as he went forth accompanied by many who were reciting [the hymns] here and there, [the people were amazed].
The young women were intoxicated and defiled by passion;
seeing that supreme beauty, all those fair-faced ones [were overcome].
Then, as those women in the Dāruvana forest approached him,
they underwent many transformations upon seeing the god who moves with the speed of thought.
O best of kings, hear from me what happened to the wives of the brahmins:
they did not realize their lower garments had slipped off as they stood with their hands raised.
Desiring to give alms in that manner, she was unable to move at all;
having seen Mahādeva, a certain woman became proud of her beauty and youth.
Then another woman, struck by the arrows of desire, forgot the child resting on her lap who had fallen asleep, as she pressed her breasts with both arms.
Sighing, another likewise did not say anything at all;
in this manner, Maheśa moved none of those women who held their husbands as their deity.
Perceiving that they had been shaken, all those goddesses hurriedly went out to the door; Maheśvara, the god, having made them assemble together, [spoke].
Having agitated the assembly of women and vanished from sight,
he was then seen by the entire host of Brahmins who had arrived there.
When all the women were agitated by Hara, wrath took possession of them;
overcome with anger, a certain brahmin ran forward, raising his staff.
One with an axe in hand and another holding a handful of *darbha* grass— having all wandered here and there through that forest— RKS 76.34.
United as one, those great-souled ones spoke these words in anger:
"If anything has been given, if any oblation has been offered, and if our gurus have been satisfied," [then let this be].
"By that truth, may the Liṅga of the God fall to the surface of the earth!"—
thus, by the power of the truth in the words of those twice-born ones.
While the god was looking on, the linga fell upon the surface of the earth; a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the people in Lokāloka, O Bhārata.
The god’s linga fell upon the very earth, causing a great destruction;
as the linga was falling, a terrible sound arose there.
The mountain peaks fall and the oceans dry up when the deity’s *liṅga* has fallen; then the gods and dānavas, along with their celestial chariots, [perish].
Having assembled together with Brahmā Parameṣṭhin, they all,
with palms joined in reverence, praised the Lord with various hymns of praise.
Then the Lord of the World, the bestower of boons upon the gods, became pleased;
for even the God had fallen to the surface of the earth by the curse when his linga had been cast down.
Having gone to the Dāruvana forest, O Bhārata, he gratified the brahmins—
Viśvāmitra, Vasiṣṭha and the others, as well as Jābāli and Kāśyapa.
Having assembled together, they all spoke to the Destroyer of Tripura:
"O Lord of the Gods, even a great multitude should not be disregarded."
And having become endowed with patience, you will be free from weariness;
for this [endurance] is the supreme sign that the wives of the Brahmins have been destroyed.
O Mahādeva, this merit shall belong to you once it has fallen [to you];
that merit cannot be obtained through the Agnihotra nor by means of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifices.
O Rudra, whatever bliss human beings shall obtain through the worship of the Liṅga,
even that which belongs to the gods, yakṣas, gandharvas, serpents, and rākṣasas— [they shall obtain it].
"By the mere word of the Brahmins, this merit shall be attained,
as well as that fruit which comes from beholding Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Rudra."
One shall obtain the entire fruit of that linga upon seeing it.
Having been addressed thus, the Lord of the World prostrated before the best of the twice-born.
Filled with supreme joy, he addressed them:
"O Brahmins, you are a moving sacred ford, waterless yet fulfilling all desires."
By the mere arising of whose words people are purified of their impurities—
there is indeed no sacred ford, no barren field, and no mountain caves [that can do so].
The Brahmin is declared to be the most excellent, by going to whom one becomes purified;
so too are all the sacred fords on earth and the rivers such as the Gaṅgā.
They do not equal even a sixteenth part of a single word of the Brahmin.
Having greeted all the twice-born, the great seer was granted permission to depart.
Then Mahādeva went to the excellent bank of the Narmadā,
undertaking a supreme vow, to dwell in the cave of Mahārbuda.
The Blessed One practiced silence, always devoted to recitation and meditation; O dear one, when his vow was completed, he established Maheśvara.
Being praised by the gods, the Lord went to Kailāsa,
where he had established Parameśvara on the bank of the Narmadā.
For that very reason, he [is called] Narmadeśvara, the most excellent;
for whatever the best person practices, that very same thing other people do as well.
Whatever standard he sets, the world follows it;
having bathed at that sacred ford according to the prescribed rite, a man whose senses are well-subdued [attains the fruit].
Having worshipped Mahādeva, one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice;
likewise, he who offers sesame seeds, flowers, kuśa grass, and water to the ancestors [attains the same].
O Pāṇḍava, seven generations of his lineage rejoice in heaven,
that best of men who feeds the Brahmins according to his ability.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, gold or even silver given to Brahmins becomes inexhaustible through the power of that sacred ford.
By touching and offering water, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice;
one should especially worship [the deity] on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days.
Having reached Narmadeśvara, one has attained the fruit of birth;
so too has he who dies by fasting, whether in the fire or in the water.
His course is irreversible, as Śaṅkara told me;
this is what he proclaims who praises the supreme Narmadeśvara.
O King, he who listens with devotion shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Glorification of Narmadeśvara," in the context of the Dāruvana forest within the Revākhaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
Then, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme Kapilātīrtha; by the mere act of bathing there, one attains the glorification of Narmadeśvara. (RKS 77.1)
O king of kings, for one who bestows a Kapila cow at that sacred ford,
[there is merit] equal to the number of pores on her body and those born in her lineage.
For as many thousands of years as there are [in the duration of that fast], a man is honored in the world of Viṣṇu, whether he enters the water, enters the fire, or practices fasting unto death.
Whoever dies at that sacred site is never again born in a womb;
such indeed, O best of kings, is the entire ordinance prescribed.
What else do you ask regarding the merit and fruit of the sacred ford?
It is auspicious, conducive to fame and long life, the supreme destroyer of all suffering.
Having heard this, O King, a man is liberated from all sins;
thence, O Indra among kings, he should go to the supreme Karañjeśvara.
"There, O illustrious one, a Daitya of great fortune and world-renowned became a perfected being (siddha).
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Who was that perfected being of great fortune and great asceticism at that sacred ford?"
"Whose son was he, what was his task, and what was the time? Tell me, O twice-born one.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"In ancient times, O King, in the first age (Ādiyuga), there was a mind-born son of Brahmā."
O King, O sinless one, after a long time, he who was known by the name Marīci— a knower of the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences— had a son named Kaśyapa.
Then a mind-born son was born, like another Brahmā in person;
he was endowed with forbearance, self-control, compassion, generosity, truthfulness, purity, and straightforwardness.
These qualities, O Bhārata, exist and shine forth in Marīci;
likewise, the multitude of virtues and fame reside in Kaśyapa, the best of the twice-born.
Having understood this, Dakṣa Prajāpati gave his own daughters to be wives:
Aditi, Danu, and likewise eleven others.
Aditi gave birth to sons headed by Indra, for whom sons and grandsons were born, and whose brothers were innumerable.
Nāgas, pretas, piśācas, winged creatures, yakṣas, rākṣasas,
lions, tigers, boars, and others such as these.
O mighty-armed one, they were born from that Prajāpati Kaśyapa;
by them, the great triple world—both the stationary and the moving—was pervaded.
Likewise, another illustrious son of Danu was born,
endowed with all auspicious marks, known by the name Karañja.
O highly fortunate one, he performed very great asceticism like Bali;
then the Lord, the destroyer of Tripura, invited him to choose a boon.
"O Karañja, great being, I am well-pleased with you, O sinless one!
Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—whatever dwells in your heart."
Karañja said: "O Lord, O God, O Destroyer of Tripura, if you are pleased with me,
then make my wealth equal to that of my sons and grandsons."
Having said, "So be it," Mahādeva, accompanied by Umā and mounted upon his bull, together with his attendants, vanished on the spot.
When the Lord had departed from sight, that Daitya, filled with joy,
installed Mahādeva under his own name and went home.
From that time forward, O King, that supreme holy site became known as Karañjeśvara;
by merely bathing there, a man is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
O Great King, at that sacred ford one should gratify the ancestors and the gods;
he undoubtedly obtains the merit and fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
But he who should practice fasting unto death at that sacred site, O best of men, [attains the highest goal].
Furthermore, whoever should give up their life-breaths in fire, in water, or even upon the ground,
shall surely dwell in heaven for twenty thousand years.
He is born wealthy in an excellent family or in a vast lineage;
he knows the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and is proficient in all the treatises.
He will be born as a king or one equal to a king; of this there is no doubt.
Endowed with sons and grandsons, he shall be free from all diseases.
All this that you asked me has been told to you, O Bhārata: the fruit of the sacred ford (tīrtha) in comparison with all other gifts, according to reason.
This supreme majesty of the sacred fords (tīrthamāhātmya), when read or heard, is meritorious, destructive of sin, auspicious, and a destroyer of suffering.
But he who causes [this] to be heard at a *śrāddha* ceremony is devoted to his ancestors;
for him, everything shall become inexhaustible—thus did Śaṅkara declare this.
Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Karañjeśvara," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS, Chapter 78.
Now begins the seventy-eighth chapter.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme Kuṇḍaleśvara,
where the god Kuṇḍadhāra attained perfection, O best of monarchs.
O best of kings, having performed extensive asceticism that caused fear to both gods and asuras, Kuṇḍadhāra now sports while residing on Mount Mandara.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: In whose lineage was he born, and whose son was that great-minded one,
by whom Śaṅkara was propitiated after performing very extensive austerities?
"O sinless one, O dear father, tell me this in detail.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Long ago, O King, in the Tretā Yuga, there was a son of Pulastya named Viśravas."
O illustrious King, through my favor, a son endowed with all the qualities of a son, Dhananjaya, was born to that daughter of Bharadvāja.
Knowing that his son had just been born, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
together with the ṛṣis and gods, was well-pleased and bestowed a name upon him.
"O sinless one, because you were born from Viśravas and have become my grandson, I have therefore given you the name Vaiśravaṇa."
He himself shall become the protector of the wealth of all the gods,
the fourth among the world-protectors, or even the inexhaustible lord of the yakṣas.
The yakṣa Kuṇḍadhāra, the most excellent lord of yakṣas,
having attained a beautiful form and youth, was born as their son with the permission of his parents.
Resorting to the bank of the Narmadā, he performed extensive austerities where the supreme Vyāghreśvara Liṅga, known as Vyāghrakheṭaka, is located.
In that very place, Kuṇḍadhāra performed most rigorous penance:
standing in the midst of five fires during the summer, and enduring the downpour of rain during the monsoon.
During the cold season, staying in the midst of water and subsisting on air for a hundred years,
he then became a single thumb when that century was completed.
O bull among the Bharatas, it revolved around the sun like a wheel;
for four and five [days], the one whose vehicle is the bull was thus gratified.
"Choose a boon, my child, whatever pleases your mind;
I shall grant it, of this there is no doubt, for I am gratified by your asceticism."
Kuṇḍadhāra said: "O Lord, if you are pleased with me and have come here desiring to grant a boon,
then let this Liṅga and this Tīrtha bear my name."
Having said "So be it," Mahādeva Soma vanished;
entering the sky, he went to Kailāsa, the upholder of the earth.
And when he had departed from sight, O Lord, that yakṣa, filled with joy,
