Those two birds, who remembered their former births, were ill-behaved yet pleasing to behold;
while crossing all the sacred fords, they beheld Nārada.
The two Gandharvas said:
"O son of Brahmā, O one of auspicious conduct, O you whose wealth is asceticism!
Tell us, by what deed indeed have we two been liberated? (RKS 82.11)
Nārada said:
On the southern bank of the Narmadā is the auspicious hermitage of Mṛkaṇḍu;
indeed, the sacred ford known as Tiryagyonivimokṣa is considered supreme.
"By being immersed in the waters of the Narmadā, everything will be accomplished there;
then Heti and Praheti, having bathed well, will assume divine forms."
By a single bath alone, the two birds attained divinity;
having bathed according to this rite and meditated upon the god Sadāśiva.
O King, while those two were constantly established in meditation after having recited the Aghora mantra,
in that interval, O King, an auspicious [being] rose up from Pātāla.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, there indeed is a Liṅga possessing the brilliance of a hundred suns;
furthermore, there is Kukkuṭeśvara alone and Mayūreśvara as well.
The two Gandharvas, seated in their celestial chariot, went to the abode of Śakra;
by bathing at that sacred ford, a man shall not be born again in this world.
Having bathed and offered water with sesame seeds for the ancestors, one attains the supreme goal;
this holds true whether one gives up one's life against one's will or even under one's own control.
There is no returning for him again to the terrible ocean of saṃsāra;
even there, he is not among the worms, moths, birds, or reptiles.
Frogs and wicked trees, when dead, go to the auspicious state.
Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "The Glorification of Mṛkaṇḍa’s Hermitage," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS, Chapter 83.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Next, there is another supreme holy site at the confluence of the Candrabhāgā.
Candreśvara, the Siddhaliṅga, and likewise Siddheśvara again.
Ghaṇṭeśvara, Mahiṣeśa, and Aśvatīrtha;
beyond that, Vṛṣasena, Hayagrīva, and Śukatīrtha.
Then, O King, one should go to the Rameśvara tīrtha, which destroys sins;
situated on the bank of the Mekalā, it is the destroyer of great transgressions.
Formerly, in the Dāruvana forest, the wives of brahmins, having been deluded by Mahādeva, gathered there while sporting.
And while contemplating liberation, they took refuge on the banks of the Mekalā;
and as they took their pleasure there, their worship of Śiva was attended by them.
As soon as the empty space was filled with offerings of blue lotus petals, bilva fruits, jasmine, *jāti*, and *kunda* flowers, the *liṅga* suddenly rose up.
The Liṅga that emerged from Pātāla, blazing with the splendor of the fire of cosmic destruction, is renowned as Ramaśvara; it arose from the one who was sporting [there].
The Lord of Gods said to the women, "Let there be release from the curse;
now, having been cleansed of all taint, let all of you go to your own homes."
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the Gods vanished right there;
a man who bathes in that sacred ford shall not be born again in this world.
Indeed, those who die by fasting in the fire do not undergo rebirth;
[for them], there is the offering of water with sesame seeds and the ritual presentation of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) for the ancestors according to the prescribed rule.
Through the performance of *śrāddha* and through giving alone, the supreme goal is attained for the ancestors;
this was established in former times by Indra, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the Giver of Wealth (Kubera).
Then, O King, by the Rākṣasa Rāvaṇa and likewise by Indrajit,
prayers were recited, austerities were performed, and various sacrifices were offered.
O tiger among kings, those who have performed these deeds have indeed attained the supreme goal;
furthermore, I shall describe another excellent and captivating sacred site (tīrtha).
Know Hariṇeśa, Siddhaliṅga, as well as Dhanurīśvara,
Bāṇeśvara, and likewise Lubdhakeśvara.
Having worshipped the forms of the Liṅgas, one shall go to Śiva;
O Yudhiṣṭhira, I shall relate an ancient narrative concerning this.
O King, a hunter named Arjuna, born of a low caste,
while wandering on a hunt, arrived at the bank of the Narmadā.
Having seen the herd of deer running again and again, they all fled; only one deer remained behind.
That deer was killed today at midday on the bank of the Narmadā;
having fallen there lifeless, he has once again assumed a divine body.
He indeed went to the world of Brahmā in a celestial chariot yoked with swans;
once the deer had departed, the hunter was then filled with anxiety.
Furthermore, many great sins have been committed by me;
to what destination shall I go? Therefore, death is better for me.
Having thought thus, O King, he then fell into the waters of the Narmadā;
at that very moment, possessing a divine body, he went to the city of the Gandharvas.
When he had departed for the world of the gods, the bow and arrow remained in the water;
these four are renowned as the *liṅgas* throughout the three worlds.
One should proclaim the five liṅgas as Hariṇeśvara, Bāṇeśa, Lubdheśa, Dhanurīśvara, and Ramēśvara as the fifth.
O King, having bathed at that sacred ford, a person shall go to the city of Śiva; there is no returning for him again to the terrible ocean of saṃsāra.
O King, sins such as the killing of a Brahmin go to dissolution;
one who dies through fasting or in half-submerged water shall attain Śiva.
Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, titled "The Account of Rameśvara, Hariṇeśvara, Lubdhakeśvara, Dhanurīśvara, and Bāṇeśvara," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS Chapter 84.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having bathed there with devotion, he who is intent upon fasting...
One should keep a vigil throughout the night and diligently bestow gifts.
One should perform the bathing of the deity with the five nectars (amṛtas), and likewise,
having performed worship according to the prescribed rule, one should apply unguents as far as possible.
One who desires his own welfare should give after examining the recipient;
his ancestors remain satisfied for twelve years, without a doubt.
The donor goes there, where the stainless God resides;
having entered the interior of the house, he should remember His name according to his ability.
He shall obtain all the merit that exists on the Blue Mountain (Nīlādri) who performs a Śrāddha at Śūlabheda on every festival day.
And listen now, O King, to the specific fruit of his merit at the end of the month—
the merit that resides in Kedāra as well as in Kubjā.
Whatever merit is found at Kanakhala and at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, whatever merit is found at the Sitāsite, and especially at other sacred fords— [all that is obtained here].
A human being obtains the merit that exists at Arbuda as well as the merit on Mount Amaraparvata,
and the fruit of all sacred fords beginning with the Gaṅgā.
At this sacred ford, one obtains merit in that manner; there is no doubt about this.
One should offer libations to the ancestors and the deities, accompanied by the prescribed rites and mantras.
Having become pure and composed, that mortal indeed delivers ten generations of his lineage, both preceding and succeeding him, as well as those to whom he gives the sacrificial fee.
Having performed the previously mentioned ritual placement (nyāsa), one should offer the eight flowers;
listen now to those [flowers] along with the eight mental mantras as declared in the scripture.
The water-born, the lunar, the fiery, the windy, and again the earthly;
the flower may be from a tree, and the seventh is that which belongs to Prajāpati.
Listen now to the determination of these, including the eighth, the *śivapuṣpa*:
the lotus-born is to be known as water, while the gentle one is milk mixed with honey.
The incense and lamp belong to Agni; the sandalwood and such belong to Vāyu;
the tubers, roots, and so forth belong to Pṛthivī; and that which consists of fruits belongs to Vanaspati.
The offering to Prajāpati, food, the flower of Śiva, and worship;
non-violence is the first flower, and the restraint of the senses is a flower.
And the third is the flower of compassion; by these the deities are satisfied.
O lord of men, one should worship at this sacred site with austerity and devotion.
One should offer an umbrella, a fly-whisk, a bed, and likewise sandals;
by that mere act of worship, the three persons are honored.
He who performs the ritual bathing of the Trident-bearer with devotion shall dwell in the heavenly world for as long as the dissolution at the end of the eon.
One should likewise anoint the Lord of Gods with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), as well as with yakṣakardama, saffron, sandalwood, agallochum, and other such substances.
Those twice-born ones who perform worship with various kinds of flowers,
[reciting] the Rudra-hymn and the Puruṣasūkta according to their own respective Sūtras in this world;
The *iṣe tvā* mantra and others, the *Jyotiḥ-brāhmaṇa*,
the *Gāyatrī*, the *Madhu*, and the *Maṇḍala-brāhmaṇa*.
Those men who with devotion recite this divine mantra born from the Yajurveda, known by the name Devavrata, have gone to that city.
In ancient times, O Great King, there was one named Andhaka, difficult to conquer,
who propitiated Śiva by attending upon him for a long period.
"The Lord God is pleased; ask for a boon, O you of noble vows!
Having received the boon, the Daitya Andhaka then ran off in great joy.
And pure people were seen with vessels filled with jewels;
his hundred thousand women were seen with vessels containing unbroken grains of rice.
The Brahmins recited mantras accompanied by auspicious sounds,
while the king was surrounded by ministers and servants, along with royal horses, chariots, and elephants.
All those who dwell in the city congratulate him;
dwelling there, joyful and well-nourished, he is not overcome by the gods.
Knowing that he had obtained the boon, the gods were then filled with apprehension;
they all united and went for refuge to Śakra.
Seeing the gods assembled, Śakra spoke these words:
"Why have you all, the inhabitants of the triple heaven, come together?"
And how has this fear arisen? Tell me, O great asuras.
The gods said:
"In the world of mortals, there was a wicked and intoxicated man named Andhaka."
And having fallen into fear because of that, they came to you for refuge;
in the meantime, a fierce Dānava, arrogant in his strength, [appeared].
Then, O tiger among kings, Andhaka, mounted upon his chariot and equipped with various weapons, went alone toward the city of Śakra.
O best of kings, it was encircled by a golden wall, adorned with various mansions,
and always impregnable to hosts of enemies.
The Asura entered there as if into his own home with ease;
then Śakra, rising up, offered him his own seat.
Andhaka sat there upon the auspicious throne of Śakra himself.
Śakra said:
"What is the reason for your arrival here? Tell me, what is your purpose?"
"O Dānava, whatever wealth belongs to me, that I shall give to you.
Andhaka said:
"I do not desire wealth, nor elephants, nor horses."
Show me today your own Airāvata,
the great elephant who is the very stage for the splendor of heaven, and the horse Uccaiḥśravas born from the sea.
O Lord of Śacī, show us Urvashi and all others, as well as the three types of musical instruments and your other personal manifestations.
Having heard these words of his, Śakra too, overwhelmed by fear,
displayed all the objects to Andhaka.
Then, O King, having arrived together with the gods, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras,
the apsarases danced there to the accompaniment of various musical instruments.
O best of kings, having seen his mind thus deluded even after beholding the apsarases at that time, all the hosts of gods were terrified.
There, in various battles terrifying with discuses and vajras,
all the gods were tormented and driven to destruction in great numbers.
The Ādityas and the Maruts who were broken in the circle of battle moved about like wild beasts in the forest when trampled by a lion’s paw.
Thus, all those gods were rendered powerless by him alone; they turned their faces away, while he incessantly oppressed the subjects in various regions and villages by force.
Milk, vegetables, and likewise clothing are taken by shaking [the source];
he does not honor their words, being intent on tormenting his subjects.
Having seized the wife of Śakra, the Dānava also went home;
thereafter, the gods and Śakra sought refuge with Brahmā.
With elephants resembling mountains, with horses like unto elephants,
and with chariots that seemed to touch the sky, yoked with lions and tigers;
Even by means of tortoises, crocodiles, deer, rams, and likewise serpents,
the gods led by Indra attained the world of Brahmā.
Having seen the god born from the lotus, they bowed to the Lord and praised him:
"Victory to you, O God, Lord of the World! Victory to you, the cause of all manifestation!"
"O Lotus-born one, O best of gods, we have come to you alone for refuge.
Having heard these anxious words of the gods whose minds were purified, [Brahmā spoke].
With a voice as deep as a thundercloud, Brahmā spoke to Vāsava:
"O gods, what is the reason for your arrival? Indeed, why is there such paleness among you all?"
"By whom have we all been insulted? Tell me all of that.
The gods said:
"There is a Dānava named Anyaka, who is arrogant because of his strength."
By him all the hosts of gods were deprived of their wealth and jewels;
O Lord, having slain the hosts of gods with axes, discuses, swords, and javelins.
Having seized Śakra’s wife by force, the Dānava departed;
then, having heard their words, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, [acted].
The Blessed One then reflected upon the slaughter of that rākṣasa;
for that sinful dānava was incapable of being slain by any of the gods or asuras.
Then all the gods, led by Śakra, offered praise:
"Victory to you, O God, Lord of Gods, who possess half of your body with Lakṣmī!"
"O Lord of Gods, protect us quickly; therefore we have come to you for refuge.
Janārdana said:
"Welcome to you, O highly fortunate ones; welcome indeed to those who speak thus."
"Tell me everything that must be done; whatever cause I desire, let him by whom this defeat was wrought go to the abode of Yama."
Thus addressed, all the gods spoke according to the truth;
trembling and with their faces cast downward, they revealed their limbs.
O Lord, we have been deprived of our kingdom and defeated by Andhaka.
"O Lord, protect [us] like a father his sons; slay the enemy here along with his sons and kinsmen.
Having said, "So be it," the Lord, whose footstool is worshipped by gods and asuras, [departed for] the Lotus-Seated One.
Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Purāṇa, in the narrative of Andhaka’s penance.
RKS, Chapter 85.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having taken up the conch, the discus, the mace, and the noose, the Supreme Lord...
He rose quickly from his bed, bestowing victory upon the gods.
Keśava said: Whether in Pātāla, or in heaven, or in the mortal realm, O gods—
I shall slay that Andhaka by whom the gods have been tormented.
"O gods, whose minds are imbued with contentment, go to your own homes!
Having heard these words of Viṣṇu, Brahmā and the others, together with Indra, departed.
Having ascended their respective vehicles, they went to heaven with hearts full of joy;
thereafter, Lord Mādhava proceeded to where Andhaka was staying.
Having gone there, Hṛṣīkeśa discharged the fiery weapon (āgneyāstra);
and having seen the blazing fiery weapon released by Keśava, [the opponent acted].
Then he discharged the supreme Vāruṇa weapon;
by that arrow of the Vāruṇa weapon, the Āgneya was then dried up.
Andhaka reflected: "By whom has this arrow been discharged?
Whose is this manly prowess? Who shall go to the abode of Yama?"
Then Andhaka, filled with rage, moving along the path of his arrows,
saw that god arrived on the field of battle and spoke to him.
"O Gavaya, you have been gazed upon by my sight;
therefore, O deer, you shall not be able to escape from the tiger here."
Just as a mouse that has come within reach of a cat cannot escape its prey,
so too you are unable to do so, even though you stand right before me.
Then [he beheld] the Lord of the gods, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace,
with four white arms, and who was engaged in a duel.
Having seen the god Gadādhara, Andhaka prostrated himself on the ground with the eight-limbed salutation (*sāṣṭāṅga*) and said:
"Victory to you, O Kṛṣṇa! You are indeed the Supreme; O Viṣṇu, O Jiṣṇu, salutations, salutations!"
Salutation to Hṛṣīkeśa, to Keśin, to the Sustainer of the World, and to Acyuta;
salutation to the one with a lotus in his navel, salutation to the one garlanded with lotuses.
Salutation always to the divine Janārdana, who wears yellow garments;
salutation to Govinda, and salutation to him who reclines upon the ocean.
Homage to the one with a formidable face, to Nṛsiṃha who roars,
to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, to the one with a smiling face, and to the bearer of the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Homage to the one in the form of the Dwarf who strode across the three worlds;
homage to the one in the form of the Boar; homage to you, whose form is the sacrifice.
O Vāsudeva, salutations to you; salutations to the destroyer of Kaiṭabha.
O Lord, son of Vasudeva, salutations to you, O leader of the gods!
O Viṣṇu, Lord of the supreme gods, Sustainer of the world, Lord of creatures!
Homage again and again to those who even offer a salutation to you.
To Vāsudeva, the wise one, the lord of all beings and gods;
to that Viṣṇu, the sacrificial boar of immeasurable splendor.
"Salutations to you again and again for the manifestation of the qualities!
The God said: 'O Lord of Dānavas, I am indeed pleased; choose a boon as you desire.'"
"I grant you a boon today, as you now request it.
Andhaka said:
"If you are pleased with me, O God, and if you desire to grant me a boon here—"
"Then, O Lord, grant me a most glorious battle.
The Blessed One said:
"How can I grant you a battle when I have been further gratified by you?"
O Andhaka, there should be no anger toward you; how could I not fight if your mind is set upon battle? Of this there is no doubt.
"In that case, go quickly indeed toward the god Maheśvara.
Andhaka said:
"By the grace of that god, I shall be victorious throughout the three worlds."
"Tell us how one may wage war against that Śaṅkara.
Having heard this from the Dānava, the Blessed One spoke as follows:
"I shall tell you how you may have battle with him:
go to the peak of Kailāsa and shake it again and again."
When that mountain was shaken, the three worlds trembled;
its peaks fell down, shattering in many ways.
O King, the four oceans have become one on all sides;
Rudra, accompanied by Umā, has his consciousness attached to sense objects.
Trembling and falling down together with Pārvatī, Śaṅkara firmly embraced the Lord of Gods, and Umā spoke these words:
For what reason does the mountain tremble, and why indeed does the earth shake?
All seven netherworlds and the seven heavens tremble as well.
"Or is it the end of the eon, O Lord? You ought to explain this to me.
Maheśvara said:
"Whose evil thought is this that has arisen, even though he is one who walks by my side?"
If this [arrow] were to strike his forehead, he would go to the abode of Yama;
however, while I was resting in meditation upon Mount Kailāsa, I was awakened.
"I shall slay him, there is no doubt—even if he were the six-faced god Skanda.
Then Andhaka thought: "Even this man knows [who I am]."
He devised a stratagem by which he might be slain in an instant;
then the gods, led by Indra and Brahmā, assembled.
Having fashioned a divine chariot endowed with all auspicious characteristics,
some gods stood upon the wheels, while others were stationed at the tip of the beak.
Some, O King, were stationed on the axle;
some were situated on the yoke-ropes; some on the chariot-pole and the tip of the banner; and others were stationed elsewhere.
Having thus fashioned it from divine materials, the Lord of the World ascended it;
and Maheśvara set forth in anger toward where the Dānava was.
He tormented the Dānavas as the sun [torments] the sky;
there, neither the sun was seen, nor the quarters of the horizon, nor the moon.
Then the king of the Dānavas discharged the fiery weapon (āgneyāstra),
by which the entire host of gods was set ablaze with arrows.
Being thus scorched by arrows, they sought refuge with the God;
thereupon, the God of gods discharged the Vāruṇa weapon.
O best of kings, by that very Vāruṇa weapon, the Āgneya weapon was neutralized;
thereafter, the Dānava released the Vāyavya weapon.
And even the god, overcome with anger, discharged the serpent-missile;
there is no doubt that Māruta was devoured by the serpents who were possessed by wrath.
Then, the exceedingly powerful Dānava released the Garuḍa-missile;
by that [missile], the serpent-missile was split into a hundred pieces and was no longer seen.
Then the God of Gods dispatched the Narasimha [incarnation];
having warded off weapons with weapons, the two fought with one another.
O dear one, a battle took place that was equal in intensity and terrifying to both gods and asuras,
fought with discuses, false arrows, iron javelins, swords, and mallets.
Likewise, with calf-tooth-shaped arrows, broad-headed shafts, and beautiful karṇikāra-tipped missiles—
even with these various weapons— the Dānavas were unable to slay him.
Then, with his fangs bared and wielding swords, iron arrows, and javelins,
he pursued her as she went along with her face cast down in shame, like a daughter-in-law seeing her mother-in-law.
Their weapons did not touch their bodies, just as when a skilled woman from Gauḍa wields them;
thereupon, casting aside their weapons, they engaged in hand-to-hand combat.
Grasping each other's hands with their own hands, they struck one another with their fists;
they fought each other with various grips, hand-blows, and other such techniques.
And the Dānava also pressed against the god’s armpit;
at that time, the god Maheśvara became motionless and fainted.
Perceiving that he had fallen into a swoon, the Dānava thought:
"Alas, alas! A grievous deed has been committed today by this sinful and evil-minded one!"
"What indeed must I do here, or how shall I proceed?
Having thus taken that Lord of Gods, he then went to Mount Kailāsa.
Having released him as he lay there, Andhaka also departed in an instant;
then Maheśvara, the God of gods, regained his consciousness.
As soon as he saw himself standing in his own palace, he thought, "I have been humiliated by that evil-minded one."
Overcome by a surge of anger, the Lord set out toward the Dānava,
grasping an iron club weighing a thousand *bhāras*.
Seeing the Dānava, the god hurled [his weapon] at his head;
the Dānava, laughing in the battle, struck him with a sword.
Having seized that excellent arrow of Kubera, the Lord of Gods struck him in the heart with it, which blazed up at that very moment.
Then that Dānava, vomiting forth streams of blood,
turned face downwards there and was torn asunder by the trident.
Then the sinner, pierced by the tip of the stake, whirls around like a wheel;
and those drops of blood that fall from his body onto the ground, [they too become stakes].
From them arose the wicked Dānavas with weapons in their hands,
and because of those Dānavas, the god became repeatedly overwhelmed.
Then Durgā Cāmuṇḍā was remembered by the God;
the terrifying goddess arrived, accompanied by ten thousand weapons.
"O Maheśvara, Lord of Gods, command me! said the goddess, who had large fangs, a massive body, tawny eyes, and long ears. RKS 85.62.
The god said:
"O blessed one, drink as much of the Dānava's blood as you desire;
and O Durgā, take with effort that which has fallen upon the earth."
"You ought to provide assistance today in the slaying of the Dānava;
then all of them shall be killed by you by the thousands with your sword."
And Andhaka, seeing those Dānavas who had met their destruction,
then praised the god Maheśvara with well-composed words.
"Stay! Stay! the one of great strength cried out to the Lord of Gods regarding Caṇḍī, as blood flowed profusely from the wound pierced by his trident.
He filled the earth, girdled by the four oceans,
even though he remained stationed in the intermediate space and stood upon the tip of the trident.
With his shoulder held high, the god, raining down torrents of blood,
filled the earth with its mountains, forests, and groves.
Although Maheśvara was warded off by blood up to his waist,
he nevertheless reached as far as the heart of the god.
Then the gods became distraught, lost their way, and fled in all directions;
he, however, crushed the eight limbs of his own body.
And eight forms of Bhairava emerged from Maheśvara;
they were all terrifying with their fangs and uttering cries of "Hā Hā!"
"Let all those with hands holding skull-bowls, as well as those with swords and those who are maimed,
drink all the blood!"— thus spoke the Supreme Lord.
The blood they had drunk was exhausted; only the red [fluid] remaining on the ground was left.
His body was withered away, reduced to nothing but bones and skin.
And the Dānava Andhaka, who travels through the intermediate space, spoke thus:
Andhaka said:
"Victory to you, O God, Lord of the World, who bears Umā as half of your body!"
Seated upon a bull-throne, with the moon as his crest-ornament,
victory to him who holds a khaṭvāṅga staff in his hand and bears the Gaṅgā upon his head!
Homage be to you, O Lord, here for the crushing of Smara;
homage again and again, O Lord of the Gaṇas, for the destruction of Pūṣan’s teeth!
Victory to You, who possess a beautiful form, yet are formless; salutations again and again!
O eternal Lord of the Universe, You are the supreme goal for the highest women.
To you who always dwell in the cremation ground, who always possess the form of Bhairava;
you are all-pervading and the creator, you are the destroyer, and none other indeed.
You are the earth and you are the directions; you are light as well as splendor. You are the wind, the Great Lord (Maheśvara) in the form of living beings among all creatures.
You are Soma, you are indeed Budha, you are Guru and likewise Bhārgava;
O Lord of the gods of gods, you are Sauri and likewise the son of the Earth.
"O Maheśvara, by your grace, all these very things— the constellations that are seen in the sky, as well as the moon and the sun— [are manifest]."
Having thus praised the God of gods in many ways,
that Dānava bowed down to Maheśvara with his two hands joined together.
Śaṅkara said: "Excellent, excellent, O great being! Ask for a boon, O Dānava.
I am the giver and you are the petitioner; I shall grant whatever you desire."
Andhaka said:
"O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to me,
then I must indeed be established in your own presence, and not otherwise."
He is smeared with ashes, has matted hair, carries a trident, possesses three eyes, and has four arms;
he wears a tiger skin as an upper garment and a serpent as a sacred thread.
"I desire all of this, O Śaṅkara, if you will grant it.
While he was speaking from the tip of the trident, Maheśvara became pleased.
Īśvara said:
"I grant you today the boon that was requested by you;
as I previously declared, you shall become Bhṛṅgirīṭi."
Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Bestowing of Boons upon Andhaka," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS, Chapter 86.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having granted the boon to Andhaka, Śaṅkara, together with him, [departed].
And accompanied by Umā, he went to Mount Kailāsa.
Then the gods, beginning with Brahmā and accompanied by Vāsava, all gathered together;
joyful and well-nourished, they bowed down to that Maheśa.
The god said:
"Welcome to you, O highly fortunate ones, whoever have come here;
the Dānava has been slain there for your sake, of this there is no doubt."
"O Grandfather, because of his blood, my pain has become stainless and is no longer seen; tell me now, what must I do? RKS 86.4.
O Brahmin, I wish to properly undertake a pilgrimage to the sacred fords, both for the sake of your son and for that other one who was slain by me; of this there is no doubt.
"Arise! Let all those who have come here depart.
Then, together with all the gods, he set out toward Prabhāsa.
Having bathed in all the sacred fords from Prabhāsa down to the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, one still does not attain purity.
Just as a cloth that has turned blue never regains its whiteness,
so too, for the black trident, purity does not arise.
Then the god Narmadā, accompanied by the gods,
went there and diligently entered both the northern and southern banks.
Having gone to the mountain named Bhṛgu on the southern bank,
O lord of the earth, Mahādeva stayed there together with the gods.
Knowing that place to be enchanting for all the inhabitants of heaven and a preeminent sacred ford (tīrtha), the god Maheśvara remained there.
He pierced the mountain with his trident; by that [act], the subterranean realm (rasātala) was split open, and the trident became stainless, with no stain visible anywhere.
The Gaṅgā emerged from Pātāla by the name Bhogavatī;
there a sacred ford (tīrtha) arose, renowned as Śūlabheda.
When the sun enters there into Rāhu, the Sarasvatī becomes a source of great merit;
it is like a second confluence there, as at the junction of the white and black waters of the Veṇī.
There, the god Brahmā himself [worships] the supreme Liṅga of Brahmeśa,
on whose southern side the god Janārdana himself resides.
And Viṣṇu himself is present there, established within the sacred seats;
and there, O King, a line made with the trident carries water.
And that water went to where the waters of the Revā river flow;
there is a highly meritorious *liṅga* renowned as Cakratīrtha.
And at Śūlabheda, the Lord of Gods, having bathed according to the prescribed rite,
considers himself pure, with not the slightest impurity remaining in his body.
And on the northern side of that very place, having reached the god of gods, the teacher of the world,
the wielder of the trident, he worshipped him with great effort.
This sacred ford is the ford of all sacred fords, supreme and superior to all other fords;
it is merit exceeding all merit, and the highest destroyer of all suffering.
Having established a sacred ford there, the God of gods, the Teacher of the World,
then appointed protectors and installed Vināyaka at that place.
One hundred and eight guardians of the field (kṣetrapālas) diligently protect that sacred site;
they create obstacles for anyone who wishes to remain there.
Some worry about their families, some worry about agriculture,
and some, devoted to the acquisition of wealth, perform service.
Other people, devoted to violence, engage in indirect speech;
others, preoccupied with wealth, pursue the wives of others.
Others also speak thus: "How can one go to sacred fords when one's wife and likewise one's children are tormented by hunger?"
The auspicious hosts of the God protect that sacred ford from those men who have fallen into the snare of delusion and whose conduct is wicked.
Virtuous people who are steadfast attain the merit of bathing especially in the Payoṣṇī,
the celestial river, and the Bhogavatī.
And having seen this meritorious confluence, like that of the white and dark waters at Veṇī,
all those gods were delighted in their hearts upon beholding that sacred ford.
Having come into the presence of the God, they describe it to one another:
"O Lord of Gods, they know this sacred site to be equal to the Gayā-tīrtha."
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a sacred site more secret than this;
for even Brahmā and the other gods, together with the deities, worship the Trident-bearer here.
The hosts of Gandharvas, Yama, Varuṇa, and Vāsava,
as well as all the gods and asuras, [honored him] with dances, songs, and hymns of praise.
O best of kings, O lord of men, where the god was pierced by the tip of the stake,
three pits filled with water were formed.
O best of men, these [mantras] of Āryāvarta are marked with the great thunderbolt;
they cause the destruction of all sins and remove all suffering.
Having bathed at that sacred ford, a person devoted to fasting is liberated from the bonds of worldly existence, even if they are devoid of initiation and mantras.
Furthermore, he who, having bathed according to the rules, [performs the rite] with the five mantras indeed— namely,
the five mantras declared in the Vedas— and likewise with jars containing gold;
O lord of men, for the twice-born, a sacred ford consisting of ten syllables, five syllables, and likewise three syllables, when used separately, is praised.
O King, whether for a member of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya castes, or for a Śūdra or likewise for a woman,
one should perform the ritual bath according to the rules after meditating upon the three deities.
The man who drinks water with the ten-syllable mantra drinks it just as if it were drunk at Kedāra; of this there is no doubt.
Joined with five *repha*s (the letter *r*) and adorned with the syllable *kṣa*,
conjoined with two *oṃ* syllables— this is the recitation here.
He who performs a bath there according to the prescribed rite, with his senses subdued,
should satisfy the ancestors and the deities with water mixed with sesame seeds.
He who performs a *śrāddha* at the five sacred sites (*pañcatīrtha*) on the Gaṅgā indeed delivers his family— ten ancestors and ten descendants.
He who, being endowed with the prescribed ritual, bestows a gift there with devotion, attains the fruit at Śūlabheda; of this there is no doubt.
The fruit of whatever good deed is performed there is indeed inexhaustible; for in the sacred field of Gayā, merit is obtained in all undertakings whatsoever.
Likewise, at Śūlabheda, one gains merit through bathing, giving gifts, and libations;
and there, he who gives gold, a cow, land, or water with devotion [attains great reward].
Food produced by agriculture, beds, garments, and ornaments;
with food and other such riches, the house shall be filled on every side.
A pair of draft animals, a pair of oxen, a plough, and two new oxen capable of bearing the yoke—
whosoever should give these gifts to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas, [attains great merit].
Having recognized one who is learned in the Vedas, of noble birth, pure, and has conquered his senses, if one gives a gift to such a person, there is no end to its merit.
In thirteen days, one [unit] becomes thirteenfold.
Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Origin of Śūlabheda," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS Chapter 87.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O Indra among kings, Uttānapāda once questioned Maheśvara.
And what kind of people, O Lord, are the Siddhas, and what kind are those who are not to be worshipped?
"O Lord, tell me this regarding the ancestral rites (śrāddha), the daily sacrifices (ahnika-yajña), and especially giving (dāna): to whom is a gift not to be given?"
The Lord said: "As is an elephant made of wood, as is a deer made of leather, so is a Brahmin who has not studied the Vedas; these three are merely bearers of names."

One who is diseased, one with deficient or redundant limbs, one who is one-eyed, one born of a remarried woman, one who has broken his vow of chastity, and those known as the Kuṇḍa and Golaka— such persons are not pure for a Śrāddha or a gift.
A buffalo-herder, a low-caste man, a thief, and especially an old man—these Brahmins should always be avoided; later, he praises honor.
If a twice-born man accepts a gift without knowledge of the proper time, a gift should not be given to him; it becomes useless and fruitless.
O King, give to the poor; never to those who are already wealthy. Medicine is beneficial for the sick; what medicine is there for one who is free from disease?
Uttānapāda said:
O Lord, what is the procedure, and how is the rite of Śrāddha performed? You should explain to me by what means the gift is bestowed.
The god said:
Having performed the śrāddha at home with devotion, well-bathed and with senses subdued, one should remain silent and offer libations as many times as the prescribed number, without exceeding it.
Then, having gone to Śūlabheda and performed his bath according to the prescribed rite,
he who should perform the śrāddha ceremony at the five locations with offerings for the gods and ancestors (havya-kavya) and so forth—
And whoever should offer the piṇḍa-oblation with milk-rice, honey, and ghee, obtains that fruit at that sacred site; of this there is no doubt.
And he who gives sandals, especially to Brahmins,
shall go mounted upon a celestial chariot, surrounded by the immortals.
And one should give an excellent house filled with the seven kinds of grain;
he dwells in the heavenly world in a most excellent golden mansion.
And he who should give a sesame-cow along with its calf according to the prescribed ritual shall dwell upon the back of the celestial vault for as long as the dissolution of all beings lasts.
Whether in a house or in a forest, at a sacred ford or on evil paths,
whoever gives water and food does not see the world of Yama.
The gift of food is inexhaustible, as are the gifts of water and land;
there has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift superior to the gift of food.
Uttānapāda said:
O Lord, tell me how the gift of a daughter should be performed;
likewise, how the acceptance [of the bride-price], the gratification, the marriage ceremony, and the wedding furnishings are to be conducted.
To whom indeed should a gift be given so that it becomes inexhaustible?
Whether it be the highest, the middling, or even the lowest, how [should it be bestowed]?
Whether it be passionate, or even ignorant, or even leading to the highest good—
the Lord said: "Of all gifts whatsoever, the gift of a daughter in marriage is preeminent."
Whoever should give with supreme devotion, having approached with effort,
especially to one of noble birth, of good character, and who is a knower of virtues.
At an auspicious moment when the ascendant is favorable, one should give away the adorned maiden;
and he who gives horses, elephants, and garments with devotion [shall likewise attain merit].
His dwelling shall be there, where that state free from affliction exists,
by which that daughter— who is dearer to him than his own life— was bestowed.
By him this entire triple world, with all its moving and unmoving beings, was given;
yet that evil-minded one does not find pleasure in bestowing wealth for the sake of a daughter.
He shall become a *karmacāṇḍāla* and, upon death, a silkworm;
he who begs for the sake of a maiden, whether he be wealthy or even destitute.
O King, that mortal becomes unfit for company and is excluded from all matters; furthermore, whoever in his house should eat, being greedy of tongue, [incurs the same fate].
"He shall become pure by means of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, or else by the Taptakṛcchra.
The King said:
"He who possesses no wealth remains [stuck] regarding the marriage of his daughter."
"And how should one perform the marriage ceremony? Tell this to me, O Lord.
The God said:
"The marriage of a maiden must indeed be performed using one's own wealth."
There is no fault for a suitor if he pronounces the name of the maiden;
a gift given after approaching [the recipient] is the best, while that which is offered upon being invited is middling.
Service and the gift [of a daughter] when being proclaimed as inferior are fruitless;
likewise, the gift of a daughter should not be given to one who is incapable.
The wise and capable one may rescue [others], just as a piece of wood cast into the water;
just like a boat, the wise one may carry [beings] to the supreme shore.
But he who, having been one who has maintained the sacred fires, accepts a gift from a Śūdra,
attains the state of a Śūdra in this very life and, upon death, is reborn as a dog.
Futile afflictions arise for a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires when he accepts improper gifts; indeed, there is no calamity for a twice-born man that does not follow from such acceptance.
All of that he shall destroy, just as a shattered boat [perishes] in the water;
acquired through the power of excessive suffering, it perishes in that very instant.
In this way, merit earned through great hardship goes to the Śūdra and not otherwise;
furthermore, giving for the sake of obtaining a reward of a hundred thousand is a transgression.
O King, that which is given to those who are merely vessels of fame becomes fruitless.
Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Giving," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS Chapter 88. Uttānapāda said: At what time, O Śaṅkara, are the śrāddha and the gift to be performed?
How should a pilgrimage to sacred fords be performed? Tell us about hospitality.
Śaṅkara said:
Just as merit for the sake of one’s father is supreme and eternal,
so too is this sacred ford (tīrtha) supremely meritorious through bathing, giving, and libations.
And they perform the *śrāddha* especially on the beginnings of the four ages;
O child, hear now of the fourteen beginnings of the *manvantaras*.
The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, the twelfth of Kārttika, the third of Caitra, and likewise that of Bhādrapada; RKS 88.4.
Likewise, the tenth day of Āṣāḍha, the seventh of Māgha,
the eighth dark lunar day of Śrāvaṇa, and the full moon of Āṣāḍha.
The new moon of Phālguna, the auspicious eleventh day of Pauṣa,
and the fifteenth bright lunar days of Kārttika, Phālguna, Caitra, and Jyeṣṭha.
Indeed, the beginnings of the Manvantaras are remembered as yielding infinite fruit,
as are the northern and southern solstices.
On the third lunar day of Kārttika, as well as of Māgha, Vaiśākha,
Caitra, and likewise on the sixth of Prauṣṭhapada.
All those times for ancestral rites (śrāddha) become inexhaustible when a gift is given;
likewise for one who has fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Madhu.
One should keep a vigil at night in the vicinity of Viṣṇu’s feet;
likewise, one should give gifts according to one's ability, such as gold, cows, and garments.
He who performs the worship of Viṣṇu with incense, lamps, food offerings, garlands, flowers, and sandalwood, as well as the recitation of the Purāṇic narrative;
That twice-born man who mutters the hymn of the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas,
being liberated from all sins, goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
At dawn, having diligently fed the twice-born, he should perform the śrāddha ceremony and give gifts according to his ability, such as gold, cows, and garments.
His ancestors remain satisfied until the dissolution of the summoned world-egg,
and the performer of the śrāddha shall dwell there where the Lord Janārdana resides.
Then, on the thirteenth day, one should go where he who dwells in the cave resides;
having seen Mārkaṇḍa-Īśāna, one is liberated from all sins.
Uttānapāda said: O Lord, you ought to tell me how the most beautiful liṅga was established by whom within the cave.
Īśvara said: O best of the twice-born, that which is renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Mārkaṇḍeśvara is the Sāmaveda consisting of the Bṛhat and Rathantara [chants].
Having recited the Atharva-veda, the Atharvaśīrṣas, as well as the Hṛdaya, the Vṛṣākapi,
and the Śivasaṃkalpa, one is liberated from all sins.
He goes to the supreme abode where the god Maheśvara dwells;
and likewise, those who perform the washing of his feet with devotion [attain that same state].
Whatever merit they obtain through the gift of a cow, there is no doubt about this;
one should feed the Brāhmaṇas there with milk-rice mixed with honey and clarified butter.
By feeding even one person, he has effectively fed a thousand;
with devotion, he should give gold, silver, and clothing to the twice-born.
By that, those gods, humans, and ancestors are satisfied;
likewise, those men who perform their ablutions with devotion during an eclipse of the moon or the sun.
And he who performs the worship of the gods, especially the recitation of mantras and burnt offerings,
should give gifts according to his ability to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas.
He who should give there the jewel of a horse, the jewel of an elephant, and likewise a man of cotton, as well as a cart filled with the seven kinds of grain;
One should give a yoked plough and two young oxen capable of bearing the yoke; and cows, land, sesame seeds, and gold should be given as desired to a worthy recipient.
A wise person desiring their own welfare should not give anything to an unworthy recipient;
for the earth sustains all beings as its very self.
Then that [land], abounding in all kinds of crops, should be given to a Brahmin.
Listen further, O Indra among kings, to what the fruit of the gift of a cow is.
As long as both the feet and the face of the calf are visible within the birth canal,
so long is the cow to be known as the Earth, until she releases the fetus.
By whatever means possible, one should present [the earth] to a Brahmin;
by that act, the entire earth, together with its mountains, forests, and groves, becomes as if given.
And she gave away that cow, which delivered twenty-one generations,
with silver hooves, a bronze milking vessel, and her calf, as she was full of milk.
O lord of men, when the moon is seized by Rāhu, meritorious people bestow gifts;
yet there is indeed a limit to the quantity of every kind of gift.
During an eclipse of the moon or the sun, there is no limit to the merit of giving;
wherever cows are seen, there indeed are all sacred fords.
One should recognize that as a sacrifice; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Furthermore, if a person, having remembered that sacred ford (tīrtha), makes a journey there, [he attains the same merit].
Alternatively, it is heard that whoever becomes an attendant of Rudra [attains this].
Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Majesty of Śūlabheda," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS, Chapter 89.
The Lord said: O lord of men, I shall relate another narrative concerning events of old.
The great seer Dīrghatapas went to heaven together with his family.
Śaṅkara said: "The very powerful Citrasena, renowned as the King of Kāśī,
dwells in his city, endowed with all objects of desire."
That city, filled with people and adorned with various jewels,
was renowned as Vārāṇasī and was situated on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
Resembling Indraprastha, it was filled with herds of cows as white as Gaurī,
crowded with many twice-born brahmins, and resounded with the chanting of the Vedas.
It was adorned with various kinds of merchants engaged in buying and selling, with watchtowers, main streets, and festive celebrations.
Adorned with divine shrines for the deities and with groves,
it was beautified by delightful clusters of various flowers and fruits, and embellished by groves of plantain trees.
To the north of that [city] is a most excellent and auspicious grove,
renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Samandāravana.
Crowded with various trees and creepers, adorned with various flowers,
and filled with many *mandāra* trees, it is therefore called the Mandāraka forest.
A brahmin named Dīrghatapas always dwells there;
because he performs ascetic penance exceedingly, he is known as Dīrghatapas.
He remains with his wife; he remains joined by his sons; all five sons stand near him and serve him.
His youngest son, however, was Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, a man of great asceticism,
devoted to the study of the Vedas, a celibate student, and endowed with virtuous qualities.
Constantly devoted to the practice of yoga and subsisting on bulbs, roots, and fruits,
he dwells always among the deer, remaining in the form of a deer.
At the beginning of the day and at its end, standing before his mother and father,
the son of the sage always offered salutations with devotion.
He went once again to that very same forest, into a mountain cave;
there he played together with young deer, though he was destined by the king’s arrow to die.
The king said:
"While he was dwelling there in that hermitage, performing very long austerities,
how did his youngest son come under the power of death?"
The Blessed One said: Listen with a one-pointed mind, O Lord of the Earth, to this wondrous tale;
for by merely hearing it, one is indeed liberated from all sins.
The great king, the ruler of Kāśī, possessed of great strength and prowess,
known by the name Citrasena, dwells in Vārāṇasī.
While dwelling there in the kingdom, he spoke these words to his ministers:
"I shall go hunting; you remain established in the governance of the realm."
"Let it be gone," said the ministers; thus addressed, that lord of the earth departed.
As he proceeded toward the forest, parasols were seen [following] behind parasols,
and a vast cloud of dust rose there, kicked up by the feet of elephants and horses.
By that very [light], the entire circle of the earth, together with the sun, was covered;
there the sun was not seen, nor the cardinal directions, nor the moon.
And no trees were seen anywhere along the mountain paths;
yet there, O Great King, herds of deer were visible.
Then all the men, including the king and the princes, fled;
their multitude was dispersed, and they quickly went in the ten directions.
King Citrasena, the lord of the earth, set out upon a single path;
he went alone to wherever those deer had gone.
Having entered that inaccessible forest devoid of birds,
crowded with anthills, shrubs, and creepers, he was no longer seen once he had gone inside.
Alone, he saw only himself—neither the horse nor the foot-soldiers;
no one here knows [this], nor do I know [it] throughout the ten directions.
Thus did King Citrasena, the lord of men, fall into such distress;
he took refuge in the shade there, resting again and again.
Afflicted by hunger and thirst, wandering through the difficult forest and mountain caves,
he then beheld a divine lake adorned with clusters of lotuses.
Upon seeing the lake, which was crowded with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks and resounded with the cries of *cakravāka* birds,
the king of kings experienced a thrill that caused his hair to stand on end.
Having taken white water-lilies, he performed his bath there,
and offered libations to the ancestors, the gods, and human beings according to the prescribed rule.
He drank the pure water as desired;
having emerged from the water onto the bank, he saw a tree nearby.
Seated there, he reflected: "What work shall I perform?
Then he saw many deer seeking shade in that forest region.
Some there were facing east, others facing south;
some were facing the direction of Varuṇa, and some took their place facing the north.
Some fall asleep, while others stand with their ears pricked up;
in the midst of the deer stands the yogi Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, a man of great asceticism.
Then, seeing the deer, the king thought of striking them;
"Having killed one deer, I shall eat it at my pleasure. (RKS 89.35)
"By eating the meat of the deer, I shall become healthy;
thereafter, I will set out for Kāśī, seeking the path."
Having reflected thus, the sovereign king then took refuge at the foot of a tree;
holding his bow with the tip of his hand, the lord discharged that arrow.
As soon as that arrow was shot, all those deer perished;
among them, however, there remained only that one of great asceticism, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga.
Pierced by an arrow, he fell and cried out, "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! He let out a cry of "Alas, alas! and said, "By whom have I now been struck down?"
Whose evil thought has arisen, by which this mind [is directed] toward me,
while I stand in the midst of the deer and have committed no offense whatsoever?
Having heard those human words, the king was filled with wonder;
he went quickly from there and beheld the Brahmin, radiant with spiritual luster.
"Alas, alas! A grievous deed has been done by me today, by which he has been slain by my hand.
The Brahmin said:
"No success whatsoever shall be yours once I have met my death."
"The guilt for my death has been laid upon you alone now that I have met my end;
my parents are aged, and my brothers are indeed ascetics."
"When I have reached my death and attained the five elements, these brothers-in-law will perish;
they will become your victims—how then can there be purification for you?"
I shall tell you a means to accomplish it, if you so deem fit.
The king said:
"O great sage, let the means that is in your mind be told to me today; I shall perform all of it with diligent effort."
Śṛṅgin said:
"I ask you: from where or who are you, and how have you come here? Are you among the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, or Vaiśyas, or perhaps an outcaste Śūdra?"
The king said:
"I am not a Brahmin, nor am I a Vaiśya; I am not a Śūdra, for I am a Kṣatriya.
Śṛṅgin said:
"Take me to the holy hermitage where those two, my parents, are."
"Announce yourself and show compassion for me, who have come as a sinner toward my son;
upon seeing me, they both will show mercy toward you."
"Or they will employ some means by which peace shall be restored.
Having heard those words of his, Citrasena, the best of kings, [acted accordingly].
Placing that brahmin upon his shoulder, he set out toward the hermitage;
yet, unable to carry him, he rested again and again.
Then he saw that brahmin unconscious and his senses impaired;
Citrasena, however, released the shadow of the banyan tree.
Then, O king of kings, having rested and speaking again and again, the great ascetic Ṛṣyaśṛṅga [continued] while he was looking on.
The knower of yoga quickly attained the state of the five elements through the practice of meditation;
he then had that brahmin cremated according to the rites prescribed by rule.
Having bathed, however, afflicted by grief, he wept and fainted;
immediately thereafter, the king fell into a state of supreme agitation.
"How shall I go home today to Vārāṇasī, for I am slain?
Possessed by the sin of Brahman-murder, I shall offer my body as an oblation into the fire."
Or rather, on the basis of the sage’s words, I shall go toward the hermitage;
having gone there, I will relate exactly what has occurred to that great seer.
Having reflected thus, that king, the best of monarchs, went to the vicinity of the hermitage,
taking with him the bones of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga.
Standing on the path of vision, Dīrghatapas said to that self-realized brahmin seer:
"Come, welcome to you; please sit upon this seat."
"O Dīrghatapas, today I am your honey-mixture (madhuparka) along with the seat.
The king said:
"I am not worthy of even the guest-offering (arghya) from a great seer of purified soul."
"O Brahmin, your son who was standing in the midst of the deer has been killed by me.
O Brahmin, punish me, the slayer of your son; chastise me with a severe penalty."
"The brahmin Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, a man of great asceticism, was killed through the delusion that he was a deer;
knowing this, O brahmin, do what is appropriate."
Having heard his words, the mother went out from the house in a state of agitation;
then, crying out, "Alas, I am ruined!", she fell upon the ground.
Afflicted by intense suffering and tormented by grief for her son, she lamented, crying out "O son! O son! with a piteous voice like a female osprey.
"O son, when shall I see you, perfected in the study of the Vedas and devoted to recitation and burnt offerings, arrive at the door of my house?"
It is said that even throughout the three worlds, sandalwood is indeed cool;
yet the embrace of a son’s body is cooler even than sandalwood.
I wish to embrace you, my most beloved son;
deprived of you, I shall go to my death in great suffering.
Lamenting thus, wretched and tormented by grief for her son,
she fainted, overwhelmed and miserable, and fell upon the surface of the earth.
Seeing his wife fallen, and being tormented by grief for his son,
that best of sages then became enraged with King Citrasena.
Dīrghatapas said:
"Go away, go away, O great sinner! Do not show your face to me.
