one who has conquered the senses should perform the *śrāddha* for the deceased right there.
And having honored those devoted to the study of the Vedas with various excellent recitations, by means of cows, gold, clothing, betel, and food; RKS 95.12.
O son of Pāṇḍu, having honored a Brāhmaṇa at that sacred ford with ornaments and gifts of fine cloth, one should provide a meal according to one's desire.
O giver of honor, there is no need for deliberation here: he who casts off his body at that sacred ford with devotion shall possess a multitude of ten million [merits]. RKS 95.14.
O lord of men, hear now the merit that accrues at that sacred ford:
as long as the bones of a person remain in the waters of the Narmadā, [so long does his merit endure].
For that long the righteous-souled one dwells in the world of Śiva, which is very difficult to attain;
then, having descended from that state, the god returns to human existence.
The illustrious lord of ten million banners is born; of this there is no doubt.
Endowed with all virtues, he is wise and has living sons.
And he shall become a long-lived man, renowned upon the surface of the earth,
[honored] by Indra, Candra, Yama, the Rudras, the Ādityas, and likewise the Vasus.
Likewise, O Lord of the Thirty-three, they were all established by the Viśvedevas on the northern bank of the Narmadā out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
That man who, for the sake of a deceased person, should cause a palace to be built— O best among the foremost of men, he shall attain a happy rebirth.
Indeed, he who performs a śrāddha here with wealth acquired by righteous means—
whether they be Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, women, or Śūdras— honors them all.
O King, those men who listen with devotion to this greatness born of the sacred ford also go to the world of Śaṅkara, which is honored by the gods.
Whatever sin he has committed shall perish within six months.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme Kumāreśvara.
Agastyeśvara is renowned as the most excellent of all sacred fords;
it was here that Ṣaṇmukha performed austerities which destroy all sins.
O lord of men, through supreme bathing and feeding, he attained perfection;
O King, he became the commander of the celestial army, the crusher of all enemies.
From that time forth, having become possessed of fierce splendor and a great soul through his service at the sacred ford,
that holy site on the bank of the Narmadā became renowned.
But he who, with devotion and one-pointed mind, having conquered his senses, [performs this] at that sacred ford on the eighth and fourteenth days, especially in the month of Kārttika—
One should bathe the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain with curd, milk, and clarified butter;
there, singing should be performed and the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍas) should be made according to the prescribed rite.
O Pārtha, whatever is given there to Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the Vedas and constantly devoted to the six duties becomes inexhaustible, O son of Pāṇḍu.
O King, this supreme sacred site, fashioned by the Moon, is superior to all other holy places;
thus has the entire fruit arising from Kumāreśvara been recounted to you.
O son of Pāṇḍu, merit is obtained from the sight of Kumāra;
having died, one attains heaven—this is the truth spoken by the Lord.
From there, O lord of kings, one should go to the supreme Agastyeśvara;
there, the highly fortunate Agastya, the bull among sages, attained perfection.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O illustrious one, how did the perfected Agastya, that bull among sages,
born from a jar and produced by Mitra and Varuṇa, attain his greatness?
"Resorting to the banks of the Narmadā, tell all of that to me.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O great king, this great question which has been asked by you—"
I shall explain that to you; listen always with a one-pointed mind.
O dear one, in the former Kṛta age, the earth stood oppressed by a heavy burden.
Desiring to inform the Lord of the Gods,
O King, they ascended to the vault of heaven and spoke to Indra of the world oppressed by the burden of the Daityas.
Indra said:
"O beautiful one, Brahmā is the creator of the world for you as well as for me;
I shall go to the world of Brahmā along with my ministers and the gods."
Then they all went to the place where that lotus-seated one was.
Bṛhaspati said:
"O Brahmā, the earth has become supportless due to the burden of the Daityas."
But unable to bear that burden, the goddess goes to the netherworld;
therefore, O lord of the earth, provide a remedy for the earth.
"O Lord of the World, this creation was brought forth by you for the benefit of all beings.
The Grandfather replied:
"I am the creator of all worlds, born from the pitcher without a womb."
Agastya, a mass of ascetic power, is capable of warding off the Daityas;
from him alone arises the strength and splendor of all the gods combined.
On one side, [the fruit] arises for the foremost of sages; there is no doubt about this.
Having heard the words of Brahmā, all the gods, together with Indra, [acted accordingly].
In the same way, O Bhārata, they related another cause:
"O Lord of the gods of gods, that which Viśvāmitra intended to do has been understood."
And for the sake of Triśaṅku, this sacrifice was accomplished by Viśvāmitra;
out of rivalry with Vasiṣṭha, he brought forth the constituent parts of the sacrifice.
Competing with one another, he created the sky and fashioned another earth,
just as the Himalaya mountain [spans] from the eastern to the western great ocean.
Pervading the earth, he stands established as the accomplisher of the purpose of the gods;
thus does this Vindhya mountain vie with the splendor of Kauśika.
O Lord of the Gods, the duties of the gods remain unfulfilled by Kauśika;
O Teacher of Your Own World, consider how to remedy these two matters.
Brahmā said: "The one preceptor for this [Kauśika] was the brahmin Agastya, the bull among sages,
who was difficult to overcome when Kauśika was treading upon a wrong path."
Agastya will indeed be the breaker of the path; of this there is no doubt.
He is the teacher and the instructor of all who possess self-control; of this there is no doubt.
The expansion of this mountain, the opening of the path for the gods,
and the governance of the brahmin Kauśika throughout the entire earth.
"Capable of all tasks, O delighter of Mitra and Varuṇa!"—
having thus made this resolution, the gods, together with Indra and the Grandfather (Brahmā), [acted].
They went together with Vasundharā to Himavat, the lord of mountains;
there they saw the brahmin standing, a yogi absorbed in meditation.
Seeing that very firm and unwavering meditation which governs the path to liberation, the gods, together with Indra, Candra, and Varuṇa, began to offer praise.
The gods said:
"O Blessed One, O Pot-born One, grant victory to the gods!
Becoming gracious and well-disposed toward us, [remove] the fear that has come upon the gods."
Agastya said:
"O gods, what task has arisen that has brought you all from afar to me, who dwell perpetually in solitude?"
"Tell me what must be done by me; I shall perform it all.
Then, [he spoke] with a voice as beautiful as a lotus pond stirred by a gentle breeze.
The slayer of Vṛtra urged the Guru with his thousand eyes.
Vākpati said:
"O highly fortunate one, previously by you, for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods..."
All the oceans were drained by the Lord according to his will for the sake of the world; likewise, all the gods were destroyed by the Dānavas, who were arrogant in their strength.
All those gods were indeed conquered by the Dānavas and turned their backs;
in order to deprive them of their boons, the oceans were dried up in the past.
Now the distressed nurse beholds this earth, the sustainer of beings;
oppressed by the burden of the Daityas, the earth has sunk into the netherworld.
"O best of the twice-born, O mass of asceticism, you must go toward the southern quarter;
O great brahmin, establish the meritorious boundary between the Narmadā and the ocean."
"Bring about the prosperity even of the Vindhya mountain and accomplish the work of the gods;
for Kauśika is your younger brother, he who leads you astray."
Agastya said:
"I shall perform the work of the gods; remain at ease, O Earth.
I am going toward the southern quarter, for I am capable of restraining my disciple."
"I shall undoubtedly restrain the growth of this mountain.
The gods said:
"Having gone toward the southern direction together with the deities, he must be seen; of this there is no doubt."
O Brahmin, when the sun is situated in Leo, for those who travel with devotion, their wealth and grain will perish and they will find no happiness; of this there is no doubt.
"And he shall be seen for the sake of the gods' authority";
having made that promise, the deities, together with the Earth, departed.
As they departed from all sides toward Agastya, that mass of ascetic power,
the earth itself trembled at the impact of Agastya’s footsteps.
Kauśika arrived with the speed of thought at the place where the ascetic was;
and Kauśika, seeing his teacher, prostrated himself before him with the eight limbs of the body.
"I am blessed; I am delighted by the sight of you, O tiger among sages.
Having taken up a vessel for the guest-offering (arghapātra) provided with curd and unbroken grains (akṣata), he said this.
Having reverently placed dūrvā grass and sandalwood in a vessel,
he who was standing at the feet of his guru then spoke these sweet words.
"O dear one, let an instruction be given; you are my servant, O best of the twice-born.
Agastya said:
"O Kauśika, abandon this obstruction to the work of the gods."
If your devotion toward me, Viśvāmitra, is unwavering, you shall not engage in any action that would cause you to be dismissed from your divine duties.
Then you should avoid all engagement in the wrong path.
Viśvāmitra said:
"The teacher is the instructor for those who possess self-control; the king is the instructor for the wicked."
"In this world, Yama, the son of Vivasvat, is the teacher of those who commit secret sins;
yet, out of rivalry with Vasiṣṭha, Triśaṅku was well-petitioned by me."
"From this day forward, O best of the twice-born, all that has been renounced by me.
Having been addressed thus, he quickly departed for the very difficult-to-reach bank of the Revā.
Having reached the northern bank, he commenced his ascetic penance there;
for the Narmadā is purifying and destructive of sins throughout the three worlds.
Having made a supreme resolve, the delighter of Mitra and Varuṇa sat down upon a stone slab and performed extensive austerities.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, the pot-born Agastya, a man of great austerity who subsisted constantly on air,
was known by the Lord as one endowed with supreme devotion.
In the twelfth year, the Lord of Pārvatī appeared before him in person.
The Lord said: "Excellent, excellent, O best of sages! The sky is illuminated by your ascetic penance."
"I am truly pleased with you, O delighter of Mitra and Varuṇa;
for I am the granter of boons to no others for ten thousand times ten thousand years."

Agastya said: O Lord of the Pramathas, who have transcended the pond of saṃsāra, who are devoid of birth in created worlds, and who are difficult for the hosts of Asuras to perceive— salutations be unto you!
The gods of the Nandi-skandha hosts, deluded, suffer in vain;
as do the sages headed by Sanatkumāra, who are praised for their vows.
O Śambhu, O Lord, they do not know your true form; salutations be unto you!
All the deities, beginning with Brahmā, meditate upon you day and night.
"They do not perceive your form, O Creator; O God, let there be salutation to you! The Lord said:
"I am pleased with you, O chief of Brahmins, for you are one whose vital energy is drawn upward and who is not born from a womb."
"I have been won over by your devotion; I am pleased along with Umā.
Agastya said:
"O Lord of Gods, if you are satisfied, if a boon is to be granted to me—"
"O Maheśvara, supervisor of dharma, if you are truly the granter of boons, appear visibly within the water at this sacred ford at all times."
"O Lord of the World, by your grace, may I always be present upon this stone on the northern bank of the Narmadā as the performer of the rites for the gods."
Having said, "So be it," the bull-vehicled Lord of Mountains also departed for Mount Kailāsa;
he was not born from a womb, being endowed with the power of yoga and the wisdom of Śiva through the strength of his *liṅga*.
Praised by the hosts of gods, he departed toward the southern direction,
to a most meritorious penance grove frequented by gods and dānavas.
The tiger among sages entered the sacred Devakambala;
Suṣamādevī remained motionless, as did the Earth.
The gods showered flowers and repeatedly uttered cries of "Victory!
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O sage of excellent vows, please tell me what merit belongs to that sacred ford."
From beginning to middle to end, together with the Brahmins and kinsmen,
it is beneficial for all ancestors, for all sacred fords, and for all living beings.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O lord of men, the day known as Śivā, occurring on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Kārttika, is declared to grant liberation to the ancestors at all times.
Having fasted with devotion and being free from desire and anger,
a man who stays by a *śamī* tree should keep a vigil at night.
Engaged in conversation with the twice-born regarding that discourse through narrations of the Dharma,
he should again bathe the Lord of Gods at night with the clarified butter of cows.
One should kindle the lamp with a full jar, or half a jar, or even half of that, according to one's own capacity; one should offer clarified butter for the lamp and cause it to be given to a Brahmin.
One should bathe the Supreme Lord with the five nectars and the products of the cow;
at dawn, one should worship brahmins who are always devoted to their own wives.
People devoted to the constant study of the Vedas and avoiding the wives of others will become constantly intent on serving Śūdras and engaged in the activities of rogues.
They fall [into hell] by giving false testimony, being constantly devoted to accepting gifts,
having a disposition hostile toward the Vedas, and being hunchbacked and always physically deformed.

O Yudhiṣṭhira, those twice-born men who have limbs that are deficient or redundant are excluded from the śrāddha; however, those whose limbs are pure according to the Vedic injunctions are always to be honored.
By means of gifts of land, clothing, and especially the gift of daughters,
they should be supported with devotion during the times of *śrāddha* and at auspicious conjunctions (*yoga*).
There, for the sake of one's own welfare, the gift of a cow should be performed—
one that has a calf, gives milk, is bright, well-nourished, and endowed with good character.
With supreme devotion, he offered a woolen blanket, as well as wooden sandals and leather shoes,
a golden necklace, a patched garment, betel-leaf, and likewise food.
Abundantly adorned with the beauty of bells and ornaments, covered with a pair of cloths, possessing horns of gold and hooves of silver, and provided with a bronze milking vessel; RKS 95.104.
Having recited it with supreme devotion until the dissolution of all that is summoned, O Pārtha, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious, its merit is multiplied ten millionfold.
Whoever reads or listens with devotion to this narrative of the sacred fords (tīrtha) is liberated from all sins and shall even dwell in the world of Śiva.
Thus ends the ninety-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Agastya-tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS, Chapter 96.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then one should go to Ānandeśvara, who is saluted by all the gods.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, it was there that the supreme bliss of Rudra was born.
I shall describe that sacred ford which brings about the destruction of the sun's sin.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O best of the twice-born, joy has indeed arisen within Rudra.
"Tell me, O illustrious one, O best of sages, in brief.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O best of kings, I shall tell you of the supreme Ānandeśvara."
Having brought about the slaughter of the Dānavas, Śaṅkara, the God of gods,
was worshipped by all the deities, as well as by the Kinnaras, Yakṣas, and Pannagas.
Having attained supreme bliss, the one whose vehicle is the bull danced;
having assumed the form of Bhairava, Gaurī was held as half of his body.
Surrounded by terrifying spirits, vetālas, and skeletons,
Bhairava dwells on the northern bank of the Narmadā, O son of Pāṇḍu, while [the other] is on the southern bank.
There, the lotus-seated Lord was installed by the delighted hosts of Maruts;
from that time forth, O God, he is called Ānandeśvara.
O lord of men, on the eighth, the fourteenth, and the full moon day,
having bathed according to the prescribed rite, one should worship the gods and anoint them with fragrant unguents.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, one should honor the Brahmins there according to one's ability;
likewise, the gift of cows and the gift of clothing should be performed there.
On the thirteenth day of the month of Vasant, one should perform the Śrāddha ceremony right there with *iṅguda*,
*badara*, or *bilva* fruits, or with unbroken rice grains and water.
One should perform the śrāddha for the pretas at the Ānandeśvara Tīrtha;
those pretas shall remain joyful until the dissolution of the world at the end of the kalpa.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, for them there shall be continuity, wealth, and happiness throughout seven births, and there shall be joy in birth after birth.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Mātṛtīrtha,
situated near the confluence on the southern bank of the Narmadā.
O Indra among kings, the Mothers were born there on the bank of the Narmadā;
there, Umā requested him [to wear] a serpent as a sacred thread.
He said to the host of yoginīs, "Alas, alas! This is not auspicious.
And he said, "I am the giver of boons, the bestower of boons upon the host of yogins."
The Yoginīs said:
"O Maheśvara, by your grace we are invincible to all the gods;
we shall become renowned upon the surface of the earth in the enumeration of sacred pilgrimage sites."
"So be it," said the Yoginīs, and they vanished right there.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O mortal, whoever at that sacred ford on the ninth day, having subdued his senses and having fasted, worships the circle of Mothers with supreme devotion,"
O Yudhiṣṭhira, those Mothers were pleased with him, as was he whose vehicle is the bull; for her who was barren, whose children had died, and who was childless.
There, the best of Brahmins, who are knowers of mantras, should commence the ceremonial bathing (snapana) with a water-pot containing gold, endowed with the five jewels and fruits.
And a woman desiring sons should bathe [the child] with a bell-metal vessel while reciting the mantra;
that woman obtains sons who are endowed with vigor and possessed of virtues.
O King, whatever desire she might contemplate, that very thing she obtains;
O son of Pāṇḍu, there is no other sacred ford superior to Mātṛtīrtha.
Immediately after that, O dear one, is the supreme Lord in the midst of the water,
renowned as Liṅgeśvara, who is saluted by gods and demons alike.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
How was that Revā not abandoned, yet abandoned by Śambhu?
For how could the wielder of the trident, the bearer of the Pināka bow, remain in the midst of the water?
"Therefore, O best of the twice-born, I wish to hear this from your words.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O son of Pāṇḍu, it is a source of wonder in this world, a firm foundation [of dharma]."
"O best of kings, I speak as a wise man out of my advanced age.
O dear one, in the beginning, during the Kṛtayuga, there was a Dānava arrogant in his strength."
Known as Kālabāṣpa, he who was invincible even to the gods and the Dānavas performed extensive penance in the auspicious waters of the Narmadā.
Worshiping Mahādeva intensely with fierce austerity,
the Blessed Maheśvara, together with his consort, was then highly pleased.
The Lord said: "O child, choose a boon; I am pleased with your devotion.
Having heard the words of the God, Kālabāṣpa spoke these words:
"The gods themselves were defeated by me through your grace, O wielder of the trident;
moreover, I was disheartened in battle, and for that reason I performed this propitiation."
"O Maheśvara, grant me this boon: that man upon whose head I place my hand shall not live in this world."
The Lord said: "O Daitya, that which you have desired shall come to pass exactly so.
Having heard these words, the Daitya rushed toward Śambhu himself.
"I shall place my hand upon your head; that word of yours is not true.
Rudra has fled, and for that reason he has gone to Keśava for refuge."
Having offered everything to Keśava, he dissolved right there.
Keśava said:
"O Mahādeva, I shall slay that wicked lord of the Daitya folk."
"O Maheśvara, I shall place my hand upon his very head";
then, having arrived in haste, he entered onto the bank of the Namadā.
And Kṛṣṇa, wearing the dress of a woman and endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great being, came into the presence of the Daitya, impelled by the arrows of Love.
Having meditated upon Śambhu in Madhumāthavaka, Suśīlā, who was everywhere devoted to Keśava, wandered through the forest everywhere, [finally reaching] a banyan tree.
Agitating the minds as it were, O delighter of the Dharma, she took her pleasure;
and that wicked Daitya Kālabāṣpa continued to run about.
He entered the delightful forest where that fair-eyed woman was;
"I shall become your husband, invincible by gods and dānavas."
“You are the mistress of the three worlds; be gracious to me, O beautiful one.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
“If you consider me your wife, and if there may be proof for me,” RKS 96.40.
The Dānava said:
"O slender-limbed one, I myself shall make an oath as my proof;
I will do that, for this is my truthful word."
The woman said:
"O highly fortunate one, do this; let your head be placed in my hand.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O Indra among kings, it was by one blinded by desire alone that the hand was placed upon his head.
At that very moment, he became ashes like a heap of straw consumed by fire;
then, a rain of flowers fell upon Keśava.
All the gods, freed from their feverish distress, went to heaven, to their own abodes;
and Viṣṇu entered the ocean of milk once Kālabāṣpa had been struck down.
Whoever should listen with devotion to this account of the Dānava,
and whoever, free from desire and anger, should perform a śrāddha ceremony right there;
By him all his ancestors have indeed been rescued from hell;
for he who gives [a gift] in that sacred field to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas.
The entire fruit of his giving surpasses that of Kurukṣetra for one who touches this linga fashioned by Śaṅkara.
But a human being who merely touches it is born as a dweller of Rudra;
for this reason, O King, the world-protectors and the deities [venerate it].
Likewise, Durgādevī and the four-armed Madhuhantā,
as well as all the foremost among the Dānavas, were also engaged in the protection of the Lord.
And they always protect [the household] through their domestic duties,
acting like sons and brothers while maintaining the nature of their relationship with the master.
But Liṅgeśvara, O king of kings, is protected even today by the gods.
Thus ends the ninety-sixth chapter, titled "The Slaying of Bhasmāsura," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS, Chapter 97.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme Dhanadatīrtha.
On the southern bank of the Narmadā, it causes the destruction of all sins.
The fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas) is obtained there; of this there is no doubt.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra, one who has conquered the senses [should perform the rite].
Having observed the fast with supreme devotion, one should keep a vigil at night;
O King of kings, one should bathe the omnipresent Lord, the giver of boons, with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
One should worship with devotion and provide songs and instrumental music;
one who desires their own welfare should worship the Brahmins at dawn.
Those who are not liberated from accepting gifts, yet are proponents of knowledge and established doctrines,
should indeed be supported with affection and devotion by their loved ones, while remaining free from criticism.
One should worship with cows, gold, clothing, and ornaments, and by the gift of elephants, horses, and chariots; thus, the destruction of all evil occurs.
By the power of Dhanada, the sin produced over three lifetimes is destroyed;
it bestows heaven upon the ill-behaved and liberation upon those who are disciplined.
O tiger among men, he shall be wealthy in birth after birth;
he shall possess noble lineage and a beautiful form, and there shall be no suffering for him at all.
They have no fear of disease; they shall rejoice from serving the Giver of Wealth (Kubera), for he indeed bestows knowledge at the sacred ford of wealth.
He goes to the world of the Sun, freed from all suffering.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall relate to you an ancient history.
Kaśyapa had two wives, unsurpassed in all the worlds;
Garuḍa is known as the son of Vinatā, and the serpents as the sons of Kadrū.
"O dear one, by means of contentment, two [daughters] lived in the house of Kāśyapa;
there were Kadrū and Vinatā, both of whom were beloved."
Kaśyapa, the lord of creatures, also sported with Vinatā;
then one day, O Pārtha, she was staying in the hermitage, looking most beautiful.
"Behold, behold, O slender-limbed one, the horse Uccaiḥśravas, possessing exceeding speed, stationed in the sky— a horse that is white all over."
To him who was running without rest, with speed like that of the mind,
Kadrū said:
"O slender-limbed one, why do you speak of this black one as white?"
"If you have spoken untruth, O blessed lady, you shall go to the world of Yama.
Vinatā said:
"Let this word of mine now be a wager between us regarding truth and falsehood."
If my word be untrue, O Kṛṣṇa— then for a thousand years he shall go about offering [himself] while remaining unaware that he is Uccaiḥśravas.
"Then indeed I shall always be a slave in your house;
but if the white horse Uccaiḥśravas [is yours], then you, in turn, shall be a slave in my house."
Thus, having spoken thus to one another, Kadrū went to her own hermitage; having arrived there, she remained at night overcome with anxiety.
O Pārtha, I have described the white-colored horse as Śyāma, that steed of darkness; I have thus described the sons [of the Sun] and the stake I have set.
Then all the serpents heard those words regarding the wager with their mother:
"She has become a slave, there is no doubt; Śveta is the one whose vehicle is the sun."
Kadru said:
"Consider how that may be accomplished so that I shall not become a slave;
you yourselves must enter into the hair-pores of Uccaiḥśravas."
"Stay for one moment until Kṛṣṇa is seen;
in a single instant, she shall become my servant for you."
May Vinatā, who was slender-limbed and devoted to truth while in a state of servitude, now attain her own place;
may all beings likewise always be happy and established in their rightful stations.
The serpents said:
"Just as you and your mother are the mothers of all serpents on earth,
so too must she not be deceived, especially since she is like a mother."
Then, provoked by those words, she became like the fire of cosmic destruction;
and as for whatever serpents there are on earth who do not carry out my command—
"Everyone will go into the mouth of the fire-eater"—
by those words, they were terrified, their hair standing on end like the bristles of a horse.
Some, overcome by the fear of Kadrū’s curse, vanished into the celestial quarters;
some vanished into the waters of the Gaṅgā, and others vanished into the Sarasvatī.
O King, some were led to the great ocean, while others entered the caves of the Vindhya mountains, taking refuge in the waters of the Narmadā under the protection of Maṇināga, the supreme serpent.
The Naga, bearing the curse of his mother, wandered with great devotion on the northern bank of the Narmadā and entered the waters of the Narmadā.
"By your grace, O Lord, I shall cross over my mother’s curse,
since I do not enter the mouth of the fire, O Master of the World."
Īśvara said:
"O child, by my command you shall not go into the mouth of the fire;
moreover, O son, you shall have your dwelling in my world."
Maṇināga said:
"O Mahādeva, please remain in this place; by way of a partial portion, may you remain in the waters of the Narmadā with a thousandth part."
"For the benefit of the worlds and in my name, O Śaṅkara," said Īśvara,
"O serpent, install your own and another liṅga by my command."
Having spoken thus, the God vanished right then and there along with Śivā.
But those who, at that sacred ford (tīrtha), being pure and self-controlled, [worship] with devotion—
O Pārtha, those who always worship on the fifth, the fourteenth, and the eighth day of the bright fortnight do not approach Yama.
With curd, honey, ghee, and milk,
people bathe Virūpākṣa, who bears half of Umā’s body.
Those who with devotion bathe the God, the burner of Kama’s limbs and the slayer of the great asuras, behold the supreme state.
O dear one, those who are devoted to the six duties and avoid intimacy with Śūdras,
even they go to the highest world, freed from all sins.
One should never honor Vratyas, those who are difficult to restrain, eunuchs, the elderly, farmers, or Brahmins who have impaired vision.
O Lord of Men, those Brahmins who drive a buffalo in the house of a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī) should be avoided from afar during a vow or a śrāddha ceremony.

O Pārtha, those who are one-eyed, those with deformed ears, those with testicles like a cow's, and even those who are physicians— these twice-born ones are to be avoided and are not to be honored at the auspicious Maṇināgeśvara.
If one desires the upward ascent of the ancestors as well as of oneself,
then indeed the twice-born, whose limbs are beautiful in every part, should always be honored.
He goes to the supreme world until the dissolution at the call [of Brahmā];
then, fallen from that heaven, he is born into a noble family.
O lord of men, whoever beholds the god Maṇināgeśvara with great devotion [should offer] a cow, a bed, as well as an umbrella, a maiden, and a female slave.
O Indra among kings, one who desires his own welfare should give [offerings] into the vessel;
he should also cause fragrant flowers and scented garments to be given.
Those men who with devotion give a lamp, grain, and a bright house equipped with all furnishings, go to the third heaven.
O King, that golden serpent which is offered at Maṇināga—
Sins dissolve like water in an unbaked clay vessel;
food prepared with the waters of the Narmadā is given to a Brahmin.
They too, liberated from sins, sport together with the deities;
being generous and endowed with enjoyments, they are always devoted to the narration of the Dharma.
Devoted to the gods, the twice-born, and their gurus, they are dedicated to visiting sacred fords;
they are devoted to their mothers, fathers, and masters, and are free from anger and malice.
O son of Pāṇḍu, those men who are endowed with all these qualities and desire heaven shall dwell in heaven.
O best of kings, this is the Maṇināga, the most excellent of all holy fords;
whoever reads or even hears this meritorious narrative of the holy ford [shall gain great merit].
He too, liberated from evil, is glorified in the world of Śiva;
poison does not affect them, and they roam about according to their will.
And for one who bathes on the sixth day of Bhādrapada and on the new moon day of Bhādra,
the attainment of the fruit of merit is described by means of this narrative.
Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Maṇināga Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS, Chapter 98.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
On the southern bank of the Narmadā, there is a most beautiful sacred site (tīrtha).
The supreme Gopāleśvara is meritorious and removes all sins.
"O King, the meritorious Liṅga emerged from the body of a cow upon the surface of the earth.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Why did the Liṅga that destroys sins emerge from the body of a cow?"
O Brahmin, please describe briefly the excellent Gopāleśvara located on the southern bank of the Narmadā, near Maṇināga.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
There, Kāmadhenu performed austerities for the sake of her son,
meditating with supreme devotion upon Maheśvara, the God of gods.
The Lord of the World, Maheśvara, was pleased with that Kapilā;
the imperishable Supreme Lord emerged from the center of her body.
Maheśvara said:
"O Goddess, Mother of the World, Kapilā, Supreme Sovereign! I am pleased.
Tell me, O Goddess of lovely countenance, why was this propitiation performed?"
Surabhi said:
"I was created by the Supreme Lord for the benefit of the worlds;
indeed, every task in the world is accomplished through my grace."
"By your grace, all the worlds behold you, the wielder of the trident;
O Śambhu, become a sacred ford (tīrtha) out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
From that time forth, O Indra among kings, that sacred ford has been renowned upon the surface of the earth;
by a single bath there, one casts off all sin.
At Gopāleśa, he who causes the gift of a cow to be given with devotion should bestow a worthy cow along with gold upon a worthy and most excellent brahmin.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, on the fourteenth or the eighth day of the dark fortnight, one should worship a young, radiant woman who is clothed, carrying milk, and accompanied by a bull.
In all months indeed, and especially during Kārttika,
one should cause [the gift] to be given with supreme devotion to a twice-born man who is devoted to the study of the Vedas.
They shall give according to the rite and receive according to the rite;
both perform meritorious deeds, and those who witness them become partakers of merit.
The offering of rice-balls (piṇḍadāna) should be performed for the deceased with sincere devotion;
by means of a single rice-ball, O King of Kings, the deceased attain the supreme goal.
For those who perform prostration to Rudra with devotion day after day,
their sin shall dissolve just like water in a broken vessel.
"O King, whoever should release a bull at that sacred ford...
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O dear one, what fruit accrues to men when the ritual release of a bull (vṛṣotsarga) has been performed?"
"O best of the twice-born, relate all of that today with effort.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"And what is the fruit of a bull endowed with all auspicious characteristics?"
I shall explain that to you; listen, O son of Dharma, O lord of men, on the full moon day of both Kārttika and Vaiśākha.
O King, having become pure by bathing and having subdued the senses, one should perform the rite of releasing a bull in the presence of Rudra for the pleasure of Dhara.
Standing in a pure place, one should release four auspicious heifers,
endowed with all the excellent marks, to the bull.
May Mahādeva, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others be pleased;
O lord of men, the number of hairs on every limb of the bull [is infinite].
For a duration equal to that number of years, one is glorified in the world of Śiva;
having dwelt in the world of Śiva, one is subsequently born again in the mortal realm.
Born into a great family abounding in wealth and grain, he was handsome and possessed of beauty, born into a lineage rich in learning and characterized by truthfulness.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, I have described to you the meritorious Gopāleśvaraka;
the Liṅga emerged from the body of a cow on the southern bank of the Narmadā.
Thus ends the ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Gopāleśvara," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS, Chapter 99.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
On the northern bank of the Narmadā, there is a most beautiful sacred site (tīrtha).
It is meritorious, removing all sins, and is indeed known by the name Gautameśvara.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, this sacred ford (tīrtha) was established by Gautama himself out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, serving as a staircase to heaven for men.
Go with supreme devotion, O King, to where the Lord, the Teacher of the World, resides,
for the destruction of your sins and the attainment of residence in heaven.
The linga increases happiness, bestows victory, and destroys suffering;
by a single offering of a funeral ball (piṇḍa), one may uplift three generations of one's lineage.
Whatever is given with devotion, whether it be small or great,
all that becomes a hundred-thousandfold by the command of Gautama.
"The supreme among all sacred fords, as spoken by Rudra himself.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"On the southern bank of the Narmadā is a most beautiful sacred ford."
There, O son of Pāṇḍu, stands Śaṅkhacūḍeśvara, renowned throughout the circle of the earth.
O Pārtha, out of fear of Vainateya, he remained on the bank of the Narmadā;
and at that sacred site, whoever, having become pure and composed, [performs worship] with devotion—
O lord of men, one should bathe Śaṅkhacūḍa with honey, curd, and ghee,
having kept a vigil at night before the deity.
Having honored Brahmins of praised vows with an offering of curd-rice,
a gift of a cow should likewise be given, which effects the destruction of all sins.
O Pārtha, even one who is bitten by a snake at that sacred ford perishes [of its venom] and,
by the command of Śaṅkhacūḍa, goes to the supreme world.
Thus ends the ninety-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Śaṅkhacūḍa Tīrtha," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS, Chapter 100.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the most excellent Parāśara.
And the high-souled Parāśara was on the auspicious bank of the Narmadā.
O descendant of Pāṇḍu, Gaurī, the daughter of Himācala, accompanied by Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, performed extensive penance for the sake of obtaining a son.
On the northern bank of the Narmadā, having been gratified by his supreme devotion,
the sage Parāśara, being pleased with him, granted him a boon.
The Goddess said:
"O best among the foremost sages, I am pleased with your devotion.
O lord of brahmins, O great-minded son of Parāśara, ask for a boon."
Parāśara said:
"O Goddess, if you are pleased with me, and if a boon is to be granted to me,
let a son be given to me quickly— one who is proficient in all the scriptures."
"And let there be a sacred ford here, O Goddess, by virtue of your boon;
O Daughter of the Mountain, please remain for the sake of benefiting the world."
On the southern bank of the Narmadā, by the one named Parāśara;
having heard the words of Parāśara, the goddess, the daughter of Himavat, [spoke].
"So be it for you, O Brahmin," having said this, the high-souled Parāśara vanished and established Pārvatī there.
He established Śaṅkara, who is saluted by gods and asuras,
worshipped by all the deities, and difficult for the dānavas to approach.

And the high-souled Parāśara, having accomplished his purpose and freed from all affliction, [resided] at that sacred ford; and whoever, being pure and with a restrained mind, [performs rites] there with devotion—
O prince, it should always be performed during the bright fortnight of the renowned month of Caitra, of Śrāvaṇa,
and likewise of Mārgaśīrṣa.
O best of the Pāṇḍavas, one should likewise worship Śaṅkara and Girijā on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, and always during solar eclipses.
Whether women or men, free from desire and anger,
having gone there to a pure place on the southern bank of the Narmadā;
Having fasted with supreme devotion, O great sage, they should perform the vow;
having kept a vigil at night, they should offer lamps according to their ability.
O Pārtha, one should honor excellent Brāhmaṇas who are accompanied by their wives and endowed with virtuous conduct and faith, with gifts of food and gold.
O best of kings, a śrāddha should be performed with garments, the gift of an umbrella, beds, betel, and food; indeed, a śrāddha of raw grain (āma-śrāddha) is highly praised.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, it is declared that raw grain is fourfold for Brāhmaṇas;
the twice-born should be honored with effort according to the procedure prescribed in the Vedas.
O King, with kuśa grass and sesame seeds measuring a span in length, and as desired,
one should face a Brahmin toward the north while facing oneself toward the south.
Having placed raw [food] upon *darbha* grass and recited this before the foremost of the twice-born:
"By the power of this sacred ford, may the deceased go to the highest world. (RKS 100.19)
May my evil be pacified; may there always be an increase in what is auspicious.
O best of the twice-born, may my lineage and circle of kinsmen always prosper.
Having thus addressed the lord of brahmins, one should give cows, land, blue cloth, gold, food, and clothing according to one's ability at the hermitage of Parāśara.
O best of the Pāṇḍavas, it should be given at the excellent hermitage of Parāśara;
even that man who hears it with devotion is liberated from his sins.
Thus ends the hundredth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Parāśara Tīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS, Chapter 101.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, one should go to Bhīmeśvara, which causes the destruction of all sins.
It is also resorted to by hosts of sages who observe formidable vows.
Having bathed at that sacred ford, fasting and with senses subdued,
one should mutter the single-syllable mantra while raising one's arms toward the sun.
The sin accumulated by that person in this life perishes at that very moment;
the sin accumulated over seven lifetimes is certainly destroyed by the Gāyatrī.
The Gāyatrī destroys the sin produced in ten lifetimes by [recitation] a hundred times, and that committed in a previous thousand lifetimes by reciting it three thousand times.
O Lord of Men, whether Vedic or worldly, whatever mantra is recited as a prayer burns away sin in that very instant, just as fire consumes straw.
Relying on that very power, one might at some time commit a sin;
yet due to ignorance, that [sin] never bears fruit for him quickly.
At that sacred ford, one should cause the gift of a cow to be given according to one's capacity;
O son of Pāṇḍu, all of that fruit becomes inexhaustible.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the excellent Nāradeśvara,
the supreme among holy places, which was established by Nārada himself.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O best of sages, by whom was this sacred ford (tīrtha) created by Nārada?
Tell me all of this, O most excellent one, if you are pleased with me.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Furthermore, the venerable sage Nārada, the son of Parameṣṭhin,
performed austerities in ancient times on the northern bank of the Narmadā.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, Śrī Mahādeva was gratified by Nārada, who had attained the state of a wooden log through the cessation of the nine channels.
Īśvara said:
"I am pleased with you, O best of Brahmins, O Lord of Yogins, O one not born from a womb.
Ask for a boon, O God, whatever resides in your mind."
Nārada said:
"O Lord, by your grace, may yoga indeed be perfected. The Lord said:
May you have yoga and devotion toward me alone at all times.
O Yogin, wander at will through the realms of heaven and the netherworld, and roam through the mortal world; you cannot be restrained by anyone.
There are seven notes, three scales, and twenty-one melodic modulations;
O Yogin, perform for me this divine dance and song which brings me delight.
And you shall always behold Kali [there], along with gods, dānavas, and kinnaras;
by my grace, your sacred ford on the surface of the earth shall become meritorious.
Having spoken thus, the god Nārada vanished;
there, O king of kings, he established the *liṅga* which brings benefit to all living beings.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O best of men, there is a supreme sacred site (tīrtha) on earth established by Nārada;
one who has conquered his senses should go to that sacred site."
In the beautiful month of Bhādrapada, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
having fasted with supreme devotion, one should perform a vigil at night.
An umbrella of auspicious characteristics should be given there to a Brāhmaṇa;
one should cause the Śrāddha rite to be offered for those who were slain by weapons.
By the power of the gift of rice-balls, they go to the supreme world;
therefore, O lord of men, a tawny cow should be given in that region.
O lord of men, by the power of this *śrāddha*— through the drinking of the waters of the Narmadā and the wealth acquired by righteous means— the [merit] of the Brahmins [is attained].
"By the power of these [deeds], may the hungry ghosts (pretas) attain the supreme goal.
Having uttered this, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the twice-born according to one's ability.
O large-eyed one, one should cause sacrificial food (haviṣya) to be given to the twice-born;
by the single gift of knowledge alone, an imperishable state is attained.
O Indra among kings, he who gives gold and sesame seeds to a brahmin at that sacred ford shall go to the third heaven.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to two unsurpassed holy places,
Dadhichanda and Madhuchanda, which cause the destruction of all sins.
O Bhārata, for that man who bathes at Dadhichhanda and offers curd to a twice-born, this [merit] attends him throughout seven births.
For him there is no disease, no old age, no sorrow, and no envy;
he is born into a vast family for as long as a thousand times ten moons.
If one offers water with sesame seeds mixed with honey to Madhucchandas,
one shall not behold the god Vaivasvata for seven births.
And for him who offers sesame seeds mixed with honey,
poverty shall never arise for his son or his grandson.
He who offers sesame seeds mixed with honey,
or he who causes a funeral cake (piṇḍa) mixed with honey to be offered;
Having bathed at that sacred ford according to the prescribed rite while facing the south,
one's father, grandfather, and likewise great-grandfather [are liberated].
"They remain satisfied for sixteen years; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Nanditīrtha."
I shall relate all that concerning where Nandin indeed attained perfection;
formerly, having placed the Narmadā in front, Nandin [sought] Maheśvara.
Performing austerities and reciting prayers, he went from sacred ford to sacred ford;
indeed, he continued on his way even after leaving Dadhicchanda and Madhucchanda behind.
Then Mahādeva, being pleased, spoke to Nandin.
Maheśvara said: "O Nandīśa, I am well-pleased; choose a boon as you desire."
"I am pleased by that austerity and by your performance of the pilgrimage.
Nandin said:
"I do not desire wealth, nor do I desire the continuation of my lineage."
O Lord of Gods, I do not desire liberation nor anything else; [I desire only] Your lotus feet, even among worms, insects, moths, and those born of the animal womb.
"May I go from birth to birth, and may my devotion to you be unshakable.
"So be it," was said by the god, the Supreme Lord, to Nandika.
Taking him quickly by the hand, Hara went to his abode;
for whoever bathes in that sacred ford and worships the Three-eyed Lord with devotion, [attains the highest state].
Whatever merit and fruit a human being obtains at the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice,
that same merit he attains who gives up his life at that highly meritorious sacred site.
Having become an attendant of Śiva, he rejoices for an imperishable eon;
thereafter, after a long time, he is born into a noble family.
May he who knows the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences live for a hundred autumns.
O Pārtha, this auspicious teaching, which grants satisfaction to all, has been told to you.
It is difficult to find for one who possesses the perception of truth, as it brings about the destruction of all evil.
Thus ends the one hundred and first chapter, titled "The Description of Nanditīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS Adhyāya 102.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme Varuṇeśvara.
O best of kings, it was there that the god Varuṇa formerly attained perfection.
By means of oil-cakes, vegetables, and leaves, and through the Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other penances,
people have attained perfection after propitiating the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain.
Having bathed at that sacred ford and offered libations to the ancestors and the gods, a person who worships Śaṅkara with devotion shall go to the supreme state.
O Pārtha, listen to the fruit of his merit when he gives a water-pot, a ritual pitcher, or even a large water-vessel together with food.
Whatever fruit a mortal obtains at a twelve-year sacrificial session (sattra), that same fruit he attains here; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
O best of kings, among all gifts, the gift of food is unsurpassed;
likewise, O best of men, water is that which brings the greatest satisfaction.
And for those men of purified soul who die at that sacred ford,
there is residence in the city of Varuṇa until the final dissolution of all things.
Having enjoyed [the fruits of that merit] there for a long time, he is born in the world of mortals;
as one who constantly bestows gifts of food, he shall live for a hundred autumns.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Agnitīrtha,
where the highly resplendent Fire-god, having performed austerities, attained perfection.
And the fire-god, who in ancient times had been made a devourer of all things by the Sage in Daṇḍaka, became purified after taking refuge on the bank of the Narmadā.
Having bathed at that sacred ford and having worshipped the Teacher of the World together with Umā with devotion, a person is liberated from all sins.
Having bathed at that sacred ford and having given gold to the Brahmins, O King, a man who offers water obtains a hundred millionfold fruit.
O dear one, by bathing at Dadhicchanda, Madhucchanda, Nandīśa, Vāruṇa,
and likewise Āgneya, one obtains that fruit and is liberated from all sins.
They are worthy of worship in the world of men, blessed and those whose desires are fulfilled,
by whom the five highly meritorious tirthas of the Narmadā have been seen.
They attained the heavenly world for as long as fourteen Indras endure;
thereafter, having fallen from heaven, they remain as righteous kings.
Completely liberated from all sins, they enjoy the immovable earth;
such is the majesty of Ākhaṇḍala resulting from service on the banks of the Narmadā.
The Gaṅgā is meritorious at Kanakhala, and the Sarasvatī at Kurukṣetra;
but the Narmadā is meritorious everywhere, whether in a village or in a forest.
He who always drinks the water of the Revā shall dwell eternally on its bank;
he has bathed in all sacred fords and partakes of the soma-drink day after day.
All rivers such as the Gaṅgā, as well as oceans and lakes, go to destruction at the end of the kalpa; yet the Narmadā alone does not die.
Thus ends the one hundred and second chapter, titled "The Description of the Five Tīrthas," in the Revā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS Chapter 103.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O high-minded one, how did the name Hanumadīśvara come to be?
The holy ford that removes the sin of killing a Brahmin is located on the southern bank of the Revā.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Well asked, O mighty-armed ornament of the Lunar dynasty!
This sacred site, more secret than the secret, has never been told by me to anyone."
Out of affection for you, yet oppressed by old age, I shall relate how a great battle once took place between Rāma and Rāvaṇa.
Pulastya was the son of Brahmā, and his son was indeed Viśravas;
from him was born the ten-necked Rākṣasa, Rāvaṇa.
Thus, by the grace of the wielder of the trident, he became a conqueror of the three worlds;
all the gods were defeated, and the wife of Rāma was carried off.
"Since Kumbhakarṇa is indeed his brother, and Sītā has taken refuge in the forest,
this wicked and dull-witted man was abandoned by Vibhīṣaṇa only after due deliberation."
He was conquered by Kārtavīrya; he was conquered by the son of Jamadagni;
he was slain by Rāmacandra, and his kingdom was likewise seized.
Then that mighty Rākṣasa was also defeated in battle by Rāma;
having gone there, the son of the Wind indeed destroyed the grove and slew the Rākṣasa.
In the battle, Rāvaṇa’s son Akṣakumāra was slain;
thus it came to pass in the Rāmāyaṇa after Sītā had been liberated.
O Pārtha, when Rāma had gone to Ayodhyā, the mighty Hanumān went indeed to Kailāsa to pay obeisance to Maheśvara.
"Stay! Stay! was indeed said by Nandin to that best of monkeys:
"For you have committed ten thousand killings of Brahmins through the slaughter of these Rākṣasas."
"O one of great strength, you shall not go [to that place] which is the meritorious seat of Bhairava.
Hanumān said:
"O Nandin, grant me a boon for the pacification of my sin."
"Having become free from all outflows, I indeed bow down to Maheśvara.
Nandin said:
"The Narmadā, the best of rivers, is meritorious and has originated from the body of Rudra."
By hearing of his life story, one attains twice the merit; by chanting it, one attains double that again;
and by bathing in the Revā, the sins accumulated over seven lifetimes are destroyed.
Therefore, dwell on the bank to the south of the confluence of the Revā,
meditating upon Virūpākṣa, who stands with a trident held in his hand.
The god, who resembles one wearing a crown of matted locks, who has a serpent as his sacred thread,
who bears Umā as half of his body, and who is seated upon the throne of the king of elephants.
While he was meditating there for many years,
Mahādeva, being pleased, arrived there together with his wife.
He spoke these sweet words in a voice as deep as a thundercloud:
"Excellent, my child! You have remained steadfast here in this arduous asceticism."
And Hanumān, seeing Hara standing there bearing Umā as half of his body, prostrated himself with all eight limbs and said: "Victory to you, O God! Salutations be unto you!"
Victory to the slayer of Andhaka, the crusher of the Asura Bāṇa!
Victory to the lord of the Bhūtapas! Victory to you whose ornaments are Bhairava!
"Victory to the destroyer of desire, who bears the Gaṅgā upon his head!
Thus was Mahādeva, the granter of boons, praised by the monkey.
Īśvara said:
"O child, ask for a boon; speak quickly what you have requested.
Hanumān said:
O Maheśvara, the sin of killing a Brahmin (brahmahatyā) arose from the slaying of the Brahmarākṣasa.
"May I indeed become free from sin through conversation with you.
Īśvara said:
"By the power of meditation on the majesty of the Narmadā-tīrtha."
"By the mere sight of my form, one becomes instantly free from sin; of this there is no doubt.

Mārkaṇḍeya said: O lord of men, hear now what occurred in former times regarding the manifestation of faith at Hanumadīśvara, at the end of the Tretā age and the beginning of the Dvāpara age.

It was crowded with various species of deer,

"In this essence-less cycle of existence, I now give the gift of my daughter.

"O father, I am Kalāpinī, staying here with my husband as my companion,

Hunters, afflicted by hunger, arrived there in that excellent forest;

The hunters quickly wrung their necks, tore them apart for consumption,

That remains of my flesh, indeed enjoyed by jackals, vultures, and crows, and the bone produced from my body, still joined with sinew and flesh; RKS 103.45.

though I am but a maiden, my face has become like the full moon.
"I am a recollector of my past births, O lord of men; I have been born into a family of kṣatriyas.

Viṣṇu consists of all the gods, and cows are born from the body of Viṣṇu;

O son of Pāṇḍu, whether they are white or tawny,

One should give brass milking vessels adorned with golden horns;

She should be given by one who desires heaven for himself while remaining in his natural state;

Having descended from the world of Viṣṇu, he goes to the house of a twice-born man;

One who hears of the auspicious Hanumadīśvara, the sacred ford that removes all sins, is liberated from the sin arising from the intermixture of castes.

RKS Chapter 104.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:

Yudhiṣṭhira said:

Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Nārada.

"And your wife remains all alone in the middle of the forest.

"He who gives food, clothing, and gold to a member of the first-born caste goes to the world of Śaṅkara; this is my truthful speech."

Freed from all sins, he goes to the world of Śaṅkara;

RKS, Chapter 105.
