addressed thus, let the messenger go quickly into the king's presence."
The messenger said:
"O Queen, King Vasu, the destroyer of enemies, has gone to a foreign kingdom.
O auspicious lady, it would not be possible to go there without water-machines."
"By his command, all the watercraft must be taken to the opposite shore";
at these words, that woman became despondent, tormented by intoxication.
Seeing the queen, a female friend said: "O Queen, why are you so distressed?
Let this letter be sent into the hand of the parrot, however that may be."
"O beautiful one, having crossed the ocean, Śakunta is traveling there;
the scribe has been summoned, so write a letter by my command."
"O Vasurāja, that chief queen will not live without you;
moreover, her fertile period has arrived—take all this into consideration."
It was written on birch bark by a scribe,
and a parrot kept within a cage was brought into that presence.
The queen said to him, "Śuka, take this letter and go. Thereupon, the bird departed quickly to the presence of King Vasu.
The letter sent by Satyabhāmā was delivered by the parrot itself;
taking it up, the lord of men reflected upon its contents and her prowess.
Having fashioned an unfailing casket, he became renowned for his prophetic insight;
he then entrusted it to Śūka, saying, "Go to the presence of the queen."
Having prostrated before Vasurāja and taken the seed, Śuka flew away;
having reached the surface of the ocean, he went as he pleased.
Perceiving that the parrot was carrying meat, O Bhārata, the hawk rushed toward him there as well; and the parrot was killed by the hawk with a blow from its beak.
While he was unconscious, that seed fell into the midst of the water;
there, a fish swallowed that seed of the king.
The fish was caught by fishermen and brought back to their own home;
when they cut it open, they then beheld the sun’s orb.
Seeing him, who resembled the orb of the moon yet possessed a radiance equal to the splendor of the sun,
all those fishermen on the bank of the Jahnavi were overcome with awe.
Filled with joy, they all went to the residence of the chief;
having delivered his son to the king, he protected his daughter.
"Therefore, O Goddess of noble form, you are certainly not the daughter of a fisherman.
Then she reflected upon those words of Parāśara.
Thus addressed by him, O lord of men, that virtuous woman gave herself [to him] and said: "O Brahmin, let this fishy odor be removed."
Then, by means of the power of yoga alone, he ignited the fire and made that young woman fragrant with divine scents.
Having performed a circumambulation of the fire, he then drew her out from the midst of the blazing flames; there, he touched the various erotic zones of her body.
O Prince, perceiving that the brahmin was eager for passion, the young woman became afraid; she suddenly spoke by day, in the presence of people.
Then, O dear one, she was meditated upon by him for a moment; and there arrived the Night of Darkness, filling the quarters of space, by whom all things were pervaded on every side.
Then, filled with wonder, that fawn-eyed maiden was enjoyed in secret by him,
who was as if heated by passion and sporting in the pleasure of union with a woman.
Then, at that moment, oppressed by the burden of her offspring,
she [beheld] there a handsome young boy with matted hair, holding a staff.
Holding a water-pot, peaceful, adorned with a girdle around his waist,
wearing a sacred thread over his shoulder, he was free from the illusory power of Viṣṇu.
For the mother, having seen her son’s restlessness, became apprehensive;
trembling, that young woman then went for refuge to the sage.
Protect, protect, O best of sages, O great sage Parāśara!
[This] brahmin, born most wonderful, wearing only a loincloth and a girdle.
[He was] with staff in hand, possessed of matted locks, and adorned with an upper garment.
Parāśara said:
"Do not fear; a son has been born [to you], yet you shall remain a maiden."
The second preparation of perfumes shall be named Satyavatī;
indeed, the king named Śaṃtanu will become your husband.
"Her first queen, the ornament of the Lunar dynasty,
go back to your own hermitage, O blessed lady, established once more in your former form."
"Do not feel dejected; you have seen the power of my knowledge.
Having said this, the brahmin departed, and that young woman remained on the dry land.
Having prostrated with supreme devotion and affection by touching the ground with eight limbs,
Satyavatī, beholding her son as he was departing, spoke to him.
"If you indeed have affection for your mother, then grant me the desired boon;
teach me something by which I may attain perfection."
Vyāsa said:
"O Ambikā, always exert yourself in the worship of the Lord.
Then, O son of Pāṇḍu, she became despondent at her son's words.
Yojanagandhā said:
"O son, because of separation from you, I shall go to my death; it cannot be otherwise.
There is no affection equal to that for a son, and there is no strength equal to that of a brother."
The son said:
"Do not despair, for what your father has spoken is indeed the truth;
you must remember me when times of distress arise, for the accomplishment of your purpose."
"I shall rescue you from calamities; please forgive me, O mother, for your son," having said this, Vyāsa departed, and the maiden also went to her father's house.
O lord of men, at the end of the Tretā Yuga and the beginning of the Dvāpara Yuga, the son of Parāśara sat there in the middle of the forest.
Vyāsa was born from Virañci and was described by Nārada as a great-souled ṛṣi, the son of Parāśara.
"Know that [he] was born to a fisherwoman on the bank of the Jāhnavī;
by the very words of Nārada, the best of the gods arrived."
Bhānu, Pitāmaha, and Śakra, surrounded by hosts of ṛṣis, each gave their blessing and exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent!"
This boy was consecrated with the birth-rites and other ceremonies by his grandfather;
he was Dvaipāyana because of his island-birth, and Pārāśarya because of Parāśara.
Kṛṣṇanāman excels even Havyādātu because of his dark body;
he was consecrated again and again by Virañci and by the hosts of sages.
Having said, "You are Vyāsa for all the worlds," they departed once more;
meanwhile, Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana commenced his pilgrimage to sacred fords.
By him the Gaṅgā was plunged into, as well as Kedāra and Puṣkara;
Gayā, the sacred site of Naimiṣa, and the Sarasvatī at Kurukṣetra.
Then the great sage Vyāsa went to Mahākāla in Ujjayinī and to Somanātha; having bathed there, he traversed the entire earth bounded by the ocean.
While wandering, O King, he reached the river Narmadā, which arose from the body of Rudra;
seeing the Narmadā, his heart rested with joy.
Resorting to the banks of the Narmadā, he performed extensive austerities;
in the summer he stood in the midst of five fires, and during the rainy season he slept upon the bare ground.
But during the winter, wearing wet clothes, he should meditate upon Maheśvara,
the creator of emission and withdrawal, the indestructible Sadāśiva.
O son of Pāṇḍu, by constantly worshipping the Siddheśvara Liṅga through the power of meditation and yoga, and by honoring that Siddha-liṅga, [one attains success].
"O Brahmin, Īśvara has become manifest before Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana; I have been gratified by you, so request an auspicious boon."
Vyāsa said: "O Lord, if you are pleased with me, O God, and if a boon is to be granted to me, then,
O All-pervading One, appear before my very eyes today on the bank of the Narmadā yourself."
"O Maheśvara, by your grace, may I possess knowledge of the past and the future.
Īśvara said:
"O Brahmin, let it be so for you through my grace; of this there is no doubt."
"Seized by your devotion, I have become manifest on the bank of the Narmadā," having said this, the God departed for Kailāsa, the most excellent mountain.
When his marriage was performed and a son was born to him,
he was attended by all the gods, led by Indra and Brahmā.
Then, having learned of the birth of a son, the best of sages,
led by Parāśara, arrived there in the course of their pilgrimage.
Manu, Atri, Viṣṇu, Hārīta, Yājñavalkya, Uśanas, Aṅgiras, Yama, Āpastamba, Saṃvarta, Kātyāyana, and Bṛhaspati; RKS 109.87.
In this manner, thousands, lakhs, and crores of various kinds—
all those most excellent among the twice-born— arrived at the auspicious and meritorious hermitage of Vyāsa.
Having seen the best of Brahmins, Vyāsa rose up with effort,
first bowing down starting with his father, and inquiring after their welfare.
Having joined his palms in reverence, he spoke these words:
"O Ānanda, my joy has been uplifted by the sight and conversation with you."
"I shall give wild vegetables and forest fruits to all of you, following the custom of my ancestors."
He bowed down to each and every one of them as they were all engaged in their respective observances; then, seeing the twice-born Dvaipāyana prostrated there, [he addressed him].
Having increased his strength with blessings of victory, they then looked at one another;
and Parāśara was gazed upon by all those preeminent sages.
"O dear one, let a reply be given to Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana.
Thus addressed by them all, the venerable Parāśara—
He said to his own son Vyāsa: "O son, those sages do not wish [to stay] on the southern bank for fear of breaking their vows."
"Indeed, you desire to eat further because of your particular faith.
Vyāsa said:
"I shall do what is appropriate for you; stay right here for a moment."
"Until I reach the river and perform [the rite] according to the prescribed rules.
Having spoken thus, he became pure and took his place on the bank of the Narmadā.
He suddenly uttered a hymn of praise; listen to it, O lord of men.
Vyāsa said:
Victory to you, O Goddess! Salutations to the giver of boons, the bestower of auspiciousness; victory to you, the crusher of sins, who wields the trident!
Victory to you, who cause the dissolution of Bhairava’s body; victory, O Goddess, who are saluted by Brahmā!
Victory to you, O daughter of Bhāskara and Śakra, who are ever-unmeasured! Victory to you, O giver of boons, daughter of the father of the six-faced one!
Victory to you, who consist of the entire collection of divine bodies! Victory to you, O daughter of the Earth, who flows toward the ocean!
Victory, victory to you, the ornament created for all the world! Victory to you, the destroyer of the poverty of suffering!
Victory to you, the increaser of sons and wives! Victory, O Goddess, remover of sins through the Sudarśana!
Whoever recites this hymn composed by Vyāsa in the presence of Śiva,
or at home with a pure disposition, free from desire and anger—
for him Vyāsa shall be pleased, and this Bull-vehicled Lord shall be pleased.
And having been thus praised, the goddess Narmadā then spoke these words:
Narmadā said:
"O, O great sage Vyāsa, I am pleased by this hymn of praise."
"Whatever boon you desire, I shall grant it all to you completely.
Vyāsa said:
"O Goddess, if you are pleased with me, and if a boon is to be granted to me—"
"You ought to grant me hospitality on the northern bank.
Narmadā said:
"O Vyāsa, you have conceived an improper thought; you are proceeding by an unlawful path."
Indra, Candra, and Yama are not able to lead you astray;
ask for something else, my child, however difficult it may be to find on earth.
Having heard these words of the goddess, Vyāsa then fell into a swoon;
his exertion had become in vain, and he collapsed upon the surface of the earth.
The entire earth, together with its mountains, forests, and groves, trembled;
then, perceiving Vyāsa to have fallen into a swoon, the gods [approached] Parāśara.
All the deities arrived, crying out "Alas!
Alas!", and as they raised up Vyāsa, they spoke to the best of rivers.
O best of rivers, you have been defiled for the sake of the Brahmins, not without cause;
one should sacrifice one's life for the sake of cows and for the sake of Brahmins.
Thus was she quickly called Narmadā by Brahmā and the other gods;
indeed, being consecrated by the waters of the Revā and purified, she bestowed freedom from distress upon all sides.
This conscious son of Satyavatī bowed down together with the gods, ending with those of the Narmadā.
Vyāsa said:
"All the sacred fords of the deities are present in you; yet the fruit [of visiting them] has been assigned to me, who am unfortunate."
Narmadā said:
"O illustrious Vyāsa, wherever the path of the mountain named Sumeru,
of Vindhya, or of any other mountain leads, there indeed I, blessed and upholder of dharma, shall go."
Thus addressed, the highly effulgent Vyāsa, accompanied by Satyavatī,
moved the preeminent sages from their own hermitages to the south.
O prince, the daughter of Rudra, possessed of great splendor, was shaken by the *huṃ* sounds of the staff-bearing [Vyāsa],
who was terrified by the *huṃ* sounds of Vyāsa.
Pointing out the way with his staff, the goddess proceeded there;
and seeing the goddess having entered upon that broad path, the gods led by Indra [followed].
They showered a rain of flowers upon Vyāsa, while the kinnaras offered hymns of praise;
the twice-born, headed by Parāśara, became filled with joy, their eyes wide open.
"What can we do here? By your greatness, we have been conquered by your deed; you are the best.
Vyāsa said:
"Having performed very extensive austerity and having given gifts of great fruit..."
This alone should be done by men: the pleasing of the virtuous;
for now, O highly fortunate ones, you are well-disposed toward those who deserve your favor.
Therefore, please stay in my meritorious hermitage; of this there is no doubt.
You shall be offered hospitality with vegetable leaves mixed with water.
And having been entreated by all the twice-born, headed by Parāśara, he said:
"Take refuge in the meritorious hermitage on the northern bank of the Narmadā."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having performed the rites of bathing and libations, those best of the twice-born then went to Vyāsakuṇḍa and properly performed the fire-oblation (homa).
Gautama, Bhṛgu, Māṇḍavya, Nārada, and likewise Lomaśa, being absorbed in meditation, offered oblations with *śrīphala* fruits and *bilva* leaves.
Parāśara, Śaṅkha, Kauśika, the sage Cyavana, Pippalāda, Vasiṣṭha, and Nāśiketu of great asceticism; RKS 109.124.
Viśvāmitra, Agastya, Uddālaka, Yama, Śāṇḍilya, Jaimini, Kāvya, Yājñavalkya, Uśanas, and Aṅgiras; RKS 109.125.
Atri, Śātātapa, Bharata, and likewise Mudgala;
Vātsyāyana of great splendor, Saṃvarta, and Śakti as well.
Jātūkarṇa, Bharadvāja, the Bālakhilyas, and others likewise,
O King, those twice-born ones, being of one mind, performed the ritual of mantra and tantra.
Then, having seen the three-eyed Lord, Vyāsa prostrated himself with all eight limbs before the Liṅga that had arisen, blazing with the splendor of the fire of cosmic destruction.
Having bestowed their blessings once more upon Vyāsa, O Brahmin, they then departed;
from that time forth, O knower of truth, it became famous as a sacred ford (tīrtha), O Pāṇḍava.
O Pāṇḍava, I shall tell you everything regarding the procedure for bathing and giving gifts, and at what time it is established for [the worship of] the brothers.
O best of kings, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Kārttika,
whatever man fasts with devotion and performs a vigil at night, [attains great merit].
One should bathe the Lord with devotion using honey, milk, and clarified butter.
Furthermore, one should worship Maheśvara with curd mixed with sugar, or with water infused with *kuśa* grass, or with fragrant sandalwood (*śrīkhaṇḍa*).
Then one should worship with fragrant flowers, bilva leaves,
kumuda, kunda, kuśa flowers, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and so forth.
One should worship the unsurpassed Lord of the Island with the utmost devotion, using *unmatta* flowers and the most excellent, gentle juices.
One should worship the Supreme Lord with flowers such as the mandāra;
by the offering of molasses and rice-porridge, the sin accumulated during the day is destroyed.
What has been earned in one month is lost by [drinking] a hundred measures of molasses-water;
that of six months is lost by a thousand, and that of a year by two thousand.
O best of kings, ten thousand sins committed since birth are destroyed by performing a bath with devotion on the full moon day. RKS 109.138.
Having performed the rite that destroys evil according to the procedure prescribed by mantra,
one should likewise know the Vāruṇa rite, which effects the destruction of all sins.
O King, one should duly gratify the gods, the ancestors, and human beings;
having bathed, one should mutter even a single Ṛgvedic verse and obtain the fruit of the Sāmaveda.
One may obtain the entirety of the Yajurveda, the Atharvaveda, and the Gāyatrī;
one should recite the eight-syllable mantra, or likewise that of the Sun or of Śiva.
Alternatively, one should worship with devotion the Vaiṣṇava mantra consisting of twelve syllables, as well as Brāhmaṇas endowed with all auspicious characteristics.
Brahmins devoted to their own duties, free from hypocrisy and greed,
as well as those with missing limbs, those with extra limbs, the outcaste, and those who serve Śūdras.
He in whose house there is a Śūdra woman, or a Vṛṣalī, or those born of remarriage, as well as the wicked who are intent on reviling their gurus; RKS 109.144.

Those who have neglected the study of the Vedas, those who are mere sophists, and those who live like crows— one should avoid such persons at a śrāddha ceremony, as well as in the giving of gifts or during religious observances.
A Brahmin who is well-learned and recites even only the Gāyatrī is better than this man who has mastered the four Vedas, yet eats all things and sells all things.
One should avoid such persons at a *śrāddha*, during a vow, or when giving gifts of gold,
shoes, clothing, a bed, an umbrella, or a seat.
Whoever should give [this] to a Brahmin with devotion, he too is honored in heaven;
for there, the cow Surabhi herself is considered to be present in the form of the sesame-cow.
Those who give sesame seeds and cows, those who give their own property, those who give black antelope skins, and those who give elephants; RKS 109.149.
Those who bestow a maiden and knowledge shall attain an imperishable world;
[they should give] two draft-oxen accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), together with grain and household utensils.
"One should cause [the gift] to be given for the sake of all desires; this is my truthful statement.
One should wrap the Lord [with thread], or else the tree of the world."
With supreme devotion, men— except for a Śūdra— should perform the circumambulation of the temple or of the Supreme Lord.
O King, there are the two islands named Jambū and Plakṣa, and Śālmali;
then Kuśa, Krauñca, Śāka, and Puṣkara as the seventh.
O King of kings, O lord of the island, that [land] extending as far as the seven oceans was surrounded by those who had conquered their senses through the ritual release of a bull, O Bhārata.
By the release of such a bull, one shall indeed attain the world of Īśvara—
specifically that bull which is white on its face, forehead, and likewise on its feet.
One that is white on the tail and the face is indeed a bringer of the vision of heaven;
such a blue one as this is said to grant auspicious lordship over an island.
O King, even those common folk, beyond counting, go to the celestial realm,
to the world of Caṇḍeśvara belonging to Sauri, in the city of the wielder of the discus.
By the power of Vyāsatīrtha, he enjoys the world according to his desire;
thereafter, he should worship the Brahmins there with devotion along with their wives.
One should give white jewels and garments to a member of the highest caste (agrajanman), having performed two circumambulations, [saying]: "May the Teacher of the World be pleased with me."
There is no kinsman equal to a Brahmin in this world and in the next,
for he protects one who has fallen into the most terrible realm of Yama.
Men who contemplate the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras, remaining at home, remember Mahadeva, the Lord of the Island, with supreme devotion.
For them, O King, no sorrow arises, nor loss, nor any ill-deed;
one should first worship the Liṅga Siddheśvara there.
Where the illustrious Siddha, the delight of Satyavatī, resides;
it was by worshipping him alone that the sage Pārāśarya attained perfection.
O King, those who give up their lives at that sacred ford go to the supreme world; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.

O Bhārata, he who dies submerged in water attains ten thousand years; he who dies in a fall attains sixteen thousand; he who dies in a great battle attains sixty thousand; and he who dies at the home of a cow through fasting attains eighty thousand years, while for one who fasts to death, there is an imperishable state.
Then, by that very yoga, the imperishable state is attained;
having gone from there to the world of the Sun, they proceed to the world of Śiva.
The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather,
having experienced [the world], behold their own kinsman as he approaches.
And he who offers water with sesame seeds into the ancestral lineages remains [in heaven],
especially on the full moon days of Kārttika, Māgha, and Vaiśākha.
And at the end, they go to heaven by the power of their respective sons.
Thus has all this auspicious fruit of being a lord of the island been told to you.
O King, that man who, having risen in the morning, either recites or hears this,
is likewise liberated from all sins and rejoices in the abode of Śiva.
O best of kings, it was established by the preeminent sages as the sovereign of all sacred fords,
granting the fulfillment of desires to all living beings on the banks of the Revā.
Thus ends the one hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Dvīpeśvara-Vyāsa Tīrtha," in the Revākhaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS, Chapter 110.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme Prabhāseśvara.
Renowned throughout the three worlds as the supreme staircase to heaven.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Tell me briefly how the sacred ford named Prabhāsa originated, which yields great fruit and serves as a stairway and path to heaven.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
The unfortunate wife of the Sun, renowned by the name Prabhā,
formerly propitiated Śambhu through severe ascetic penance.
Subsisting on air, she remained for a year devoted to meditation upon Śiva;
then, O son of Pāṇḍu, Mahādeva was pleased with her radiance.
He said, "O child, tell me why you are suffering; what is your purpose?
There is no difference at all between me and the sun."
The Lord said: "O Śambhu, there is no other god who anywhere nourishes his consort;
he is described as both possessing qualities and devoid of qualities, yet free from material substance."
"O Maheśvara, whether he be beloved or even hateful, a husband is indeed a deity for women; yet I have been consumed by my own misfortune in the midst of the world."
"And because you have not obtained the happiness of a husband, O Maheśvara, I shall suffer on your account. The God said:
"By my power, you shall become the beloved of the Sun."
Pārvatī said:
By your word, she shall not become your beloved in the solar realm;
her suffering there will indeed be in vain—what then need be said of Prabhā?
At the word of the Goddess, Rudra meditated upon the Sun, the destroyer of darkness;
the Sun arrived from the sky upon the northern bank of the Narmadā.
Bhānu said:
"O God, destroyer of the demon Andhaka, why have you been summoned?
The God replied:
O Bhānu, protect your radiance with supreme contentment.
"O Destroyer of Cold, may you dwell eternally in the temple of Prabhā.
Having thus obtained boons from the God, Prabhā established Śaṅkara there.
"O sinless one, remain here with a portion of yourself and manifest this sacred site.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O son of Pāṇḍu, this is the Liṅga of all the gods that has been established."
This [place] named Prabhāseśvara is difficult to find in all the worlds;
as for whatever other sacred fords there may be, they indeed bear fruit only in their own time.
O Indra among kings, Prabhāsa also bestows the fruit of merit immediately;
however, on the seventh day of the month of Māgha, it becomes especially fruitful.
O King, he who causes a horse to be given there according to the prescribed rite for a Brāhmaṇa attains the world of Indra or else goes to the realm of the Sun.
O Pāṇḍava, misfortune is destroyed there by the mere act of bathing;
moreover, he who with devotion bestows the gift of a maiden at that sacred site [attains great merit].
O son of Pāṇḍu, he should cause [the wealth] to be given to a Brāhmaṇa for the purpose of marriage—
specifically to one who is of equal age, of noble birth, learned, and likewise wealthy.
O Great King, whoever gives [this gift], even if burdened by great sins,
their sin shall perish like salt in water.
The sin arising from treachery toward one's master, the sin resulting from theft, the sin of giving false testimony, and the sin of those who observe the vows of outcasts; [all these are removed].
The sin arising from hypocrisy, from cutting down trees, from approaching those who should not be approached, from being a village cheat, or from being a poisoner or a slanderer.

O King, whatever sin arises from the sale of knowledge, that which originates from improper association, the terrible sin arising from treachery toward one’s wife, and that which arises from treachery toward all— [may they be destroyed].

Whatever sin there is in killing a Brahmin, whatever sin there is in seizing land, whatever sin there is in killing a cow, and [the sin] regarding the murder of a guru, a fire, or a Brahmin— [all these are removed].
O King, there are the two islands named Jambū and Plakṣa, and Śālmali;
likewise Kuśa, Krauñca, Śāka, and Puṣkara is the seventh.
O Pāṇḍava, that sin goes to dissolution through the gift of a daughter;
having then pierced the world of the Sun, one shall go to the auspicious realm.
Residing in the world of Rudra, he sports for as long as fourteen Indras [reign];
when all his sins have been exhausted, he becomes Śiva through his very being.
O son of Pāṇḍu, that holy site of Prabhāsa continues to exist;
having obtained the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice, one realizes the truth of what was spoken by the Lord.
The gift of a cow is a source of great merit that brings about the destruction of all sins;
there, one should likewise respectfully behold a water-cow that is visibly fragrant.
The giver of sesame seeds and a milch-cow, likewise the giver of a horse,
and the giver of a daughter or knowledge, shall attain the imperishable world.

O best of kings, one who desires all objects of wish should then cause a cow to be given away, covered with a cloth of earth-colored wool, accompanied by milk, and provided with grain and household utensils.
O King of kings, O lord of the island, that land of Bhārata, bounded by the seven oceans, was surrounded by those who had conquered their senses after performing the ritual release of a bull.
It should be performed at all times, but especially on the fourteenth day.
Thus ends the one hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Prabhāsa Tīrtha," in the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
RKS, Chapter 111.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the southern bank of the Narmadā.
It was established under the name of Vāsuki, destroying the entire flood of sins without exception.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O dear one, for what reason was it established on the southern bank?
Tell me the entire truth in its completeness, along with the underlying cause of dharma."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
